about: How each study was done, for the Atlas paper pages: who took part, the task, the design problem and a paraphrase of the prompt, what was measured, the method, and the main finding. Extracted by AI (Claude) from each paper's methods section in the atlas_corpus PDFs, written in its own words; 'Not reported' where the paper does not say. No PDF text is stored here. n = number of human participants (null if not reported or not people).

1.who: GPT-3 (no human participants); two expert raters scored outputs against crowdsourced baseline
1.task: Model generated 100 solutions for each of 12 design problems under base, zero-shot and few-shot prompts; compared with crowdsourced solutions
1.problem: 12 problems, e.g. travel exercise device, milk frother, time measurement
1.prompt: Produce 100 design solutions for a stated need, such as a lightweight exercise device for travel, a way to measure time, or a powder-spreading device
1.measured: Expert-rated feasibility, novelty, usefulness (0-2); computational similarity to human set (nearest-sample distance) and diversity (convex hull volume of embeddings)
1.method_detail: Expert ratings on 3 of 12 problems; embeddings for all 12
1.finding: GPT-3 solutions were rated more feasible and useful but less novel than crowdsourced ones, and few-shot prompting with human examples made outputs more similar to the crowdsourced set.

2.who: GPT-3.5 (no human participants); two mechanical engineering graduate students rated outputs
2.task: Model was prompted with an adaptive or innovative cognitive-style description and asked for 10 solutions to each of three design problems; raters scored every solution
2.problem: Three problems: securing belongings in public, one-handed food container opening, lightweight travel exercise device
2.prompt: Acting as a more adaptive or more innovative individual, generate 10 unique solutions to each of three stated design needs
2.measured: Rater-scored feasibility and paradigm relatedness (paradigm preserving vs modifying); inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa)
2.method_detail: Zero-shot prompting with Kirton adaption-innovation theory description
2.finding: Adaptive prompts yielded more feasible, paradigm-preserving solutions, while innovative prompts yielded more paradigm-modifying but less feasible ones, though without strong paradigm shifts.

3.who: 107 volunteer senior biomedical and mechanical engineering students in capstone teams of 5-6
3.task: Completed a 5-item psychological safety survey at the start, after the first semester and after the second semester of a two-semester capstone sequence
3.measured: Individual and team psychological safety (Edmondson survey, 5-point scale), compared across time and by mentor type (industry vs academia)
3.method_detail: Longitudinal, three time points; 8 full teams completed all three surveys; each team had a faculty or industry mentor
3.finding: Psychological safety did not change significantly over the two semesters, and industry-based and academia-based mentors made no significant difference.

5.who: 103 completed survey responses from MIT instructors (97 instructors and lecturers, 6 teaching assistants)
5.task: Answered an online survey with open-ended questions on barriers, helpful resources and changes in including social, policy and ethical content in their courses; responses were coded
5.measured: Barriers to including social, policy and ethical considerations, desired resources, changes over time; engineering vs non-engineering and design vs non-design courses
5.method_detail: Online Qualtrics survey, open coding with two raters (kappa 0.82-0.92); 231 courses in 29 departments
5.finding: Instructors increasingly see these topics as important, but barriers include perceived irrelevance, lack of time and lack of teaching materials, so more resources and institutional support are needed.

7.who: 10 employees of a global engineering and service company (3 managers, 4 information gatherers, 3 receivers)
7.task: Took part in hour-long semi-structured interviews about how user understanding is gathered, communicated, stored and received; transcripts analyzed thematically
7.measured: Methods for gathering and communicating user information, communication challenges, storage of past user information (21 initial themes)
7.method_detail: Semi-structured, one representative project at one company; first six in person, last four by video
7.finding: Communication was hindered by differing disciplinary backgrounds, lack of shared time and many handovers, and user information from past projects was stored locally or in people's heads and hard to find.

8.who: Three prior datasets: 186 papers, 20 capstone teams (members not reported), 15 global health design practitioners
8.task: Synthesized a literature review, capstone report and interview analysis, and interviews of practitioners to build a framework of contextual factors and their use in design
8.problem: Global health and industry-sponsored capstone projects; practitioners' global health devices
8.measured: How context was investigated and reported in literature, contextual factors novices and experienced designers considered, and when in the design process
8.method_detail: Systematic review of 186 papers; 10 capstone reports plus 10 teams interviewed (90 min); 15 practitioners interviewed (90 min)
8.finding: The paper proposes a preliminary framework defining contextual factors (classifications) and strategies for applying them in design stages, drawn from three prior studies.

10.task: Ran an LLM workflow (problem to TRIZ parameters, contradictions, inventive principles, solutions) on 37 classic and 10 post-2023 TRIZ cases, comparing prompt strategies and models; plus one in-pipe robot case
10.problem: 47 published TRIZ cases across product design, engineering, manufacturing, sustainability, ergonomics, service; in-pipe robot case study
10.prompt: Case descriptions were given to the model, which had to identify contradictions and generate inventive solutions
10.measured: Recall and precision of generated contradiction pairs against published cases, GPT-4 vs GPT-3.5 comparison, similarity of generated solutions to original solution (embedding visualization)
10.method_detail: Four prompt strategies compared (chain-of-thought best); temperature 0
10.finding: Chain-of-thought prompting gave the best contradiction recall (0.69), GPT-4 outperformed GPT-3.5, and generated solutions closely matched original ones while suggesting additional implementation mechanisms.

13.who: 40 mechanical engineering undergraduate and graduate students (18 men, 22 women)
13.task: Sketched ideas for two prompts, 20 minutes each, one with pen on paper and one on an iPad, with order of tool and prompt varied across four groups of 10
13.prompt: Sketch as many ideas as possible for a low-resource peanut sheller that avoids damaging peanuts and states a power source, and for a quick, easy-to-use milk frother
13.measured: Sketch quantity, sketch quality, smoothness, proportion/accuracy, understandability; gender differences
13.method_detail: Within-subject tool comparison, counterbalanced; sketches rated
13.finding: Sketch quantity and understandability did not differ between tablet and paper, but paper sketches scored higher on overall quality, smoothness and accuracy, with no gender differences.

14.who: 40 mechanical engineering undergraduate and graduate students (22 women, 18 men; 27 graduate)
14.task: Sketched ideas for a peanut sheller and a milk frother, 20 minutes each, one on iPad and one on paper (counterbalanced); idea chaining was coded
14.problem: Peanut sheller (shelling and sorting) and milk frother
14.prompt: Generate as many ideas as possible for a peanut sheller that also sorts shells, and for a milk frother
14.measured: Concept chaining (sequential iteration on an idea) by tool and prompt, for primary and secondary functions
14.method_detail: Within-subject, counterbalanced tool and prompt order; coding of sketch sequences
14.finding: Tablet sketching was linked to significantly more concept chains for both prompts, especially for the primary shelling function, but not for the secondary sorting mechanism.

18.who: 39 university students and employees who wear glasses (21 male, 18 female)
18.task: Rated 5 eyeglass frames from 1-10 shown as hand drawings, CAD solid models and polished renderings (each twice), then rated physical frames, while wearing eye-tracking glasses
18.measured: Preference ratings and their consistency with ratings of physical models across representation styles, eye-tracking gaze areas
18.method_detail: Within-subject survey with Tobii eye tracking; subgroup of participants with engineering background
18.finding: Preferences for CAD solid models were inconsistent with preferences for physical frames, but this difference did not appear among engineering-background participants, and physical models drew more semantic responses.

20.who: 44 third-year mechanical engineering students (36 male, 8 female)
20.task: Drew mental models of a hair dryer, clothes dryer and vacuum cleaner, tore down a hair dryer in groups of 3 for an hour identifying components and functions, then redrew the models
20.problem: Hair dryer teardown; mental models of hair dryer, clothes dryer, vacuum cleaner
20.prompt: Take apart a hair dryer following a packet and identify each component and its function
20.measured: Mental model scores before and after, component identification (e.g. motor inclusion), functional reasoning
20.method_detail: Single-group pre-post study within a thermodynamics course session
20.finding: Mental model scores did not change for any product, so no transfer was seen; teardown improved component identification, especially the motor, but worsened functional reasoning.

21.who: 48 students in 24 pairs (secondary analysis of an earlier experiment)
21.task: Pairs jointly adjusted slider inputs to hit target outputs in coupled parameter design tasks as fast as possible, with limited visibility and face-to-face talk; action sequences were analyzed
21.problem: Abstract cooperative parameter design tasks with 2 or 4 variables
21.prompt: Pairs, each controlling some input sliders and seeing some outputs, must jointly reach all target regions as quickly as possible
21.measured: Task completion time, design strategies from action time, size and variation (principal component analysis), task order, number of variables, English ability, experience
21.method_detail: Secondary analysis of 192 pair-task observations; regression on strategy factors
21.finding: Strategies with short, small and steady actions significantly reduced completion time, while lower English ability and less experience were linked to worse performance.

22.who: 12 undergraduate students trained as design interviewers
22.task: After online ethnography training, did 36 practice interviews on grocery decisions and 18 field interviews on kidney disease care in Zimbabwe; interview quality was scored three ways
22.problem: Practice: consumer health food choices; field: dialysis service model for End Stage Kidney Disease
22.prompt: Practice: pretend to work for a food company and explore consumers' health food practices and opinions
22.measured: Calculated interview quality score from coded best-practice skills, expert ratings (1-10), amount of information gained
22.method_detail: Coding of recorded practice and field interviews, compared against expert scores and information gained
22.finding: The calculated scoring method had no strong relationship with expert ratings or information gained, so its metrics were revised and it may be better used for novice feedback.

23.who: 60 students in a project-based design course (28 in fall 2019, 32 in spring 2021) in 17 teams
23.task: Wrote three individual reflections (weeks 3, 8, 15) about project goal, need, constraints and success during a semester service-learning design project; text analyzed for mood
23.problem: Community service-learning UX projects: Smart City technologies; reducing social isolation of older adults
23.measured: Individual and team mood from affect words in reflections (LIWC) across three project phases
23.method_detail: Longitudinal text analysis of reflections in two course cohorts
23.finding: Time significantly predicted changes in team mood across the project but not changes in individual students' moods.

24.who: 60 students in a project-based design course (28 in fall 2019, 32 in spring 2021) in 17 teams
24.task: Wrote three reflections during a semester community design project; divergence of team members' mood language was related to project grade and peer evaluation scores
24.problem: Community service-learning UX projects: Smart City technologies; reducing social isolation of older adults
24.measured: Team mood divergence (tone, positive tone, negative emotion) vs project grade and quality of collaboration (peer evaluations)
24.method_detail: Longitudinal text analysis of reflections (LIWC) with regression on course outcomes
24.finding: Greater divergence among teammates' emotional tone, positive tone and negative emotion was linked to lower project grades, but not to peer-rated quality of teamwork.

26.task: Judged 7 autonomous-vehicle behavior trials (including one failure) in immersive VR by walking a crosswalk, then in non-immersive video, rating trust, risk and comprehensibility
26.problem: Pedestrian crossing in front of an autonomous vehicle
26.prompt: Decide when it feels comfortable to cross as the vehicle approaches, then rate trust, risk and comprehensibility on 1-7 scales
26.measured: Pedestrian trust, perceived risk, comprehensibility of vehicle behavior, in VR vs video across 7 trials
26.finding: VR produced higher trust and risk ratings than video with equal comprehensibility, but the relative effect of vehicle behaviors was the same in both media.

28.who: 14 startup founders from an NSF I-Corps program
28.task: In a design thinking workshop, ranked own and (after interviewing a random partner) the partner's chair preferences, ideated, built a cardboard chair for the partner, who tested it
28.problem: Chair for a partner, built from cardboard
28.prompt: How might we redesign the seating experience for our partner using only cardboard
28.measured: Preference accuracy (match of predicted vs actual partner preferences) as a proxy for empathic ability, user satisfaction with the prototype
28.method_detail: Workshop session with pre- and post-surveys, random pairing
28.finding: Preference accuracy may capture how well designers identify user needs, but no statistically significant link to user satisfaction was found.

29.who: 4 synthetic chemistry researchers at one university
29.task: Observed on video doing 7 steps in 6 syntheses, then completed NASA TLX and free-response surveys per task; tasks were broken into sub-tasks and coded
29.measured: Tasks and sub-task typologies for liquid dispensing and solids handling, self-reported burden (NASA TLX), free-response comments
29.method_detail: Direct observation with hierarchical task analysis plus survey
29.finding: Ten lab tasks were identified, with 40 liquid-dispensing and 18 solid-handling typologies, and perceived burden depended strongly on reagent properties such as toxicity.

33.who: Two language models, GloVe and MiniLM (no human participants); 15 lab members gave similarity triplets, 7 authors wrote design descriptions
33.task: Embedded text descriptions of 10 milk-frother sketches with the models and compared the embeddings with a human triplet-based similarity embedding, testing free-form and function-behavior-structure templates
33.prompt: Original students were asked to sketch a device to froth a basin of milk
33.measured: Triplet violation rate, pairwise and centroid distances between LLM and human-derived embeddings
33.method_detail: 360 majority-voted triplet comparisons from 15 raters as baseline
33.finding: Templates covering several design facets (function, behavior, structure) replicated human similarity judgments slightly better and more consistently than free-form or single-facet descriptions, with about 36% triplet violations.

34.who: 10 junior mechanical engineering students (7 male, 3 female)
34.task: After brief concept-map training, built a concept map of one chosen problem domain with a smart pen (8-36 minutes, no time limit); pen-stroke recordings were coded second by second
34.problem: Concept map of a problem domain (Indian River lagoon pollution, cellphone effects, rural-to-urban migration)
34.prompt: Construct a concept map capturing what you know about one of three societal or environmental problem domains
34.measured: Eleven activity codes and four element codes (nodes, edges, labels) per second, crosslink formation, temporal grouping, clustering of elements
34.method_detail: Pilot protocol study with smart-pen recordings
34.finding: Participants built maps in bursts of elements, with conceiving entities differing from conceiving relations, higher generation rates at the start or end of sessions, and wave-like patterns within clusters.

35.who: 36 participants: 16 undergraduates, 14 graduate students, 6 industry professionals
35.task: Rated which of two 3D chair and table parts was more similar to a reference part, in 25 triplet trials for visual and 25 for functional similarity (order counterbalanced), and described their criteria
35.problem: No design problem (similarity judgments of 3D-model parts as inspirational stimuli)
35.prompt: Judge which of two parts looks (or functions) more like a reference part
35.measured: Human similarity embeddings (visual and functional) compared with deep-learning embedding distances; consistency and alignment; stated criteria
35.method_detail: Triplet rating task with 16 parts per stimulus set, compared with computational embeddings
35.finding: Human and AI similarity were largely consistent at a coarse level, agreeing most on clearly dissimilar pairs and less on what drives high similarity.

36.who: 32 deep-tech startup founders (22 male, 10 female) from an NSF I-Corps program
36.task: Completed a psychological safety survey, then a 30-minute one-on-one video interview naming current obstacles and resources they could use against them; interviews coded for resource accuracy
36.problem: No design problem (founders' own venture obstacles and resources)
36.measured: Individual perceived psychological safety (7-point scale), obstacles and resources by category, resource accuracy (ability to identify meaningful resources)
36.method_detail: Survey plus semi-structured interviews with deductive coding
36.finding: Founders who perceived their team as more psychologically safe were better at identifying meaningful resources to overcome their obstacles.

38.who: GPT-4 and GPT-4V (no human participants); crowd workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk wrote the component descriptions (number not reported)
38.task: Models were given text, image, sketch or combinations of five mechanical components with dimensions and wrote CAD programs, which were run and compared with ground-truth shapes
38.problem: Five mechanical components: shafts, nuts, flanges, springs, gears
38.prompt: Generate a CAD program for a component from its description, image or sketch with dimensional information
38.measured: Syntactically correct CAD programs (success rate), shape accuracy by intersection over union, by input modality and component type
38.method_detail: Synthetic dataset with 1,123 crowdsourced descriptions; a debugger step was added
38.finding: Both models showed potential for CAD generation, with GPT-4V performing best on text-only input over text plus image, though complex parts like springs and gears remained hard.

43.who: 40 second- to fourth-year mechanical engineering undergraduates (20 per condition)
43.task: Sketched as many concepts as possible alone for 30 minutes (half told to draw people in sketches), then wrote who each idea is for and who would use it
43.prompt: Design a way to help people move households, considering one or more moving-day challenges and the physical setting
43.measured: Length and depth of reflections on intended users, consideration of social and physical context and user preferences, claims that a design is for everyone
43.method_detail: Between-subjects, intervention vs control in four one-hour sessions
43.finding: Drawing people in concept sketches led to longer, deeper reflections on users and context, and sharply fewer claims that a design is for everyone.

47.who: 8 staff (business development, technology and planning leads) from 4 new-business projects at one Japanese manufacturer
47.task: Took part in 60-minute online semi-structured interviews, rated their prototyping practice on 5-point scales and explained the scores; project documents were also reviewed; coded with grounded theory
47.problem: No design problem (four projects: battery device, video distribution, measurement system, smart glasses)
47.measured: Factors hindering prototyping in early new business development (mindset, rapid iteration, communication with stakeholders)
47.method_detail: Grounded theory with document review; single company case
47.finding: Prototyping skill depended on individuals and tacit knowledge, and development teams were reluctant to communicate with customers, which hindered effective prototyping.
47.note: Methods say eight interviewees but limitations say six subjects; eight used

48.who: Coauthors as proof-of-concept MEG subjects (number not reported)
48.task: Proposed four brain-imaging decision tasks of rising complexity (letter go/no-go, hue ordering, ranking 15 designs, autonomous-vehicle trust decision) and showed preliminary MEG recordings from the first three
48.problem: Proposed decision tasks, including ranking 15 designs on multi-attribute information
48.measured: Open quantum model parameters fit with MEG prefrontal activity time series, time to converge, vacillation during a decision
48.method_detail: Modeling framework with preliminary MEG proof-of-concept data, no full experiment
48.finding: Preliminary MEG data suggest decision time is shorter than the span from trigger to response, so brain activity can constrain open quantum decision models; more subjects are needed.

49.who: 13 students from a 23-student design thinking course (7 non-engineering, 6 engineering majors) in six teams
49.task: Rated their individual experience 1-10 after each of five human-centered design phases, then drew a final journey map of the whole process, with qualitative comments
49.problem: Team design thinking projects in a six-week online project-based course
49.measured: Self-reported experience ratings per design phase, first vs final journey map ratings, discipline and team differences, qualitative themes
49.method_detail: Longitudinal self-report during an online six-week course
49.finding: Early research phases were rated less positively than later phases, and engineering and non-engineering students differed in retrospective ratings, especially for the Analyze phase.

50.who: 24 graduate mechanical engineering students analyzed (26 volunteered): 9 facilitated, 9 unfacilitated, 6 nominal
50.task: Generated ideas for 30 minutes into a morphological matrix of 8 sub-functions, in facilitated groups of 3, unfacilitated groups of 3, or alone; then did workload and psychological safety surveys
50.problem: Device or method to reduce lunar dust buildup on astronaut suits
50.prompt: Generate ideas for 8 sub-functions (remove, collect, dispose of dust, user input, energy, storage, feedback) of a lunar dust mitigation device, following brainstorming rules
50.measured: Number of ideas, perceived task load (NASA TLX), psychological safety (not asked of nominal participants)
50.method_detail: Three between-subjects conditions with trained facilitators; small samples
50.finding: Trained facilitation raised idea quantity over unfacilitated groups but not above nominal individuals, and also lowered perceived task load and raised psychological safety.

52.who: 40 households surveyed plus interviewees (sanitation officials, desludgers, manual scavengers, masons, farmers, academics; number not reported) in three Indian municipalities
52.task: Field study with semi-structured interviews, 40 household questionnaires, and gas measurements in 13 septic tanks using a prototype empty-alert sensing device lowered into tanks for about 2 hours
52.measured: Sanitation chain practices and stakeholders, household emptying habits and preferences, tank gas concentrations (CH4, CO, CO2, H2S) vs years since emptying
52.method_detail: Field study in Maharashtra, India: interviews, questionnaires, device testing
52.finding: The device should be introduced only where a working fecal sludge treatment plant exists, with stakeholders varying by municipality, and should detect hydraulic retention time rather than years since emptying.

53.who: 56 participants (29 women, 24 men, 3 nonbinary), mostly engineering students recruited from university lists
53.task: Made two sets of 30 pairwise choices of the more comfortable-to-hold mug, steering a Bayesian optimizer alone or with aggregate data, then validated results
53.problem: Drinking mug (five shape parameters), comfort to hold
53.prompt: Choose which of two mugs looks more comfortable to hold, repeatedly, then compare the optimized designs
53.measured: Validation choices against random designs for individual, aggregate-informed and aggregate-only models, ratings and rankings of optimized mugs, decision-making survey
53.method_detail: Interactive Bayesian optimization; aggregate initialized from simulated data (25 people) or earlier participants (31)
53.finding: An aggregate model captured shared comfort perceptions well, but combining aggregate data with each person's own decisions gave designs best aligned with individual perceptions.

57.who: 28 members of the public (13 in an online dialogue, 15 in an in-person dialogue) recruited via Craigslist in Madison
57.task: Took part in two-day, four-hours-per-day open-framing dialogues with individual reflection, report-outs and small-group discussion on energy transitions and fusion energy, then did a post-event survey
57.problem: No design problem (public framing of fusion energy as sociotechnical system)
57.prompt: Discuss environmental concerns, energy sources, and fusion energy benefits and drawbacks, guided by facilitators in breakout groups of 5-7
57.measured: Participant post-survey Likert ratings and free responses on the dialogue process, recruitment, facilitation and materials
57.method_detail: Two pilot participatory technology assessment dialogues, one online and one in person; preliminary observations
57.finding: Participatory technology assessment dialogues appear promising for eliciting public framings, understanding and concerns about a design context, though the small samples mean results are preliminary.
57.note: Text once says 12 participants in the first dialogue; table shows 13 online and 15 in-person, which were used

58.who: A U.S. Navy ship design program (several hundred engineers in dozens of teams; exact number not reported)
58.task: Researcher took part in and documented a large ship design program using set-based design: team structures, ways options were ruled out, coordination across teams, and a point-based virtual prototype
58.problem: Design of an entire large U.S. Navy surface ship
58.measured: Conceptual structures guiding the process, organization, mechanisms for eliminating options and coordinating system-level choices, lessons learned
58.method_detail: Participatory action research inside the design program
58.finding: Set-based design could be run at whole-ship scale, with a point-based design acting as a virtual prototype, though reasoning across differing abstraction levels in parallel teams was a key difficulty.

59.who: 147 first- and second-year engineering students from two North American universities (156 consented)
59.task: Clustered the elements of three household products into subsystems for fault troubleshooting, each product shown in a different representation; then completed self-efficacy and need-for-closure surveys
59.problem: Clustering mixer, hair dryer and toilet models into subsystems
59.prompt: As a design team manager, group the elements of each malfunctioning product into subsystem clusters, with each element in exactly one cluster
59.measured: Cluster sizes by representation (function structure, function graph, component graph), design self-efficacy (9 items), need for closure (15 items), demographics
59.method_detail: Mixed between- and within-subjects design with product and representation as variables
59.finding: Cluster size did not differ by university, gender, class year or first language and was not correlated with design self-efficacy or need for closure.

60.who: 40 U.S. and U.K. engineering students recruited online via Prolific
60.task: Rated 45 design prompts (in randomized groups of five by category) on whether the problem is clear and how essential its skill is to engineering creativity; prompts analyzed for linguistic features
60.problem: 45 idea-generation prompts in three groups: ability differences, transportation and mobility, social and environmental systems
60.prompt: Develop as many design ideas as you can for a stated need, such as helping people with hearing impairments join group conversations
60.measured: Perceived understandability, perceived essentiality to creativity, confusing words, text readability and other linguistic characteristics, word prevalence
60.method_detail: Online rating survey of prompts, about 15 minutes, with regression on linguistic features
60.finding: Prompt objective categories differed little in perceived understandability and creativity, and neither objective nor linguistic characteristics predicted how respondents rated prompts.

62.who: 10 fourth-year mechanical engineering students (2 female, 7 male, 1 non-binary)
62.task: Individually spent 60 minutes designing a 3D-printable smartphone stand while wearing eye-tracking glasses; use of sketches, CAD and other representations was coded
62.prompt: Design a fully 3D-printable solution for hands-free phone viewing that uses minimal print material and prints quickly
62.measured: Time and transitions across design representations (eye tracking), solution creativity, solution performance (build time and material)
62.method_detail: Eye-tracking lab study with qualitative comparison of high vs low creativity and performance designers
62.finding: Designers with highly creative solutions spent more time on CAD, especially late in the task, while designers with high-performing solutions spent more time sketching.

63.who: 30 participants (26 with valid post-surveys), mostly under 25 and novice designers
63.task: Chatted with the AIDA chatbot, which assessed each idea for validity, novelty and feasibility and gave feedback, fallbacks or examples, for up to two idea rounds; pre- and post-interaction surveys
63.prompt: Describe your idea for a new, innovative but feasible sustainable washing machine in full sentences, then try again with a different focus
63.measured: Task completion and idea counts, expert-rated novelty and feasibility (1-5), perceived usefulness, enjoyment, effort, trust in the chatbot, gender and age differences
63.method_detail: In-person lab validation of a baseline chatbot version, no comparison condition
63.finding: Participants interacted smoothly with AIDA and mostly rated it useful, enjoyable and trustworthy, though male and under-25 participants were more skeptical of it than females and those 25 or older.

64.who: 9 stove users interviewed in five Himalayan villages, one of whom co-designed a stove with the team
64.task: Interviewed and observed users, ran a baseline water boiling test, then built a clay stove with a chimney together with one user and tested it
64.problem: Traditional clay cookstove modified with a chimney to cut household air pollution
64.measured: Stove usage patterns and preferences, user tacit knowledge, indoor smoke reduction, retention of traditional stove features
64.method_detail: Field co-design with one user, supported by interviews in India and Nepal
64.finding: Co-designing with a stove user yielded a chimney design that reduced household air pollution while keeping valued traditional features and showed users' capacity for innovation.

66.who: 33 design instructors and educators (of 38 summit attendees) from 17 U.S. organizations; 30 pre-survey, 24 post-survey, 20 postcards, 13 interviews
66.task: Attended a three-day design justice pedagogy summit; completed pre- and post-surveys, wrote reflection postcards, and 13 were interviewed four months later; syllabus makeathon artifacts analyzed
66.problem: Embedding design justice into design courses and activities (summit syllabus makeathon)
66.prompt: Reimagine your course or activity to embed equity and justice; postcards prompted what you will do, what we should do, and what not to forget
66.measured: Confidence in embedding design justice, valued summit components, planned actions, impact stories, community building
66.method_detail: Mixed survey, interview and artifact data around one summit, short and four-month follow-up
66.finding: Participants gained confidence in embedding design justice over the summit, valued the community built, and planned to share knowledge and deepen engagement.

68.who: 118 Amazon Mechanical Turk respondents; 9 designers and design researchers helped build the attribute vocabulary
68.task: Sorted 16 vase silhouettes and 16 walkway canopy designs into five like-dislike groups by visual appearance; designs combined four form attributes at two levels each
68.prompt: Rate each design by visual appearance only, not function, from strongly like to strongly dislike
68.measured: Individual form preferences by attribute (conjoint utility functions for width, length, curvature, complexity) and consistency of preferences between products
68.method_detail: Rating-based conjoint analysis; vocabulary of 67 syntactic terms from a 9-person workshop
68.finding: Individuals' form preferences were consistent between vases and canopies for about 61% of cases, supporting a shared vocabulary of syntactic attributes for measuring aesthetic preference.

69.task: Read a makerspace user persona and walkthrough, recalled and rated obstacles, then rated the space and user; six conditions varied user gender and task stereotype
69.problem: Makerspace user needs (pain points in a woodworking or crafting walkthrough)
69.measured: Recall and severity ratings of pain points, perceptions of the makerspace and user (fun, creativity, competence), assumed user gender
69.method_detail: Online between-subjects survey, six conditions (persona gender by task stereotype)
69.finding: Students assumed a user of unknown gender was a man even in feminine-stereotyped tasks, and spaces used by women were rated more fun, though competence ratings did not differ by gender.

70.who: A 10-person NASA design team (engineers and designers); 7 completed a survey, 6 were interviewed
70.task: Researchers observed a six-week speculative design sprint on future sustainable airports (10 meetings, field notes, journey map), then interviewed six members about their generative AI use
70.problem: Envisioning a sustainable airport 50 years ahead and backcasting needed developments
70.prompt: Envision an ideal sustainable future airport 50 years from now and later backcast the developments needed
70.measured: When, how and why generative AI was or was not used, AI literacy (5-item scale), factors influencing use, coded strategies
70.method_detail: Ethnography with follow-up semi-structured interviews and inductive coding
70.finding: Three generative AI strategies emerged, intimate co-design, selective delegation and minimal use, shaped by factors such as familiarity, perceived quality and productivity, and unintended consequences.

71.who: 19 engineering students, first-year undergraduate to fourth-year graduate
71.task: In a design thinking workshop, sketched cardboard chairs for a partner, were told cardboard was halved mid-task, then redesigned and built; pre- and post-surveys
71.problem: Cardboard chair designed for a partner
71.prompt: How might we redesign the seating experience for our partner using only cardboard
71.measured: Resilience, perceived scarcity of time, money, skills, mentors and resources (pre-survey), perceived design performance, whether the concept changed after induced scarcity
71.method_detail: Mixed-methods workshop with an induced halving of material mid-task
71.finding: Perceived scarcity of time in daily life predicted perceived design performance, while resilience had no significant effect overall, though two resilience items differed strongly between those who changed their concept and those who did not.

74.who: 24 students recruited (22 graduate, 2 undergraduate); 23 analyzed, in three groups of about 8
74.task: Worked 30 minutes with an AI cognitive assistant (Daphne) to explore satellite constellation designs; after 15 minutes one group did a 10-minute reflection questionnaire, one read an unrelated article, one continued
74.problem: Satellite constellation design for soil moisture monitoring (assigning 5 instruments to 5 orbits)
74.prompt: Improve the science benefit and cost Pareto front of constellation designs and learn which features drive good designs
74.measured: Design performance gain, designer learning of driving features, forms of human-AI collaboration
74.method_detail: Between-subjects: reflection vs incubation vs control; one incubation participant excluded
74.finding: Incubation improved design performance significantly more than reflection, and the interventions led to different ways of collaborating with the AI assistant.

75.who: 3 long-standing assistive technology industry professionals (interviewees); process applied to 4 orphan device projects (team members not reported)
75.task: Developed a four-step process for turning one-off assistive technology prototypes into small-batch products, applied it to four devices, then interviewed three professionals about its value
75.problem: Four orphan assistive technology devices advanced to small-batch production
75.measured: Professionals' views on the process's value for low-volume products, user engagement, and fidelity of small-batch designs; lessons learned from the cases
75.method_detail: Four case examples plus separate interviews with three professionals
75.finding: All three professionals saw the process as valuable for low-volume products and for communicating with commercial partners, while authors say long-term success remains unproven.

76.who: 15 older adults in the Boston area (5 male, 10 female; mean age 75)
76.task: Did a Timed-Up-and-Go test, rated own difficulty standing, were interviewed, and reacted to eight look-and-feel and works-like sit-to-stand assistive prototypes; a physical therapist rated videos
76.problem: Sit-to-stand assistive devices for older adults
76.prompt: Rate how likely you would be to use each prototype if it helped you stand up, and describe what you would want from such a device
76.measured: Timed-Up-and-Go time, self-rated and therapist-rated standing difficulty, likelihood of use per prototype, interview themes
76.method_detail: Home or lab sessions of 60-90 minutes combining assessment, interview and prototype feedback
76.finding: Therapist ratings tracked mobility performance but older adults' self-ratings did not, and they preferred discreet, light, flexible devices regardless of their demonstrated need.

78.who: 15 professional designers (10 men, 5 women; industrial design, architecture, mechanical engineering; mean 8 years experience)
78.task: Thought aloud while sketching an outline concept for a future entertainment system, wearing a 14-channel EEG headset; verbalizations were coded as spontaneous, deliberate or metacognitive and matched to EEG segments
78.problem: Personal entertainment system of the future (open sketching task)
78.prompt: Propose and sketch an outline design for a future personal entertainment system
78.measured: EEG band power (alpha 1, alpha 2, beta 1 and others) by Triple Process Theory process type and sub-category
78.method_detail: Think-aloud protocol coding time-locked with EEG; preliminary analysis
78.finding: Metacognitive processes showed higher alpha 1, alpha 2 and beta 1 power than spontaneous or deliberate ones, suggesting metacognition helps balance cognitive effort during design.

79.who: 30 designers (15 novices with 3-4 years of design education, 15 professionals with 8+ years); GPT-3 generated stimuli; one expert scored sketches
79.task: Used GPT-3 to generate design proposals (fixed keywords, FBS-template prompts, or free-form questions by group), then completed and sketched a concept within 30 minutes; sketches scored against a reference concept; interviews
79.prompt: Sketch a leg sports rehabilitation device based on GPT-3-generated content, within 30 minutes
79.measured: Concept scores relative to an award-winning reference on novelty, feasibility, usability, functionality, cost (5-point), plus interview feedback
79.method_detail: Three conditions: fixed prompt, function-behavior-structure templates, free-form; novice and professional designers
79.finding: The function-behavior-structure decomposed prompting approach produced concepts rated more creative and reasonable than fixed-keyword or free-form GPT-3 use.

80.who: 69 experienced automotive designers at one company across three separately recruited activities: 47 survey, 16 annotation task, 6 workshop
80.task: Surveyed designers on keyword use, had them pick car wheels that best match keywords, and ran a three-day workshop (brainstorming, interaction-mode poll, paper-prototype testing); a diffusion-based generative AI system was then built
80.problem: Conceptual automotive design (car wheels, text and image inspiration); generative AI design assistant
80.prompt: Pick the top 10 of 25 car wheels that best represent a keyword such as dynamic; in the workshop, generate image inspiration for keyword prompts
80.measured: Usefulness and common use of design keywords, wheel selections per keyword, preferred interaction modes with generative AI, how text and image inspiration is used
80.method_detail: Survey, annotation task and workshop, with system development informed by them
80.finding: Designers use keywords to set design directions and share vocabularies within their context, use images to convey feelings, and want AI tools that fit team workflows, informing the diffusion-based system.

81.who: 38 robotics conference attendees (39 recruited; 9 bachelor's, 17 master's, 11 doctoral), age 19-56, 0-17 years robotics experience
81.task: Designed a ground robot in the Build-a-Bot software for 15 minutes after a 5-minute practice, repeatedly switching between shape, operation and test modes; design decisions were logged
81.problem: Ground robot to cross uneven steps
81.prompt: Build the fastest, most efficient ground robot to cross an environment of uneven steps (framed as a competition)
81.measured: Frequency of design iterations, iteration strategy, vulnerability to design fixation, effect of robotics expertise
81.method_detail: Logged software behavior at a conference booth, no manipulated conditions
81.finding: Participants iterated by testing and modifying designs, but expertise did not significantly affect iteration frequency, and participants at all levels were prone to fixating on their initial concept.

82.who: 67 adults in three art-based workshops (41 music festival attendees, 26 technology university affiliates); 60 of them later completed the survey
82.task: Made drawings and writing on environmental attitudes in workshops, then months later rated emotions toward 5 eco-feedback sketches and completed attitude scales
82.problem: Eco-feedback product sketches for electricity conservation
82.prompt: Respond with drawings and writing to open prompts about environmental attitudes and individual conservation behavior
82.measured: Pro-environmental attitudes and behaviors (scales), self-reported positive and negative emotional intensity toward experimental vs control sketches
82.method_detail: Three phases: workshops with content analysis, sketch design, follow-up survey months later
82.finding: Users with positive conservation attitudes reacted most strongly, positively to positive and negatively to negative framing, while neutral or negative-attitude users still responded negatively to negatively framed designs.

83.who: 33 design thinking conference attendees (28 assigned to five teams, plus 5 expert facilitators); students, faculty and staff
83.task: Worked in five facilitated teams through a three-hour design thinking workshop on a child learning challenge; audio of 15+ hours was coded for behaviors and surveys given before and after
83.problem: Learning experience for a six-year-old first encountering addition
83.prompt: Re-imagine the learning experience for children learning addition for the first time, for a given child persona
83.measured: Coded facilitator and participant behaviors (Markov transition probabilities), team climate, trust, psychological safety, facilitator efficacy
83.method_detail: Audio behavioral coding plus pre- and post-surveys across five teams
83.finding: Facilitator involvement led to participant engagement and support, clarification led to participant questions, and facilitator behaviors correlated positively with trust and psychological safety.
83.note: Unclear whether the 33 includes the 5 facilitators; 28 participants were assigned to teams

84.who: 64 survey respondents: 37 community members, 12 implementing partners, 15 research team (Kenya, Uganda)
84.task: Completed pre- and post-workshop short-answer surveys during co-design workshops; researchers coded responses for knowledge gained, enjoyment, challenges and suggestions
84.problem: Contraception access via self-injectable DMPA-SC (four sub-projects)
84.prompt: Kenya: explore direct-to-consumer provision through e-commerce and retail pharmacies. Uganda: use social communication and support to enable desired contraceptive use
84.measured: Knowledge and skills gained about human-centered design, mindsets that resonated, enjoyment, challenges, suggestions to improve workshops
84.method_detail: Qualitative coding and thematic analysis of 214 pre/post surveys across five workshops
84.finding: Co-designers learned about human-centered design and enjoyed the workshops, but time constraints and language barriers limited successful co-design.

85.who: 27 lay users and 25 design-background participants at MIT; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 tested
85.task: Users wrote a product comment and self-reported goals and needs; designers (6 comments each) and LLMs inferred those goals and needs, compared by embedding similarity
85.problem: User goal and need inference for everyday products (cleaning, travel, digital entertainment)
85.prompt: Users: describe experience with a product and your underlying goals and psychological needs. Designers: infer a user's goals and needs from the comment
85.measured: Empathic accuracy: cosine similarity of inferred do-, motor- and be-goals and 13 psychological needs to user self-reports
85.method_detail: Human benchmark from 24 users' comments and 20 designers' inferences vs standard, chain-of-thought and tree-of-thought prompts
85.finding: GPT-4 matched human designers at inferring users' goals and needs, sometimes exceeding them, and chain-of-thought or tree-of-thought prompting did not raise accuracy.

89.who: Engineers from two aerospace companies (number not reported)
89.task: Each supplied 6-12 documents they use daily; authors classified terms in them, and engineers marked search-useful terms and ranked search attributes 1-5
89.measured: Term categories in documents (Object Content Profiles), ranked importance of attributes for searching for documents, drawings and CAD models
89.method_detail: Text analysis of about 5,000 terms in engineers' documents plus ranking survey
89.finding: Text documents need a wider range of descriptive attributes than drawings and CAD models for search, and the three document types showed distinct content profiles.

92.who: 3 analyzed groups of 3-5: final-year design students and professional engineers (total not reported)
92.task: Groups discussed and jointly evaluated ready-made concept solutions against criteria to choose the best; sessions videotaped, transcribed and content-coded
92.problem: Selecting among conceptual solutions to an industrial design issue
92.prompt: As a group, evaluate the generated conceptual solutions using supplied criteria and select the most effective one
92.measured: Types of concept-selection activities (12 main) and time spent on each
92.method_detail: Lab workshops of 45-90 minutes; 2 further pilot workshops not analyzed
92.finding: Groups' selection work divided into 12 activity types; little time went to weighting criteria, and professionals spent more time than students on raising evidence.

104.who: 32 product development staff (team members, managers, others) in 6 Silicon Valley companies
104.task: Took part in semi-structured, audio-recorded interviews on organization, teams, development process, projects and collaboration
104.measured: Collaboration problems, activities used to improve product development efficiency, and perceived practice
104.method_detail: Coded qualitative interviews during 1998; abstract says 36 interviews, methods and results say 32 interviewees
104.finding: Collaboration problems recurred across the companies, and the authors derive guidelines and a support-structure framework for more efficient product development.
104.note: abstract states 36 interviews; body states 32 interviewees

107.who: 20 graduate students (UT-Austin, MIT) plus 4 undergraduates in each of 2 further experiments (UMR)
107.task: Each student built a functional model of a product with the derivation method, then converted it to the functional basis vocabulary
107.problem: Functional models of a slotted toaster, power screwdriver and toy dart gun
107.prompt: Derive a product functional model from customer needs, first without and then with the functional basis; toaster students used their own toasters
107.measured: Repeatability of models: share of sub-functions found by many students, chain ordering, number of sub-functions, modeling errors vs authors' control model
107.method_detail: Preliminary classroom experiments at three universities; unclear if the same 4 undergraduates did both UMR tasks
107.finding: Students produced highly repeatable functional models, with half of sub-functions found by over 70 percent of them, but errors exposed weaknesses in the functional basis definitions.

116.who: 2 of 4 multidisciplinary charrette groups (architects, technologists, faculty); numbers not reported
116.task: Groups developed usage scenarios and requirements for learning spaces; videotaped sessions of two teams were transcribed, segmented and coded
116.prompt: Respond to two of five loosely stated design challenges by developing usage scenarios that reveal requirements for the learning spaces
116.measured: Share of information-handling (generate, access, analyze) vs social-interaction (elaborate, verify, navigate) activity segments
116.method_detail: Protocol analysis of two 1 hr 6 min transcripts with a new coding scheme
116.finding: Social interaction made up about 45 percent of utterances in both teams despite very different process styles, so tools for distributed teams must support social exchange as well as information.

119.who: Australian automotive (14 companies) and maritime (13 companies) design firms; respondent numbers not stated
119.task: Companies completed a mailed survey on teams, design practice and concurrent engineering use; 10 of them (5 per sector) gave follow-up interviews
119.measured: Team makeup, design process type, concurrent engineering tools and practices, perceived impact on 17 performance measures
119.method_detail: Mail survey with follow-up interviews; automotive 14 of 27 invited, maritime 13 of 23 surveyed
119.finding: Automotive firms reported extensive concurrent engineering with positive performance effects, while the custom, one-off maritime industry lagged and was advised to adopt more concurrent engineering practice.

120.who: Stanford ME310 student teams (45-60 students yearly, four years of logs); interviews unspecified
120.task: Web-server access logs of an archive of past and current project documents were analyzed, plus open-ended interviews with some engineers
120.measured: Access hits to prior-year vs current-year files, process vs product files, timing against deadlines, correlation of usage with team performance, interview themes
120.method_detail: Quantitative log analysis over four academic years plus qualitative interviews
120.finding: Students rarely reused prior-year files (under 10 percent of hits), mostly opened process files around milestones, and usage correlated more with team performance over time.

128.who: 30 mechanical engineering students in 15 two-person teams (7 control, 8 experimental)
128.task: Designed, built and tested a Lego device in 75 minutes after a 15-minute familiarization; the experimental group did extra system level design activities
128.problem: Lego device to move a golf ball onto a target
128.prompt: Use only the supplied Lego parts, storing the only energy in the materials, to bring a golf ball to rest near the target center with few parts
128.measured: Normalized accuracy score and piece count, composite outcome, and a system level design index from design records
128.method_detail: Pilot lab study, random assignment of teams to control or SLD protocol, ANOVA and t-tests
128.finding: Emphasizing system level design did not change outcome scores and students were hard to constrain, though a post hoc index linked more system level design to better outcomes.

130.who: About 110 high school students in classes at four schools
130.task: Took a mechatronics course taught with six selected design methods (or fewer/none in comparison schools) and built robots for a contest
130.problem: Mechatronic robots, mainly fire-fighting robots, for a shared contest mission
130.prompt: All teams received the same robot mission; the paper does not quote the brief
130.measured: Contest ranking, expert evaluation of designs, design tests, peer evaluation, attitude questionnaire, science grades, interviews
130.method_detail: Course designed with design methods, then compared across schools teaching all, some or no methods; student counts summed from class sizes in the paper
130.finding: Teams taught the full set of design methods placed highest in the contest and earned better expert ratings and science grades than teams taught fewer or none.

139.who: 8 home blender owners (3 men, 5 women, ages 20-48), observed in US homes
139.task: Sketched their blender and described its parts, then made a cold drink with it while thinking aloud on video; tasks analyzed step by step
139.problem: Kitchen blender use and product architecture
139.prompt: Make a cold drink with your own blender using supplied ingredients, no instructions, talking aloud
139.measured: Task flow, parts drawn, subtasks per part, affordance levels and attributes linking technical functions to user tasks
139.method_detail: Illustrates the Function-Task Design Matrix method with semi-structured interviews and videotaped observation
139.finding: Users described their blenders through about 63 percent of visible parts, and the observations let the authors map functions to tasks and affordance levels in the matrix.

142.who: Consumers interviewed on lighting and boiling products (11 and 15 surveys; overlap not stated)
142.task: Used each product, gave interview comments, then rated likelihood of use (1-5) and ranked products for each described usage context
142.problem: No design problem (product preference study of lighting and boiling products)
142.prompt: Imagine needing to boil water or get light in a described usage context, such as backpacking, and say how suitable each product is
142.measured: Product preference per usage context, links between context factors and chosen product attributes (e.g. mass and transport mode)
142.method_detail: One-on-one interviews and online reviews to find contexts, then interactive preference surveys
142.finding: Customers preferred different products in different usage contexts, and attributes of the preferred products tracked context factors such as transportation mode.

151.who: Senior mechanical engineering students from 14 teams (12 teams of five, plus controls)
151.task: Generated peanut-sheller ideas for 40 minutes in teams, with ideas shown to all or rotated, as words only, sketches only or both
151.problem: Hand-powered peanut shelling device for developing regions
151.prompt: Design a device to shell many peanuts quickly and cheaply with little damage, without electricity, for places like Haiti and West Africa
151.measured: Quantity of ideas (words and sketches), idea quality, ideas gained from teammates
151.method_detail: 2 (display: view all vs rotate) x 3 (words, sketches, both) factorial design, two teams per condition
151.finding: Rotating ideas among teammates yielded more ideas than posting all at once, participants gained many ideas from teammates, and quality rose as teams built on ideas.

152.who: 1 lead construction engineer as decision maker (authors say method also used with others)
152.task: Gave value functions and stated preferences between hypothetical drills; inconsistent preferences were flagged by the consistency check and corrected
152.prompt: Choose the best drill among alternatives using number of operations, price and weight
152.measured: Consistency of stated preferences, derived attribute weights, resulting preferred drill and the decision maker's agreement
152.method_detail: Worked demonstration of a preference consistency check within a decision method
152.finding: The consistency check exposed inconsistent preferences in the decision maker's statements, and the corrected weights picked a drill he confirmed matched his real priorities.

153.who: 32 undergraduate engineering students at Caltech, mostly juniors (18 without, 14 with sketching instruction)
153.task: Did three sketching tasks at term start, then kept sketch logbooks during a class design-build project; sketch counts and grades were correlated
153.problem: Mechanical product of own choice (e.g. can opener, spice dispenser)
153.prompt: Pick a project from an approved list or propose one, then design and build it in the machine shop
153.measured: Sketching skill scores (bicycle recall, hand drawing, box visualization), number of logbook sketches, design outcome (project grades and external ratings)
153.method_detail: Preliminary correlational study with Spearman rank correlations
153.finding: Drawing facility scores went with more sketches, mechanism-recall skill went with fewer, and sketching ability showed no notable relation to design outcome.

154.who: 38 students: 11 engineering, 10 industrial design graduate, 17 psychology or consumer science
154.task: Took seven tests (creativity mode, constructive perception, visual reasoning, spatial perception, two idea generation tests, design task); design task was 25 minutes with visual clues
154.prompt: Design a head- or face-worn binocular used with both eyes and manual lens adjustment, drawing on two of five visual clues
154.measured: Personal creativity mode, constructive perception, visual reasoning, spatial perception, idea generation, design originality and usefulness (0-5 each)
154.method_detail: Correlational lab study comparing three groups with different design education
154.finding: Constructive perception and visual reasoning were each related to creative design performance, yet the two abilities were not correlated with each other.

160.who: Graduate product family design students in 5 teams of 4-5 (class size not stated)
160.task: Dissected families of four products, listed common, variant and unique parts, photographed them, and computed the Product Line Commonality Index for another team's family
160.problem: Commonality in families of cameras and coffeemakers
160.prompt: Dissect each product to its lowest level, classify parts as common, variant or unique, and compute a commonality index
160.measured: Variability in Product Line Commonality Index across teams and its sources
160.method_detail: Classroom dissection activity doubling as a repeatability study; three product families (Kodak and Fujifilm cameras, Mr. Coffee makers)
160.finding: Commonality index results varied between teams because of different dissection levels, omitted parts and different factor values, so firm rules for dissection and scoring are recommended.

188.who: 14 auto industry practitioners: 5 engineers, 4 studio designers, 3 market researchers, 2 engineer-suppliers
188.task: Each gave a half-hour recorded interview answering open questions about three product stimuli; responses were transcribed and coded
188.problem: No design problem (perceptions of products and vehicle parts)
188.prompt: Questions on important aspects and purpose of everyday colanders, a vehicle exterior body side molding and a door system
188.measured: Perceived importance of product aspects, styling vs function emphasis, perceived value, goal conflicts across disciplines
188.method_detail: Three-part open-ended interview study with coded responses; the authors call it ethnographic
188.finding: Engineers, designers and marketers described the same products in different terms, creating perceptual gaps that drive goal conflict and call for user-centered process and negotiation.

195.who: 21 academic and industrial designers and mechanical engineering design students (UT Austin, Missouri-Rolla)
195.task: Built a functional model of a Nerf ball blaster freely, then again after reading a method manual, then modeled an original human-powered radio power supply
195.problem: Functional models of a Nerf ball blaster and a human-powered radio power supply
195.prompt: Make a functional model from customer needs, first by any method, then with the method manual; also design a human-powered radio power supply
195.measured: Repeatability of functional models: percent of correct and need-weighted sub-functions, flow connectivity, redesign vs original design
195.method_detail: Three-part repeatability experiment with a baseline, method-instructed and original-design condition
195.finding: The derivation method made functional models more repeatable, including for novices and original design, though flow connections between functions stayed inconsistent.

197.who: 1 engineering design student, from a larger study of 45 students and 15 professionals
197.task: Designed a conceptual solution with free tools and no think-aloud, recorded and interviewed; one sketch sequence analyzed
197.problem: Laser welding device for sheet metal in car manufacturing
197.prompt: Devise a mechanism that moves a laser at a set speed and distance along a complex-shaped metal sheet, keeping the beam at right angles to the surface
197.measured: Modality and abstraction level of sketch elements (geometry, symbols, words), reinterpretation of sketch and resulting concept change
197.method_detail: Qualitative analysis of one sketch and sketching sequence; authors say mechanisms could not be verified in the setting
197.finding: Combining geometric and functional elements in a sketch let the designer reinterpret it, which changed the whole concept; the mechanism is proposed as a hypothesis, not verified.

205.who: 89 undergraduate engineering students in four groups
205.task: Developed solutions to two problems from an initial idea given as sketch or text, then described them; controls brainstormed or worked alone
205.problem: Bicycle lock and book retrieval device
205.prompt: Develop the supplied initial idea for a bicycle lock and for a book retrieval device, working in sketch form or text form depending on group
205.measured: Fluency, quality, novelty and variety of ideas, expressiveness of each representation, visual vs verbal thinking survey
205.method_detail: Crossover of sketch and text representation with brainstorming benchmark and individual control; ANOVA with judge scoring
205.finding: Graphical representation produced more novel and higher-quality ideas than textual representation, supporting the claim that sketching aids idea generation.

218.who: A software design-process system (no human participants); compared with an industrial case study
218.task: A Signposting-based system with CFD and standard analysis codes automatically designed a steam turbine in a lab test; results compared with an industrial case
218.problem: High pressure steam turbine aerodynamic design
218.measured: Validity of the proposed process model, isentropic efficiency of the resulting design, design time
218.method_detail: Laboratory test of an implemented system, plus a case study of the original steam turbine's development
218.finding: The tested approach raised isentropic efficiency by 1.3 percentage points and cut design time by an order of magnitude compared with an industrial case.

226.who: 14 senior and graduate mechanical engineering students (4 protocol study, 10 experiment)
226.task: Thought aloud on video for 30 minutes while designing; in the experiment four groups were given function, form, behavior or knowledge stimuli
226.problem: Improved oars or propulsion for a human-powered boat
226.prompt: Oars are hard to maneuver, tire novices and rock the boat and splash; design a better human-powered watercraft propulsion
226.measured: Design entities, cognitive processes and design operations in protocols; number of ideas stimulated by each stimulus type
226.method_detail: Think-aloud protocol analysis to build a cognitive model, then a 10-person stimulation experiment
226.finding: Ambiguous stimuli prompted more ideas: behavior stimuli produced about twice as many ideas as function stimuli, and designers showed identifiable patterns of creative behavior.

231.who: 1 experienced designer (ship general arrangement) in a 2 hr 45 min recorded session
231.task: Worked on the general arrangement of a vessel while all CAD drawings were recorded; protocol analyzed for design and learning activity elements
231.problem: General arrangement of an offshore patrol vessel
231.measured: Elements of design and learning activities (knowledge change, learning goals, triggers, transformers) and links between them
231.method_detail: Protocol analysis of a single designer used to evaluate a proposed learning-in-design model
231.finding: The single protocol supported a model (LinD) in which design and learning activities link through epistemic, teleological and temporal links, though the authors call the evidence subjective and limited.

238.who: 42 junior mechanical engineering students at Osaka University, in teams of three
238.task: Designed, built, drop-tested, analyzed and redesigned a paper shock absorber over about two months; end-of-course questionnaire
238.problem: Paper shock absorber protecting a clay cone in a drop
238.prompt: Build a shock absorber from eight sheets of drawing paper and stick glue, within set size limits and three hours of production, to protect a clay cone in a fall
238.measured: Students' questionnaire responses on enjoyment, what they learned and fruitless parts; instructor observation of decisions and errors
238.method_detail: Course description with first-year outcomes and questionnaire; no formal controlled evaluation
238.finding: Students enjoyed the project and began to see how individual knowledge falls short in system-level design decisions, though the authors say outcomes still need careful evaluation.

253.who: 2 design practitioners (24 sessions in total); one session's decision sequence illustrated
253.task: Designed structure and control strategy for a controller-domain plant; reasoning steps were traced in notebook sketches and session records
253.problem: Paper-smoothing plant control (also active shock absorber)
253.prompt: Design a plant and control strategy that turns raw wrinkled paper into smooth paper of even thickness (vaguely specified problem)
253.measured: Sequence of problem reinterpretations (framing) and solution steps, recurring reasoning patterns
253.method_detail: Protocol-style illustration of a proposed framing model using extracts from 24 sessions
253.finding: Designers repeatedly reinterpreted vague problems through analogy-based shifts in the concepts they committed to, which the authors formalize as three framing patterns.

269.who: 20 engineers and graduate students with mechanical engineering degrees (Helsinki University of Technology)
269.task: Independently split four products into modules with function-structure heuristics or modular function deployment; matrix clustering was run by algorithm
269.problem: Modularizing four products: intraoral camera, electronic pipette, CT and MRI injector heads
269.prompt: Partition each product into modules using the assigned modularity method, starting from the same function structure
269.measured: Agreement of module boundaries across three methods, repeatability of each method (68% to near 100%)
269.method_detail: Comparison of three modularity methods on the same inputs
269.finding: The three methods partitioned the same products differently with almost no shared module boundaries, and repeatability ranged from 68% (modular function deployment) to near perfect (computerized matrix clustering).

283.task: A team-based multiagent algorithm and a baseline were run on a bulk manufacturing process-planning problem; performance and component effects were tested statistically
283.measured: Solution quality, successful solutions found per unit time, statistical effect of agent interdependency components
283.method_detail: Agent-based configuration design benchmark from earlier literature
283.finding: The collaborative team algorithm improved solution quality by 65 percent and found solutions about ten times faster, with agent interdependencies the most consistent driver of the gain.

287.who: Freshman engineering students in 53 two-person teams (about 106) at Missouri-Rolla
287.task: Teams developed mousetrap concept variants from needs, black box, functional model and morphological matrix, using the new representation, a textbook technique, or no technique
287.prompt: Create a better mousetrap, given customer needs, a black box, a functional model and a morphological matrix
287.measured: Concept feasibility, originality and detail, rated by blind graduate student judges
287.method_detail: Validation of a new product architecture representation against two control groups; t-tests
287.finding: Teams using the new representation produced more feasible and more detailed concepts than both control groups, with no difference in originality.

296.who: 24 upper-level engineering students in a Caltech design course
296.task: Designed and built an individual robot over 10 weeks; sketches in logbooks and morphology charts were counted and correlated with contest outcome
296.prompt: Design and build an electro-mechanical robot device for a variation of capture the flag, competing in teams of two
296.measured: Number and timing of concepts and sketches, dimensioned drawings, novices' prior fabrication experience, design outcome
296.method_detail: Correlational analysis of logbooks and morphology charts from a project course
296.finding: Dimensioned drawings made early in the project and prior fabrication experience correlated significantly with better outcome, while sketch quantity alone showed no such link.

298.who: 199 undergraduates: 177 psychology volunteers (lab) and 22 mechanical engineering students (design)
298.task: Generated ideas in two sessions with or without an interruption (incubation) between them; only the second session's ideas were compared across lab and design levels
298.problem: Alien-planet tools (lab task); spring-powered ping-pong ball transporter (design task)
298.prompt: Lab: invent novel non-motorized tools for an alien species. Design: build a spring-powered device sending a ping-pong ball farthest, using listed materials
298.measured: Quantity and quality of ideas in the second session, correlation of incubation effect between lab and design experiments
298.method_detail: Aligned lab and design experiments testing one ideation component, incubation; 82 incubation and 95 no-incubation lab participants
298.finding: Incubation raised the effectiveness of ideas in both the lab and design experiments, and the results correlated across the two levels, supporting the alignment approach.

299.who: 6 Bath and 9 Canterbury mechanical engineering students on a linked project (15 total)
299.task: Bath team developed concepts for a home assistance device; Canterbury students studied two brief issues individually; all exchanged work online and by videoconference
299.problem: Automated human assistor for elderly people living at home
299.prompt: Conceive devices that increase mobility and help within a single floor of the home, scoped from surveys of elderly people and carers
299.measured: Staff observations of communication, timing and support difficulties; student survey of project appeal
299.method_detail: Pilot of a two-university collaborative design project in 2002; Canterbury course survey covered 53 students
299.finding: The linked project succeeded in both courses, but differing calendars, time zones and remote student support were hard, and an open-ended brief appealed to only 30 percent of surveyed Canterbury students.

304.who: 18 aerospace engineering designers (2-42 years' experience) at two UK companies
304.task: Described the function of each component and feature in an assembly they knew while being interviewed; 207 descriptions were compared with two function taxonomies
304.problem: No design problem (describing functions of existing aero-engine and aircraft assemblies)
304.prompt: Break down a familiar assembly and describe the function of each part, shown example verbs and flows but free to use own words
304.measured: Share of function descriptions matched directly or indirectly to two function taxonomies, reasons for mismatch, what designers referred to
304.method_detail: Structured interviews across 17 assemblies, with comparison to Szykman and Hirtz et al. taxonomies
304.finding: Both taxonomies matched about 90 percent of descriptions, the later one more often directly, but designers talked about issues and process far more than function (only 7 percent).

309.who: 12 senior mechanical engineering capstone teams of 3-4 students (total students not reported)
309.task: Kept paper design journals over a 15-week project; hours were coded by activity and design level and related to project quality and client satisfaction
309.measured: Hours in 12 activity-by-level categories, design quality rubric score from practicing engineers, client satisfaction, productivity
309.method_detail: Journal coding with factor analysis and multivariate regression across 12 projects
309.finding: System-level idea generation and system-level problem definition best separated more from less productive teams, while early conceptual design and late detail work were not associated with productivity.

312.who: 15 third- and fourth-year mechanical engineering students, same group in both studies
312.task: In two-hour sessions, read descriptions of biological phenomena, marked relevant information, extracted strategies and turned them into concepts; second study added parsing of each phrase
312.prompt: Develop alternative ways to get clothes clean that avoid hazardous solvent wastes, using biological phenomena as analogies
312.measured: Strategies extracted (correct, incomplete, incorrect), analogous vs non-analogous similarity, fixation on words or on solutions
312.method_detail: Two follow-up studies; participants were told which similarity types to avoid; only written responses analyzed
312.finding: Telling participants which similarities to avoid cut non-analogous concepts and fixation, but difficulty mapping biological structure onto the problem persisted.

314.who: 18 project staff (leaders, systems engineers, acquisition staff) on an international submarine project
314.task: Took part in two-hour semi-structured interviews; researchers also joined the project team and reviewed project documents and diary notes
314.problem: No design problem (use of a requirements management tool in submarine development)
314.measured: Actors' needs for requirements tools and information, introduction, training and use of the tool, requirements management process
314.method_detail: Interviews, participant observation and documents in one defense project during 2003
314.finding: Introducing the requirements tool met difficulties from underestimated training time and project time pressure, pointing to the need for in-house support and introduction guidelines.

325.who: Mechanical engineering capstone students in 14 teams of 2-4 at Montana State (50 design journals)
325.task: Kept design journals over a semester of industry-sponsored projects; hours were coded by activity and design level and regressed on client satisfaction and design quality
325.measured: Hours per activity at concept, system and detail level; client satisfaction questionnaire; design quality rubric rated by practicing engineers
325.method_detail: Multivariate regression on journal-coded process data from 14 projects; n counts the 50 journals, assumed one per student
325.finding: Client satisfaction rose with problem definition time and fell with concept-level analysis, while system-level idea generation and refinement best predicted design quality.

330.who: 57 senior mechanical engineering students in self-selected teams of 4-7 at UC Berkeley
330.task: Kept individual design journals and submitted team deliverables over a four-month product design course; all sketches were coded on type, medium, dimensionality and detail
330.measured: Sketch volume, type, medium, 2D/3D, annotation and detail level over time, concept sketch variety, design outcome and class grade
330.method_detail: Analysis of 57 journals and 459 team documents including 260 concept sketches, with an inter-rater check
330.finding: Total sketches and 3D sketches mattered more for outcome later in the process, and an individual's journal sketch count correlated significantly with class grade.

337.who: 7 graduate mechanical engineering students (grammar built from 30 products)
337.task: Drew a function structure for one product unaided, then for another product guided by the grammar rules; a blind grader scored all structures
337.problem: Function structures of household products (e.g. electric knife, air pump)
337.prompt: Draw the function structure of a given product, first without and then with the grammar rules as a guideline
337.measured: Function structure quality (consistency, detail, completeness, creativity) scored by a blind grader
337.method_detail: Small validation of a 69-rule graph grammar; rules derived by hand from 30 products
337.finding: Function structures made with the grammar rules scored higher (average 8.5 vs 4.8) than those made without, especially for students who did poorly unaided.

349.who: 32 people: 30 focus group members (car, truck, mixed) and 2 development engineers
