349.task: Discussed nine open questions on what makes products innovative and valuable in 90-minute focus groups; later reviewed a seat system case against the proposed method
349.problem: No design problem (innovation factors); illustration on a seven-seat SUV seat system
349.measured: Factors that facilitate innovative products and product value, how requirements and solutions relate to intent
349.method_detail: Three audio-recorded focus groups with feedback on results, seminars, and one industrial case
349.finding: Focus groups yielded factors that promote innovation, which the authors condense into a reason-based method that challenges requirements and solutions on value and innovation.

356.who: 60 mechanical engineering students in 20 teams of three (field follow-up count not reported)
356.task: Teams drafted a design principle in 90 minutes; some paused midway to name and rate task aspects
356.problem: Engineering design task (content not stated); field follow-up on a domestic appliance
356.prompt: Create an innovative solution to a technical task from a written list of product requirements
356.measured: Expert-rated technical innovativeness, errors, unmet requirements, overall innovativeness
356.method_detail: Three conditions (explication, no explication, dummy explication), 8, 8 and 4 teams analyzed; then a field application in a course
356.finding: Explicating tacit team knowledge did not raise innovativeness but produced fewer errors and better-met requirements, giving higher overall solution quality.

358.who: About 606 undergraduates: about 350 engineering (design runs), 256 psychology (lab runs)
358.task: Generated ideas individually in two sessions, with different groups per run receiving manipulations of six ideation components in the second session
358.problem: Spring-powered ping-pong ball transporter (design); alien-planet tools (lab)
358.prompt: Design: build a device powered only by a spring to carry a ping-pong ball farthest. Lab: invent simple tools for an intelligent species on another planet
358.measured: Quantity, quality, novelty and variety of ideas, best quality and novelty; alignment of lab and design results
358.method_detail: Aligned design and lab experiments on six ideation components, with factorial runs for three of them
358.finding: Incubation helped consistently, suspending judgment raised quality but cut quantity, lab and design results aligned in 59 percent of cases, and idea quantity correlated with quality.

359.who: 8 designers: 4 expert designers and 4 student designers
359.task: Took a creativity mode test and a think-aloud warm-up, then designed alone 60 minutes; video, voice and sketches were coded
359.problem: Small water play tool for kindergarten children
359.prompt: Design a play tool for kindergarteners that uses properties of water in its mechanism, easy for children to touch, ideally usable by a group
359.measured: Design information and design process codes, personal creativity mode, solution quality scores
359.method_detail: Dual-coding protocol analysis of eight sessions, a case study
359.finding: Expert designers distributed their design activities more effectively than students, and individual creativity modes could be linked to observed design activity patterns.

360.who: 10 male volunteers: 7 engineering students, 2 university staff, 1 company engineer
360.task: After training, each completed three cable harness design tasks (20-30 minutes each) in an immersive stereoscopic system; interaction logs from the third task were analyzed
360.problem: Cable harness design in an immersive 3D system (Co-Star)
360.prompt: Task 3: revise a completed cable harness design in the product model (five subtasks such as adding cables)
360.measured: Share of time and action sequences in design, system operation, navigation, information and process integration; unproductive activity; idle time
360.method_detail: Logged user-interaction analysis during a system evaluation, with interviews
360.finding: Navigation took 41 percent of activity and system operation 23 percent versus 27 percent for design, with 28 percent of time idle, pointing to navigation and operation as improvement targets.

361.who: 137 design students in two experiments (90 and 47 recruited; 64 and 42 analyzed)
361.task: Generated ideas for 45 minutes with pencil color switched; or for 40 minutes with common or novel examples shown early or midway
361.problem: Ball-moving device (Exp 1); automatic houseplant watering device (Exp 2)
361.prompt: Exp 1: devise a device that moves balls from a field to a goal. Exp 2: devise a device watering houseplants weekly for a month
361.measured: Number of ideas, new solution categories reached, commonness of categories, effect of example timing and commonality on performance
361.method_detail: Exp 1 single-factor over time intervals; Exp 2 factorial of interval, example commonality and exposure timing
361.finding: Designers started with the most common solution categories and moved to novel ones over time, and the timing of example exposure affected performance more than whether examples were common.

362.who: 4 student design teams at Stanford, Olin and Strathclyde (member and respondent counts not reported)
362.task: Answered a Likert-scale survey on information sources and their use, just before a paper-bike race, after a two-week global collaborative design exercise
362.prompt: Build a bicycle from paper materials in two weeks and race it, with access to digital libraries, wikis, coaches and past prototypes
362.measured: Percent of information from digital libraries vs social and physical sources, and how it was used across Bloom's cognitive processes
362.method_detail: Participatory survey designed with former students; used to build a conceptual framework for design learning
362.finding: Survey of four teams informed a framework for measuring design learning from digital library use; the paper reports no headline quantitative result.

363.who: Aerospace engineers: 12 in a diary study, 10 observed 7 hours each (overlap not stated)
363.task: Diary participants logged information requests for weeks with weekly interviews; observed designers thought aloud about requests needing an external search during their normal work
363.problem: No design problem (variant design work on aero-engine parts)
363.measured: Information requests (245 diary, 241 observed) classified by objective, subject, response process, response type, reasoning direction, behaviour type
363.method_detail: Ethnographic participation, diary study with interviews, and shadowing observations twelve months apart
363.finding: Six categories were needed to characterize information requests, and about half of observed requests had high-level objectives such as generation, analysis or evaluation, needing reasoning rather than simple lookup.

364.who: 10 people: 5 mobile phone users and 5 phone-maker design experts
364.task: End users were interviewed and described making a call and their phone's parts; experts then reviewed that data and simulated affordance options
364.prompt: Users: describe the task of making a phone call and what the phone's parts do. Experts: assess user findings and propose affordance options
364.measured: Perceived architecture, user tasks, affordance levels and attributes, experts' changes to function-task interaction groupings
364.method_detail: Two investigations evaluating the Function-Task-Interaction methodology
364.finding: Users' mental models of the phone fed the function-task matrix, and experts made affordance-based modifications, supporting the method for early product architecture work.

366.who: 12 phone users in Finland: 3 blind, 3 deaf, 3 ordinary, 3 with severe impairments
366.task: Kept a photo diary on a theme for about two weeks, then took part in contextual inquiry and open-ended discussion
366.problem: No design problem (mobile phone user needs)
366.prompt: Photo diary assignment about mobile phone use, followed by discussion of use and needs
366.measured: Mobile phone needs expressed by disabled vs ordinary users and needs only disabled users reported
366.method_detail: Qualitative comparison of three user groups; authors note the small sample
366.finding: Blind and deaf users shared the needs of ordinary users and also voiced additional needs ordinary users did not yet have, making them valuable lead users.

368.who: Graduate students (11 in pilot) and senior mechanical engineering students (main experiment; total not reported)
368.task: Memorized descriptions of source products worded generally or domain-specifically, then a week later solved design problems in phases, finally told which products were analogous
368.problem: Travel exercise weights, bullet raft, flour sifter (each with an analogous source product)
368.prompt: Generate solutions to three open-ended then constrained design problems for which a previously studied product could serve as an analogy
368.measured: Share of participants finding a valid analogy-based solution at each phase, by description type
368.method_detail: Pilot (5 vs 6 participants) and larger main between-subjects experiment; two raters, about 80% initial agreement
368.finding: General (domain-neutral) descriptions of source products helped more participants find the analogous solution on the hardest problem, but the effect was weaker or absent on problems relying on visual information.

369.who: 4 undergraduate engineering researchers at two universities
369.task: Generated concepts manually with morphological matrices for three design scenarios, then compared them with Concept Generator software output and tested its robustness to altered function chains
369.problem: Hot/cold thermal mug, human-powered power supply, wall-climbing toy
369.prompt: Design a mug that adds or removes heat, a human-powered power source for audio-visual devices, and a toy that moves on a magnetic wall
369.measured: Overlap between student and software solutions, number and feasibility of software concepts, robustness to function chain changes, student reports of strengths and weaknesses
369.method_detail: Qualitative student evaluation of an early design tool plus later quantitative comparison of solution sets
369.finding: The software produced many viable concepts beyond those the students generated and was fairly robust to chain changes, though gaps in repository data and interface limits were identified.

375.who: 7 usable participants (senior undergraduate, Master's and PhD engineering students; 3 female, 4 male)
375.task: Thought aloud for 30 minutes while designing a micro-gripper from text and images of leaf abscission, with or without a function structure diagram, then a recall interview
375.problem: Microgripper that releases a tiny screw despite surface adhesion forces
375.prompt: Develop a gripper concept that overcomes sticking from surface forces when picking up and tightening a 0.6 mm screw, using leaf abscission as inspiration
375.measured: Design classification, analogical reasoning types, observed difficulties, interview feedback on the biological representations
375.method_detail: Think-aloud protocol with control and intervention group (function diagram)
375.finding: Understanding the biological phenomenon and extracting strategies from it were both hard; the function diagram helped somewhat but was cumbersome, so extraction is better done by a third party.

379.who: Senior mechanical engineering students across three experiments (total not reported)
379.task: Memorized analogous product descriptions in domain-general or domain-specific wording, then later solved design problems; third experiment varied wording of both product and problem
379.problem: Six design problems with analogous source products, e.g. travel weights, flour sifter
379.prompt: Generate many solutions to open-ended and constrained design problems, then identify and use analogies from the earlier products
379.measured: Share of participants producing analogy-based solutions across phases, by representation of product and of problem
379.method_detail: Two between-subjects experiments plus a 2x2 factorial experiment over three semesters
379.finding: General descriptions of the analogous product made later analogical use more likely, and success was highest with a domain-specific problem description paired with a general product description.

380.who: 3 fourth-year mechanical and industrial engineering students
380.task: Thought aloud for 15 minutes per problem while generating concepts with a worksheet of WordNet-derived stimulus words; transcripts coded by part of speech and keyword-in-context
380.problem: Three problems: aligning mating parts, insulating houses with snow, storing coal compactly
380.prompt: Develop concepts for each problem, performing a functional decomposition and reviewing the provided stimulus words first
380.measured: Part-of-speech use of stimulus words, relation of stimuli to new ideas expressed
380.method_detail: Verbal protocol analysis with keyword-in-context content analysis
380.finding: Stimuli given as verbs were often used as nouns, but new ideas were introduced more when stimuli were used as verbs or noun modifiers.

382.who: 12 senior mechanical engineering capstone students in 2 teams of 6
382.task: Kept a bound design journal through a summer capstone course; researchers scanned pages weekly and coded each sketch for level of detail, design stage and text content
382.problem: Capstone design projects (specific projects not reported)
382.measured: Sketch level of detail, design stage and week of entries, text content levels, documentation habits
382.method_detail: Pilot analysis of design journals using adapted coding schemes
382.finding: Journals showed uneven time spent across design stages, strong individual differences in sketching and documentation commitment, and widespread indifference to journaling.

386.who: 106 practicing designers and engineers (mostly engineers, managers and product designers)
386.task: Completed a 12-question online survey rating familiarity with and usefulness of design methods, outcome measures and tools for their latest project
386.measured: Familiarity and use of design methods, importance of project outcome measures, usefulness of design tools, respondent demographics
386.method_detail: Email-invitation survey, Dec 2006 to Jan 2007, piloted with 4 people
386.finding: Practitioners knew need finding, storyboarding and brainstorming best and found them useful, knew formal methods like TRIZ less, and valued customer feedback most as an outcome measure.

390.who: Undergraduates at three universities (53 Penn State, 16 Missouri-Rolla, 193 Buffalo; respondents fewer)
390.task: Dissected products and built CAD models or wiki reports in a digital repository, then gave feedback surveys; Buffalo compared wiki groups with hard-copy control groups
390.problem: Product dissection projects (bicycle, small engine, cordless drill, disposable camera)
390.prompt: Dissect a product and document it digitally (CAD models in a repository or a wiki report); control groups wrote conventional reports
390.measured: Student ratings of repository and website use, exposure to digital tools, understanding of the product, communication, creativity, and learning (Likert survey)
390.method_detail: Classroom implementation of cyberinfrastructure with survey feedback and wiki-group vs control comparison (t-tests)
390.finding: Students barely used the repository when it was optional, but wiki groups at Buffalo reported significantly better exposure to digital tools, product understanding and communication than control groups.

395.who: 6 expert aerospace designers (transcripts reanalyzed from an earlier study of 12)
395.task: Researchers re-read about two hours of design-activity protocol transcripts per designer to find reasoning questions and relate them to strategic questions and a problem-solving model
395.problem: Real company aerospace mechanical design tasks (variant design)
395.measured: Reasoning and strategic questions in transcripts, mapped onto generation, analysis and evaluation steps of a design model
395.method_detail: Protocol analysis of existing think-aloud transcripts from industry designers
395.finding: Strategic questions are used to formulate, develop and refine reasoning questions, and together the two question types describe how designers progress a design task.

410.who: Capstone project-course students in 8 teams (number of students not reported), plus course discussion-board data
410.task: Teams did pre- and post-test mini design projects four weeks apart, half with targeted feedback in between; discussion-board text was used to predict grades
410.problem: Build a paper glider; build an egg-drop protective case
410.prompt: Design and build within one class period, spending play money on materials: a glider judged by air time, and a case that keeps an egg intact when dropped two flights
410.measured: Correct completion of defect forms, overlap of student and instructor faults, design performance; correlation of discussion-board language features with instructor grade
410.method_detail: Pilot pre/post experiment with random assignment of groups; plus corpus-based prediction of productivity
410.finding: Targeted feedback marginally improved correct defect-form use, though not significantly in a small sample, and linguistic patterns in discussion posts predicted grades far better than post counts or length.

430.who: 12 aerospace design engineers (6 novices under 2 years, 6 experienced over 8 years)
430.task: Thought aloud for 90-120 minutes while working on their own real design tasks, followed by a short interview; analogy segments in the transcripts were coded
430.problem: Real aerospace mechanical variant design tasks, conceptual and detail stages
430.measured: Purpose of analogies, analogical distance, reasoning processes, stage of problem solving, by experience level
430.method_detail: Protocol analysis of audio-recorded think-aloud sessions in industry (about 3,370 coded segments)
430.finding: Novices mostly transferred information directly without engaging design issues, while experienced designers used analogies to solve or identify problems and to reason about component function and behavior.

433.who: 6 male engineering students (undergraduate, Master's, PhD); 2 graduate raters
433.task: Thought aloud 15 minutes per problem generating concepts from stimulus words; on one problem 3 got clashing stimuli, 3 agreeing; raters scored novelty
433.problem: Three problems: aligning a bushing and pin, insulating houses with snow, storing coal
433.prompt: Generate concepts for each problem after reviewing the stimulus words given on the worksheet
433.measured: Part-of-speech use of stimulus words, rater-scored concept novelty (0-10)
433.method_detail: Small between-subjects think-aloud study; verbal protocol coding with two raters
433.finding: Participants given incongruent stimuli used them more often as verbs, and their concepts were rated as more novel than those from agreeing stimuli.

434.who: 41 professional engineers and designers in 5 project teams at a packaging innovation company
434.task: Teams of 6-9 brainstormed (stimuli added after 40 minutes in 4 of 5), members drew 6 concepts alone, a review meeting chose gate ideas; ideas traced on video
434.problem: Five real packaging projects for customers (details confidential)
434.prompt: Generate solution ideas for each project's company brief
434.measured: Idea production rate over time, which brainstorm ideas reached stage-gate concepts, effect of stimulus type versus no stimulus
434.method_detail: Real industrial projects tracked; stimuli varied (random or guided, internal or external); no standard controls
434.finding: Idea production stayed steady for 60 minutes, but ideas that reached gate concepts dropped sharply after the first 20 minutes, and stimuli raised the share of appropriate ideas used.

440.who: Senior design class students in an experiment and in redesign teams (numbers not reported)
440.task: Control group generated analogies and ideas freely for 90 minutes; WordTree group used the taught method for 60; separate redesign teams also applied it
440.problem: Peanut shelling device for the developing world; commercial product redesigns (e.g. cat litter box)
440.prompt: Develop a device to shell peanuts for use in third-world countries, identifying analogies and many ideas
440.measured: Number of analogies identified, number of ideas, search strategy (terms outside the problem domain), share of analogies used in solutions, team opinion survey
440.method_detail: Controlled two-condition experiment (t-tests) plus uncontrolled evaluation on team redesign projects
440.finding: The WordTree method led designers to identify significantly more analogies and search more widely, without changing idea count, and redesign teams found unexpected analogies, though few analogies reached final solutions.

444.who: 84 introductory design students in 24 groups (40 without, 44 with templates)
444.task: After a lecture on functional modeling, with or without component templates, groups of 2-4 disassembled a toy and modeled it functionally in a 50-minute class
444.problem: Functional model of a Bumble Ball toy
444.prompt: Disassemble the product and develop a functional model of how it works
444.measured: Function structure and component identification mistakes, number of functions, subsystems represented, flow-conservation mistakes across 24 models
444.method_detail: Two course sections compared; classroom between-groups design
444.finding: Models built with component functional templates had fewer mistakes, more functions and more subsystems than models without templates.

456.who: 60 industrial design students (shape makers) and 20 evaluators (graduate students, designers)
456.task: Students each made a foam-cube shape expressing emotion words; 20 evaluators rated aggressiveness of 12 shapes (1-10), compared with a hand-built fuzzy logic model
456.problem: Abstract 3D foam shapes expressing emotions (massive/static, light/friendly, dynamic, aggressive/edgy)
456.prompt: Create a shape from a foam cube that best represents the given pair of emotion words
456.measured: Human aggressiveness ratings of shapes versus fuzzy model output (correlation)
456.method_detail: Design exercise to collect shapes, then rating study to validate a rule-based fuzzy model
456.finding: A fuzzy logic model of geometric features predicted human ratings of aggressive shapes fairly well (correlation about 0.88), suggesting geometry-to-emotion design rules are possible.

457.who: 30 adults aged 23 to 61 (16 male, 14 female) taking online surveys
457.task: Chose preferred vehicle front-end forms from sets of three in a 36-question survey, then a personalized 10-question check with high, neutral and low predicted-utility designs
457.problem: Vehicle front-end form (headlight and grill) drawings
457.prompt: In each question pick the one of three vehicle forms you prefer
457.measured: Individual utility function weights from discrete choice analysis; share of verification choices going to predicted high, neutral and low utility designs
457.method_detail: Two-stage online discrete choice survey with design-of-experiments stimuli
457.finding: Individual utility functions predicted preference well: high-utility designs were picked 78 percent of the time, neutral 19 percent and low-utility designs 2 percent.

458.who: 71 senior mechanical engineering undergraduates (18 control, 17 clocks-before, 18 devices-before, 18 devices-during)
458.task: Generated time-keeping device designs for 5 minutes, took a break, then 10 more; read news filler, clock or distant-device descriptions before or during the break; recall quiz
458.problem: Time-keeping devices built from household objects
458.prompt: Come up with as many conceptual designs for time-keeping devices as you can using only the listed household items
458.measured: Number of designs, functional repeats, solutions in each of 15 functional categories, by condition
458.method_detail: Four-condition between-subjects paper-packet experiment run in two class sessions; coding kappa 0.87
458.finding: Highly similar information helped even when given up front, while distantly related information only influenced solutions when given during a break after problem solving began, supporting an open-goals effect.

459.who: 57 graduate multidisciplinary new product development teams at one university (members not counted; 36 teams interviewed)
459.task: Researchers tracked 13-week team projects over four years through observation, artifacts, group interviews and surveys, coding how teams framed the problem and shared understanding
459.measured: Team framing path (need-based framing versus team agreement), decisions and their justifications, themes from interviews
459.method_detail: Four-year field study of student teams: interviews coded by two researchers, artifacts, and survey data
459.finding: Teams followed a few common paths through framing and agreement, from which the authors derived four themes to help teams navigate early product development.

469.task: Submitted one concept each on a web forum, voted for six, then picked one, in a control mode and a parliamentary mode where the crowd set its own process; survey
469.problem: Personal protection device (keep bad people and things away from your personal space)
469.prompt: Design a device that protects your personal space by keeping threats away from your immediate surroundings
469.measured: Votes on concepts, survey responses on time spent, preference versus individual work, design quality, clarity of instructions
469.method_detail: Case-study style classroom test of a forum tool in control and parliamentary modes; 18 of 42 did not finish all work
469.finding: Students received the forum system well and the crowd generated and selected concepts quickly, with most spending less time than on individual work and preferring the crowd mode.

472.who: 64 R&D engineers at an automaker (survey) plus interviewees (number not reported)
472.task: Document review of meeting minutes and change orders, semi-structured interviews of 60-90 minutes with four decision scenarios, then a web survey sent to 150 engineers
472.measured: Decision methods used by role, where decisions are made, perceived need for structured methods and expert support
472.method_detail: Document study, interviews and web survey at one vehicle manufacturer
472.finding: Most respondents resolved decisions with unstructured methods, were unsure where decisions were made, and wanted more structured methods, expert support and training.

476.who: 92 senior mechanical engineering students in 23 teams (8 control, 8 poor, 7 good)
476.task: Teams solved a design problem in one hour after instructions with no example, a poor example or a good example; talk and notes analyzed with Latent Semantic Analysis
476.problem: Low-cost peanut sheller for farmers in Haiti and West Africa
476.prompt: Design a low-cost, easy to make peanut sheller for small farmers, reaching about 50 kg per hour without electric power
476.measured: Team convergence over time (Latent Semantic Analysis), quality of final designs
476.method_detail: Three-condition between-team experiment with random assignment of pre-formed teams
476.finding: A poor example slowed team convergence and lowered design quality, while a good example did not change convergence versus control but did lead to higher quality solutions.

480.who: 16 graduate mechanical engineering students at one university
480.task: After a refresher, identified the product from function structures at three abstraction levels (10 minutes per packet) using pictures of 48 products; noted time and keywords
480.problem: Identifying a shop vacuum, rice cooker and sander from function structures
480.prompt: Identify which product each function structure models, using only inputs, outputs, functions and flows
480.measured: Correct product identification, time taken, keywords that helped, by abstraction level of the function structure
480.method_detail: In-class within-subject user study with mixed packets of three representation types; pilot with four people
480.finding: Models written in free-language terms with environmental context were far easier to identify than ones in the controlled functional vocabulary, and more functions in a model helped match similar products.

481.who: 52 survey participants in total (30 engineering undergraduates in phase 1; remainder in phase 2)
481.task: Rated similarity of pairs on a 7-point scale: 32 pairs of simplified shapes varying five design elements, then pairs of real product images
481.problem: No design problem (perceived similarity of shapes and product images)
481.prompt: Rate how similar the two items in each pair look
481.measured: Perceived similarity as affected by shape, shape angularity, orientation, texture, color and pattern (ordinal logistic fit)
481.method_detail: Two-phase full factorial similarity survey; 100% response in phase 1
481.finding: Keeping shape (especially angularity), texture, color and pattern the same significantly raised perceived similarity of a pair, so a coherent family look can be built from those elements.

486.who: 195 adults (102 online, 93 in person), about half women
486.task: Viewed 17 vehicle silhouettes one at a time, rated environmental friendliness, familiarity and nature inspiration, and chose favorites
486.problem: Vehicle silhouettes (perception study, no design task)
486.prompt: Rate how environmentally friendly each vehicle shape looks, how much it resembles everyday vehicles and how nature-inspired it seems, and pick the two you like best
486.measured: Perceived environmental friendliness, preference, familiarity, inspired-by-nature rating and sorting
486.method_detail: Taguchi design-of-experiments stimuli; main effects and interactions analyzed; online and in-person versions
486.finding: Perceived environmental friendliness can be modeled from silhouette features, and some new designs were rated greener and more nature-inspired than the Prius-shaped plant.

490.who: Staff at 2 family-owned furniture firms in Brazil and Portugal (number not reported)
490.task: Made 13 visits to the Brazilian firm and spent months at the Portuguese firm: 106 hours of observation, interviews and document review of product development practice
490.measured: How new products are developed, customer need identification, use of structured methods, lead times, difficulties in product development
490.method_detail: Exploratory qualitative multi-case study following Yin, still in progress
490.finding: Neither firm had a formal product development process, products came from reverse engineering or rough drawings with price as the key requirement, and long lead times showed little flexibility to customer needs.

495.who: 4 individuals who reverse engineered two machined parts
495.task: Each person first did a dimension-extraction rate test, then measured and recorded all dimensions of two parts in enough detail to recreate them, timed throughout
495.problem: Reverse engineering the dimensions of two metal parts
495.prompt: Extract and record the dimensions in enough detail that the product could be recreated
495.measured: Time to extract dimensions versus predictions from the exponential and linear time-to-reverse-engineer models
495.method_detail: Small empirical validation of newly proposed analytical metrics adapted from resistor-capacitor circuits
495.finding: The proposed metrics estimated barrier and time to reverse engineer well, with the exponential model tracking actual extraction time better than a linear one.

496.who: 3 robotics team members, 12 junior aerospace engineers in 3 teams, and the author
496.task: Review drawing on three qualitative field studies of diagramming software: robot test-rig design, aerospace engineer training with DRed, and a graduate concept design project
496.problem: Humanoid robot motor test rig; aerospace engineering tasks; graduate concept design project
496.measured: Barriers and catalysts to adoption, benefits for cohering perspectives, design flow and documentation, limits of diagram languages
496.method_detail: Literature review plus three qualitative studies (participant observation, semi-structured interviews, document collection); n counts only those described
496.finding: Hypermedia diagramming tools helped integrate perspectives, support design flow and document work, but adoption was limited by tool and language constraints and by capturing how information is experienced.

497.who: 5 senior mechanical engineering students at one university
497.task: Identified blurred textbook mechanism diagrams, with or without labels, by circling areas to de-blur on a tablet, thinking aloud and sketching, up to one hour
497.problem: Recognizing 14 mechanical engineering textbook diagrams (28 versions)
497.prompt: Identify the original image and describe the qualitative behavior of the objects, uncovering as little of the image as possible
497.measured: Time and difficulty to identify diagrams, where users selected (heat maps), verbal reasoning, effect of labels
497.method_detail: Controlled lab testing of a new think-aloud tablet method; qualitative, too few for statistics
497.finding: Labels and arrows sped recognition and resolved ambiguity, attention went to dense point clusters at object interfaces, and confirmation bias appeared, forming the basis of a cognitive model of diagram understanding.

498.who: 72 mechanical engineering capstone students in two course sections (38 standard, 34 experimental)
498.task: Hand-sketched concepts for homework; the experimental section got a 45-minute lesson on sketching importance between two assignments; sketches coded for detail, subject and complexity
498.problem: Paper boat built from paper pieces; semester-long capstone design projects
498.prompt: Sketch and annotate several concepts for your design project (five for the standard section, four for the experimental section)
498.measured: Number of sketches per student, sketch complexity level, sketch subject matter and detail type
498.method_detail: Quasi-experimental classroom intervention with a comparison section; ANOVA on sketches per team member
498.finding: Students sketched at a low skill level, and a short lesson on sketching importance raised sketch content and complexity but lowered the number of sketches per student.

504.who: 41 fourth-year mechanical design students (37 usable) and 1 doctoral-level rater
504.task: Solved three design problems in one hour using pairs of biological descriptions retrieved with functional, biologically meaningful or both keywords; a rater judged analogy use
504.problem: Three engineering design problems paired with biological phenomena
504.prompt: Develop a concept for each problem using the supplied biological descriptions as inspiration, forming analogies by mapping source to target
504.measured: Percentage of correct analogies formed per stimulus, by keyword group; recognition of causal relations in descriptions
504.method_detail: Three-group between-subjects study with written data only; one independent rater
504.finding: Keyword type did not clearly change results; descriptions with easily recognized causal relations drove correct analogical transfer, while complex or passive wording hindered it.

508.who: 13 graduate product design teams in one course (students not counted)
508.task: Teams wrote mission statements, interviewed and observed users, and submitted user-needs summaries; researchers coded these documents for how users talk about sustainability and trade-offs
508.problem: Thirteen team projects (e.g. fast food for teens, waste-free refrigerator, solar installation, hospital urinal redesign)
508.prompt: Student teams wrote a mission statement for their product problem, then researched potential users' needs (client-posed or self-chosen topics)
508.measured: How users define sustainability, interaction of sustainability with other needs, trade-offs and barriers to adoption, mission statement emphasis on sustainability
508.method_detail: Document analysis of student team user research, plus one team's mission-statement story
508.finding: Users rarely put sustainability first: top functional needs such as safety and performance easily trumped it, and perceived higher price was a main barrier to choosing sustainable products.

510.who: 3 co-authors acting as the designer (no outside participants); algorithm tested in automated runs
510.task: Ran 4000 automated search runs with simulated judgments, then 21 sessions where the authors compared necktie knot candidates in up to 10 dialogs against a target
510.problem: Necktie knot designs generated by a 15-rule graph grammar
510.prompt: Compare candidate tie knots shown in dialog windows and choose which is closer to the target knot
510.measured: Distance of the final suggested design from the target design (percentile among all designs), across algorithm settings
510.method_detail: Interactive stochastic search tested with simulated users (4000 runs) and 21 human-in-the-loop runs
510.finding: The stochastic grammar search consistently found designs within the 99.8th percentile with at most 30 pairwise comparisons, both with automated and human evaluators.

512.who: HTM networks (no human participants); architecture students answered a survey (5 returned in one group)
512.task: Two networks trained on silhouette chair backs by three historic designers (consistent or inconsistent sets) classified unseen chair backs; students described styles and guessed designers
512.problem: Recognizing the style of chair backs by Hepplewhite, Stickley and Greene & Greene
512.prompt: Students wrote at least three statements characterizing each designer's style from training images, then gave first and second guesses with certainty for test images
512.measured: Network belief in each style category versus human guesses and certainty, agreement between HTM and humans
512.method_detail: Model trained and tested on 128x128 images, compared against a small human survey
512.finding: The memory network recognized chair-back style much like humans did, struggling with inconsistent training data and performing accurately with consistent data, supporting its use for automated design evaluation.

519.who: 20 employees of one company making oil-rig equipment (design engineers, service engineers, design managers)
519.task: Took part in one-hour semi-structured interviews about how they use and develop design procedures; transcripts coded, with document analysis of explicit procedures
519.measured: Use of and divergence from explicit and implicit procedures, reasons for divergence, knowledge flow, coder reliability (Cohen's kappa)
519.method_detail: Single-company inductive study with coding, KJ analysis and document analysis
519.finding: Engineers followed implicit procedures (historical, social and others) alongside written ones, so procedure design needs a user-oriented approach and managing both explicit and implicit procedures.

520.who: 30 practicing designers in 15 pairs from German, Indian and Chinese companies
520.task: Pairs thought aloud together designing on paper for 2-5 hours, then were interviewed; recordings coded by design activity and compared across cultures
520.prompt: Develop a device for baking biscuits suitable for household use, working together and voicing your thoughts
520.measured: Design activities (problem analysis, sub-functions, selection criteria, solution improvement) linked to cultural characteristics, in 9 analyzed processes (32 hours)
520.method_detail: Lab protocol study in three countries; exploratory with 3 cases per culture analyzed
520.finding: Design processes differed between German, Indian and Chinese designers in ways that could be linked to cultural characteristics, such as Indian designers analyzing user situations in more depth.

521.who: Graduate trainee teams (3 teams of 4) and expert designers at one aerospace firm
521.task: Researchers audio-recorded 7 consultation meetings between trainee teams and experts during their projects; transcripts coded for design activity and conversational flow, with correspondence analysis
521.problem: Trainee team design and make projects for internal customers
521.measured: Design activities performed by novices versus experts, conversational flow (who initiates and provides information), relations between the two codings
521.method_detail: Field study with protocol analysis of audio-recorded meetings at Rolls-Royce
521.finding: Solution analysis was done collaboratively, novices mainly drove solution explanation and requirement finding, and experts mainly supplied organizational information and process and past-design discussion.

522.who: 13 multidisciplinary graduate product design teams of 4-6 members at one university (total students not reported)
522.task: Worked on a semester-long product project in four phases; team emails were scanned for feeling words and surveys measured relationship conflict, compared with performance
522.measured: Share of emails using feeling language (791-word dictionary), relationship conflict from team surveys, team performance
522.method_detail: Longitudinal field study of student teams with email text analysis and surveys; no control group
522.finding: High-performing and low-conflict teams used much feeling language, high-conflict teams used it but suppressed it after feedback, and medium-conflict teams started low and built up over the semester.

523.who: 41 senior mechanical engineering undergraduates in 9 teams of 3-6 (volunteers for extra credit)
523.task: In a 2-hour scripted session, teams used mind-maps and 6-3-5, with or without a WordTree step and a Transformation Design step (2x2), then searched the web for analogies
523.problem: System to tag and track a vehicle and then act on it (military or law enforcement)
523.prompt: Create concepts for a system that can tag and track a vehicle and later perform an effect on the target when desired
523.measured: Number of concepts generated per team and person, novelty and diversity of solutions
523.method_detail: 2x2 factorial design with ANOVA; teams randomly assigned to four conditions
523.finding: Transformation Design raised the number of concepts by 25 to 31 percent, while WordTrees did not change quantity but produced more distinct, novel and diverse solutions.

525.who: 37 fourth-year master's industrial design engineering students (13 control, 12 line-drawing, 12 photo)
525.task: Sketched solutions individually for 60 minutes after seeing only the brief, or the brief plus a line drawing or photo of an existing solution; short questionnaire
525.problem: Device to pick up a book from a high shelf
525.prompt: Design a device that lets people retrieve a book from a shelf above their reach, easy to use, manufacturable with existing technology and minimal book damage
525.measured: Number of ideas, design fixation (reproductive, contextual, analogical similarity to example), quality (ease of use, manufacture, book damage), originality
525.method_detail: Three-group between-subjects study with coded sketches
525.finding: Both example groups showed strong fixation on the pictured solution with lower originality but similar idea counts, and the richer photograph caused no more fixation than the simple line drawing.

535.who: 5 undergraduate engineering students in a summer research program
535.task: Studied an online platform planning tutorial, solved two individual case assignments and answered a questionnaire after each; outcomes scored with data envelopment analysis
535.problem: Product platform planning for a family of power tools (three cases of rising complexity)
535.prompt: Solve platform planning case assignments from the online tutorial using function diagrams, assembly diagrams, customer needs and market-segment data
535.measured: Instructional effectiveness (learning node) and efficiency (service delivery node) of each case assignment, student perceptions, design outcome quality versus expected solutions
535.method_detail: Small classroom evaluation analyzed with two-stage data envelopment analysis (8 case-solving instances)
535.finding: The efficiency analysis showed the second case was generally more efficient than the first and identified which case assignments and activities needed improvement, though results are preliminary with only five students.

537.who: 20 students in team-project design classes (17 freshmen, 3 juniors; 14 male, 6 female)
537.task: Played a repeated prisoner's dilemma game choosing to contribute or not, with grades or grade points as payoffs, 20 or 40 rounds; rated team-class importance before and after
537.problem: No design problem (cooperation game simulating free-riding in team projects)
537.prompt: Each round choose whether to contribute to a team project or not, knowing the grade outcomes for a team class and an individual class
537.measured: Percentage of rounds where both players chose to contribute, change in rated importance of team-project classes
537.method_detail: Pilot with three payoff and round conditions; assignment not fully random; sessions with missing players excluded author data
537.finding: With grade payoffs and 40 rounds, mutual contribution was highest and students rated team-project classes as more important afterward, suggesting the game may teach the benefit of contributing.

538.who: 30 sophomore mechanical engineering students (25 usable), plus a jury of 5 graduate student raters
538.task: Given one of two equal-size morphological charts, wrote and self-rated 8 concepts in 30 minutes on cost, cleanability and part count; jurors rated the top concepts
538.problem: Burrito folding device (dispense filling, fold tortilla)
538.prompt: Using the provided chart of functions and means, develop eight integrated concepts and rate each on low cost, ease of cleaning and number of parts
538.measured: Jury-rated quality of participants' best three concepts, by chart shape (3 functions with 5 means versus 5 functions with 3 means)
538.method_detail: Random assignment to two charts across two class sections; each concept rated by three jurors
538.finding: The chart with fewer functions and more means per function, offering fewer total combinations, led to significantly higher-rated concepts than the larger chart.

544.who: 40, 18 and 30 participants across three studies (overlap not stated)
544.task: Felt simulated rotary switches and rated pair similarity (0-4), did threshold discrimination tests, and rated switches as like, don't know or don't like
544.problem: Automotive rotary switch feel (travel versus effort profiles)
544.prompt: Rate how similar two switches feel; later rate how much you like each switch
544.measured: Perceptual dimensions of switch feel (multidimensional scaling), discrimination thresholds, preference as a function of travel, detent torque, friction and shape ratio
544.method_detail: Psychophysical studies with design-of-experiments stimuli on a haptic simulator
544.finding: Four parameters (travel, detent torque, friction, shape ratio) explained most perceived variation in rotary switch feel, enabling a quality function from physical design to pleasantness.

548.who: 57 senior mechanical engineering students (of 94) in 14 teams
548.task: Teams of 4-6 applied a contextual needs method while redesigning consumer products, then rated its usability and usefulness in a web questionnaire; a hand-warmer case illustrated it
548.problem: Consumer product reverse engineering and redesign; PersonaWarmth portable hand warmer for students in China
548.measured: Perceived usability and usefulness of the contextual needs method (Likert ratings), case study insights on usage context
548.method_detail: Method development with a design case study and a classroom survey assessment (other course assessments not reported here)
548.finding: Students largely agreed the context method was understandable and useful, and the hand-warmer case showed it surfaced context details, such as classroom heating and hot-water access, that shaped the design.

550.who: 3 experienced designers (one existing two-hour team protocol from the Delft workshop)
550.task: Researchers re-analyzed a three-designer team transcript, coding favorable and unfavorable appraisals by target and aligning them with design cognition patterns
550.problem: Frame for attaching a backpack to a bicycle
550.measured: Appraisals of product, process and people (positive or negative), alignment with the formation of shared understanding
550.method_detail: Linguistic appraisal analysis of one team protocol, coded jointly by two researchers
550.finding: Patterns of affective appraisal lined up with how the team formed shared understanding, suggesting an interplay between affect and cognition, though one transcript cannot show causation.

554.who: 20 undergraduate student volunteers (10 engineering, 10 non-engineering; 11 male, 9 female)
554.task: Interviewed individually for about 45 minutes about a two-person tent: verbally without it, using it normally, or using it in an extraordinary way (empathic lead user)
554.problem: Redesign of a two-person camping tent
554.measured: Latent customer needs uncovered, compared across verbal, articulated use and empathic lead user interviews
554.method_detail: Trial interview study with three interview conditions; one product
554.finding: Empathic lead user interviews, where customers experienced the product in radically new ways, uncovered significantly more latent needs than verbal or ordinary use interviews.

557.who: 16 senior mechanical and aerospace engineering undergraduates in 8 teams of 2 (4 control, 4 protocol)
557.task: Pairs in separate rooms chose machines and laid out a production line via text chat only, with free chat (control) or a structured negotiation protocol, in about an hour
557.problem: Manufacturing line for a two-part water filter (filter body and grid)
557.prompt: Each partner chooses machines for their part of the process, resolves issues using each other's option lists, and lays out machines in a shared factory space
557.measured: Number of design alternatives, cost and space performance score, collaboration efficiency, number of exchanges, communication logs
557.method_detail: Two-group between-subjects study of a negotiation protocol; communication logs coded
557.finding: The structured negotiation protocol led teams to explore more alternatives and collaborate more efficiently, but the design performance score did not differ significantly with so few teams.

567.who: 173 first-year engineering students in 28 teams of about 6 (18 experimental, 10 control teams)
567.task: Teams formed from creativity-mode test results; experimental teams did self-awareness and teamwork activities, then all sketched subway improvement ideas for 60 minutes on video
567.problem: Subway improvement (conceptual design); small-business planning as warm-up
567.prompt: Generate and sketch ideas for improving the subway; warm-up: decide how to start and run a small business with $100,000 near a university
567.measured: Creativity of team designs (novelty and resolution, rated by 3 professors), team interaction categories (Interaction Process Analysis)
567.method_detail: Experimental versus control teams; interaction analysis of one diverse and one uniform team
567.finding: Teams that did the teamwork practice activity scored significantly higher in novelty and resolution than control teams, and interaction patterns differed between diverse and uniform creativity-mode teams.

575.who: Staff at one large automaker, executives to designers (number not reported)
575.task: One researcher embedded for a year observed meetings and shadowed staff across functions with frequent interviews, building a decision model and a part differentiation matrix
575.problem: No design problem (corporate product development decision making in automotive)
575.measured: Decisions made at each stage of product planning, conflicts between disciplines, part complexity and lifestyle impact for differentiating parts
575.method_detail: One-year on-site observation and interviews at one automaker, plus comparison with other companies' processes
575.finding: The company drove development mainly by cost and technology, and a six-phase decision model with a part differentiation matrix would focus emphasis on decisions that most affect customers' emotional response.

576.who: 8 graduate students in mechanical or industrial and systems engineering
576.task: Thought aloud while designing concepts for two problems, one creative and one routine; sessions videotaped and coded for mental iteration loops
576.problem: Human-powered snow transport device (creative); two-shaft speed-reduction power transmission (routine)
576.prompt: Creative: design a human-powered personal vehicle for snow with steering and braking. Routine: design a 2000 to 100 rpm transmission fitting a 2 x 1.6 m box
576.measured: Number of problem-redefinition, idea-stimulation and concept-reuse iteration loops per session, from coded verbal protocols
576.method_detail: Think-aloud protocol analysis testing a cognitive activity model of conceptual design
576.finding: Designers iterated far more on the creative problem (about 16 loops per session) than the routine one (about 4.5), with concept reuse making up a larger share of loops in routine design.

582.who: 6 designers: 3 mechanical engineering students and 3 experts with over ten years of experience
582.task: Thought aloud for two hours while designing and dimensioning a support, ending with a final sketch and a short interview; sessions videotaped
582.problem: Support device for a hydraulic piston fixed to the ground
582.prompt: Design and dimension a support for a hydraulic piston that must carry a 90 kN axial load, placed beside an installation on the ground
582.measured: Coded basic design tasks and their order (strategies and tactics), use of rules like clarity, simplicity and safety, attention to life-cycle factors
582.method_detail: Verbal protocol analysis of embodiment and detail design in a lab setting
582.finding: Experts followed a similar strategy, thinking early in concrete parts and solving interfaces quickly, but treated evaluation and checking as secondary and neglected factors beyond cost and manufacturing.

590.who: 8 designers from earlier think-aloud sessions: 4 experienced (2+ years) and 4 novice
590.task: Thought aloud generating concepts, picked one and detailed it; researchers coded transcripts by SAPPhIRE abstraction level and scored variety and novelty
590.problem: Hole-making machine or utensil-cleaning device (one problem per designer)
590.prompt: Design a portable machine making holes of varying sizes in metal, plastic or wood, or a device cleaning all kinds of kitchen utensils for a large urban family
590.measured: Number of ideas at each SAPPhIRE abstraction level, variety and novelty of the concept space (1-7 scale), their correlation
590.method_detail: Secondary analysis of 8 existing transcribed think-aloud design sessions
590.finding: Variety and novelty of concepts correlated strongly with the number of ideas at higher abstraction levels, and the correlation weakened at lower levels.

593.who: 23 junior and senior mechanical engineering students (12 teams of two, each building own device)
593.task: Designed, built and tested an electromechanical device over a ten-week course with four milestones, logged weekly hours, then entered a public contest
593.problem: Electromechanical device built from a materials kit for a final competition
593.measured: Part count at each of four milestones, change in part count, weekly hours on design, fabrication, debugging and class, final grade, contest ranking
593.method_detail: Spearman rank correlations of prototyping data with two outcome measures, Caltech course
593.finding: Prototypes with fewer parts, and fewer parts added over the project, went with better contest results, and spending more total time did not predict a better outcome.

594.who: 11 subjects (10 men, 1 woman); 10 kept for semantic ratings
594.task: Described 15 physical glasses, sorted them by similarity, rated each on 17 adjective pairs, then made pairwise comparisons to score glasses against an ideal product
594.measured: Perceptual space (multidimensional scaling), semantic dimensions (factor analysis), pairwise-comparison scores and AHP satisfaction ranking of existing and new glasses
594.method_detail: User tests illustrating a proposed method combining psychophysics, marketing and decision theory
594.finding: The combined method gave a ranked assessment of new glass designs against an ideal product and flagged which semantic attributes a weaker design should improve.

605.who: 37 junior and senior undergraduates in a bio-inspired design class (16 biology, 21 engineering)
605.task: Studied one biological system per exercise as text, text plus graphics, or text plus SBF model, then answered 5-7 questions in 15 minutes
605.problem: Understanding biological systems (lotus leaf, basilisk lizard walking on water)
605.prompt: Read the packet describing the biological system and answer questions about it, from fact finding to abstract problem solving
605.measured: Percent correct answers on fact-finding, spatial, complex-reasoning and abstract-problem questions by representation type; self-reported familiarity
605.method_detail: Classroom pilot, each student got two different representation types, treatments alternated across neighbors
605.finding: SBF models gave more accurate answers to complex and abstract causal questions than text or diagrams, while diagrams were better for spatial questions, so no single representation suited all inferences.

606.who: 30 users: university teaching staff, research assistants, PhD and Master students in mechanical engineering
606.task: Solved 9 industrial problem cases within 8 hours, one group with the BOB-UP software procedure, the other with classical cause-effect chains
606.problem: 9 industrial technical problems (steel roller, bottle-cap valves, circular saw, Venturi wear, etc.)
606.prompt: Reformulate each problem, identifying the element suffering the undesired effect and the element causing it, with or without the BOB-UP procedure
606.measured: Correct identification of the suffering element and its operative zone, and of the causing element and its zone
606.method_detail: Preliminary two-group comparison of a new software-supported method; group sizes not reported
606.finding: BOB-UP users gave more concise descriptions and pinpointed the affected zone more often (75% versus under 40%), but finding the causing element at the right detail level stayed weak.

608.who: 60 Texas A&M students (40 undergraduate, 20 graduate), 12 per condition
608.task: Generated many solutions by sketching, building wire or plastic models, or sketching after building training; tested and marked functional ideas
608.problem: Small object to bind ten sheets of paper together
608.prompt: Design an object that binds ten sheets of paper without damaging them, made of up to 9 inches of steel wire or moldable plastic depending on condition
608.measured: Expert-rated novelty and variety of ideas, percentage of functional ideas, timing of ideas
608.method_detail: Between-subject lab study, five conditions (sketching, metal building, plastic building, and two constrained-sketching controls)
608.finding: Novelty and variety dropped only in the costly plastic-building condition, supporting a sunk-cost explanation of fixation, and building physical models produced a higher share of functional ideas.

609.who: 45 students (41 seniors) in an interdisciplinary biologically inspired design class, in teams of 4-5
609.task: Worked in teams on semester bio-inspired design projects while researchers observed and built an information-processing model
609.problem: Nine semester-long biologically inspired design projects
609.prompt: Each team picked a problem suited to a biologically inspired solution and developed a final design from biological sources
609.measured: Observed design processes (problem-driven versus solution-driven), analogy use, representations; compared to TRIZ, case-based design and design patterns
609.method_detail: In situ classroom study of Fall 2006 course, summarizing earlier data collection
609.finding: Bio-inspired design follows problem-driven and solution-driven routes with cross-domain, often compound analogies, summarized in a macrocognitive model.

610.who: 158 senior mechanical engineering students at two universities (46 at UMD, 112 at UT Austin)
610.task: Interacted up to 20 minutes with alarm clocks (subject groups also used blindfold, earplugs, mitts), then each generated three concepts in modified 6-3-5
610.prompt: Design a next-generation alarm clock for the contemporary marketplace
610.measured: Concept originality (maximum feature-level) and technical quality (minimum feature-level), t-tests of subject versus control
610.method_detail: Subject versus control groups run separately at two universities (UMD 18 vs 28; UT Austin 54 vs 58)
610.finding: Students who first experienced the product under impaired conditions produced significantly more original concepts at both schools, with no loss of technical quality.

613.who: 17 Texas A&M engineering students (16 senior undergraduates, 1 graduate)
613.task: Sketched ideas alone for 40 minutes using two sets of example analogies, marked analogous ideas, then answered questionnaires
613.problem: Quick, low-cost peanut shelling without electricity
613.prompt: Devise methods or devices to shell peanuts quickly, cheaply and without electricity, using the supplied analogy examples
613.measured: Total ideas, analogous and non-analogous ideas, emergent features, semantic distance of domains (WordNet), perceived usefulness of analogies
613.method_detail: Between-subjects, four conditions (nutcracker, food peeler, debarker, depilator as second domain), 3 to 5 per condition
613.finding: Participants rated distant-domain analogies as less useful, yet distant domains produced at least as many ideas and emergent features as close ones, and problem-domain-only analogies did worst.

614.who: 58 fourth-year engineering students (31 in Group A, 27 in Group B) after dropping 3
614.task: Each worked alone for 30 minutes per problem using a biological description with a causal-relation template, with or without mapping rules, to generate concepts
614.problem: Separating paper from plastic in mixed recycling; protecting a lunar laser device from dust
614.prompt: Develop concepts for sorting paper and plastic from mixed collection, and for keeping lunar dust off a lens cover, inspired by a given biological text
614.measured: Correctness of analogical transfer and creativity of concepts, rated by two independent raters; correlation between them
614.method_detail: Two-group comparison of design aids, random assignment, University of Toronto course
614.finding: Groups did not differ significantly on average scores, but only the group given mapping rules showed a significant link between correct analogical transfer and concept creativity.

616.who: 14 participants in a preference study and 7 in an fMRI study (overlap not stated)
616.task: Chose between vehicle silhouettes, specification sets, or both, in conjoint trials; seven also made form-function tradeoff choices in an MRI scanner
616.problem: No design problem (preference judgments about vehicle form and function)
616.prompt: Pick the preferred option among vehicle designs, specification groups, or combined form-function pairs
616.measured: Form, function and combined utility models, fit to self-reported ratings, brain activation during form-only, function-only and conflict choices
616.method_detail: Two-stage conjoint analysis followed by fMRI task
616.finding: Combined form-function choices were more complex than either alone, with conflict trials activating emotion-related regions such as the ventral striatum in addition to reasoning areas.

619.who: Students in a senior interdisciplinary biologically inspired design course over several years (number not reported)
619.task: Teams did semester-long projects while researchers observed, collected journals and reports, and one author joined a team as participant observer; data fed an information-seeking model
619.prompt: Each team identifies a problem a biologically inspired solution could address and develops a design from biological cases
619.measured: Online information-seeking behavior of designers, foraging costs, time spent finding biological sources
619.method_detail: In situ classroom observation since 2006, including participant observation in 2008; leads to a model and the Biologue tool
619.finding: Finding biological inspiration online was slow and costly, taking longer than all downstream design activity, which motivated tagging articles with structure-behavior-function models.

622.who: 26 car show attendees (18 men, 8 women) after excluding 8 of 34
622.task: Rated 30 computer-generated car side-profile designs on sportiness, ruggedness, aerodynamics and fuel efficiency using a 5-point scale
622.measured: Ratings versus computed drag coefficient, center of gravity and volume, inter-rater reliability, effect of 12 shape parameters
622.method_detail: Computer survey at a vintage car show with 5 shared cars for reliability
622.finding: Consumers judged aerodynamic performance reliably and accurately, seeing small, low, low-center-of-gravity cars as sportier and more aerodynamic, and taller cars as more rugged.

623.who: 22 practicing designers and design researchers plus 17 design students (interviews and a survey)
623.task: Practitioners took a tools survey (11) and interviews (15, plus 2 sets of notes); students were interviewed (4, plus notes on 13)
623.measured: Range of tools used, sharing semantics (private, personal, public), formality, stage of use, capture-reflect-share cycle
623.method_detail: Survey plus semi-structured interviews, with coding of tool mentions and student course documents
623.finding: Designers use a wide mix of tools whose sharing and formality differ, and sharing follows a cycle of capture, reflect and share that tools should support.

627.who: 7 people in two workshops: 3 teachers (users) and 4 development team employees (designers)
627.task: Each group built a 3D model of its view of an existing portal from given materials, then disassembled and grouped elements
627.problem: Existing online resource portal for school teachers (Opettaja.tv)
627.measured: Number and type of model elements and entity groups, differences between user and designer perceptions, participant feedback on the method
627.method_detail: Test of the Participatory 3D modeling method, 2-3 hour workshops
627.finding: The method captured both views: users modeled a wide experience around the product with 16 elements, while designers modeled product features and technical solutions in detail with 51 elements.

628.who: 11 Rolls-Royce professionals, from junior engineers to chief designers
628.task: Gave 90-120 minute semi-structured interviews, in groups of up to three, about using a map-based rationale tool
628.measured: Value of tool features and methods in practice, emergent themes on creativity and knowledge management
628.method_detail: Qualitative theme analysis of transcripts after eight years of tool use
628.finding: Engineers often saw mapping as the path of least resistance for organizing unstructured ideas and conflicting views, though its flexibility makes standardizing methods hard.

630.who: 7 graduate students from mechanical, electrical and computer engineering (empirical part of a methodology review)
630.task: Designed a train litter-disposal system while protocols were recorded; protocols were segmented and encoded using the environment-based design process
630.problem: Litter-disposal system for a train passenger compartment
630.prompt: Design a system letting passengers deposit garbage conveniently and cleaners collect it easily
630.measured: Whether the protocol data fit the environment-based design process, and differences in performance across subjects
630.method_detail: Protocol analysis summarized briefly within a broader overview of the design methodology
630.finding: All seven protocols could be encoded with the environment-based design process, and performance differed in how well subjects identified environment components and conflicts.

632.who: 6 senior student design teams at the US Air Force Academy (one member each, from 40+ students)
632.task: Rated a 21-statement six-point Likert survey about their product usage context and said whether their concept sketches included a transformable device
632.problem: Each team's own senior design project (varied)
632.measured: Agreement with context statements linked to transformation indicators, compared with whether teams chose transformable concepts; indicators also refined by analysing products
632.method_detail: Deductive team survey plus inductive study of existing transformable and non-transformable products
632.finding: Almost all teams planning transformable designs strongly agreed with several indicator statements, giving preliminary support for context-based indicators of when to transform.

636.who: 17 participants: 8 industry design experts and 9 senior engineering students; two cases shown
636.task: Thought aloud alone for up to an hour on a design problem, writing or sketching as desired; transcripts were notated into a problem-map framework
636.measured: Problem maps of attended entities, attributes and relations over time; differences between expert and novice problem formulation
636.method_detail: Think-aloud protocol study, analysis still in progress; two participants illustrated
636.finding: Problem maps showed the problem and solution spaces evolving over time, with a richer set of attended attributes and relations for the expert and more unattended attributes for the novice.

638.who: 40 engineering students (14 graduate students, remainder senior undergraduates)
638.task: After 30 minutes of training on a function model or function interaction model, sketched solution concepts for 30 minutes, one concept per sheet
638.prompt: Design a home-use burrito-folding machine for a party that meets listed functional requirements and human activity requirements such as easy to install, use and clean
638.measured: Quantity of concepts, quality scores by external panel against functional and non-functional requirements
638.method_detail: Two-phase classroom study; undergraduates randomly split by model, graduate students alternated between models
638.finding: Function model users produced more concepts, while function interaction model users produced higher quality concepts.

639.who: 1 engineering graduate student wearing an EEG headset
639.task: Rested five minutes, then solved a design problem on a tablet, no time limit, with six-channel EEG, screen and video recorded
639.problem: Arranging seven beds and a desk in a children's cottage bedroom
639.prompt: Fit seven beds and a desk into the room for seven children so the arrangement meets each child's needs
639.measured: EEG band power (delta, theta, alpha, beta) at six scalp channels across design activity segments
639.method_detail: Single-subject pilot to validate an EEG experiment protocol
639.finding: The subject showed more visual-thinking effort during solution generation than evaluation, suggesting EEG can complement protocol analysis of designing.

641.who: 14 participants, fourth-year undergraduates to second-year PhD students at University of Toronto
641.task: After three training problems, thought aloud while solving three 15-minute design problems, with similar, opposite or no stimulus words; concepts rated
641.problem: Bushing-and-pin centering, snow as house insulation, coal storage at a power plant
641.prompt: Develop a concept to center mating parts without high accuracy; a way to use snow as extra house insulation; a way to store coal near a plant
641.measured: Novelty, usefulness and cohesiveness of concepts for similar, opposite and no-stimulus conditions
641.method_detail: Verbal protocol experiment, 10 stimulus and 4 control participants, used to critique verbal protocol methodology
641.finding: Stimuli did not raise concept creativity, which prompted a review of verbal protocol limits in design research and design-specific guidelines for using them.

642.who: 3 engineering graduate students forming one design team
642.task: Discussed three carafe options until consensus while thinking aloud, and filled out five preference surveys about every 10 minutes; transcript coded with two formal methods
642.problem: Choosing a coffeemaker carafe (glass, stainless steel, plastic)
642.prompt: As a retired coffee connoisseur on a fixed income, choose a carafe and filter for a coffeemaker within a 35 dollar budget
642.measured: Team preferences for alternatives from APPRAISAL linguistic coding and Preferential Probabilities from Transcripts, compared with surveys; consistency of attribute assessment over time
642.method_detail: One 50-minute team session, transcript of the carafe discussion analyzed
642.finding: The two linguistic methods gave comparable preference assessments, and how the team evaluated a given attribute could change substantially over time.

644.who: 30 design consultants and clients (average 14 years of experience) from 25 companies
644.task: Gave one-to-two hour semi-structured interviews on project success and failure, then an 82-item questionnaire; clients rated their last three consultants
644.measured: Meanings and metrics of project success, client willingness to recommend consultants (Net Promoter style), common failure modes
644.method_detail: In-depth interviews with a stratified non-representative sample plus questionnaire and pilot rating data
644.finding: Practitioners define success in many ways, client willingness to recommend varies widely across projects, and several recurring failure modes explain gaps between client expectations and results.

646.who: 29 IIT Kanpur graduate students (18 English, 11 Telugu); software learned word associations
646.task: Handled pegs in tight and loose holes and described the interaction in English or Telugu; word frequencies linked to fit
646.prompt: Describe the interaction between the peg and the hole, without lifting the block from the table
646.measured: Conditional word frequencies for tight versus loose cases, words most associated with each in English and Telugu
646.method_detail: Human narrative corpora (1099 and 904 English words) used as input to an embodied-symbol approach; participant overlap not stated
646.finding: Words such as tight and loose in English, and equivalents in Telugu, were readily associated with fit situations, though Telugu narratives focused more on the action than the state.

649.who: 43 Texas A&M students (39 senior undergraduates, 4 graduate students)
649.task: Generated as many paperclip ideas as possible by sketching, building from steel wire, building and testing, or sketching after building training, within a three-hour session
649.prompt: Design a small steel wire object, at most 9 inches of wire, that securely binds ten pages together without damaging them
649.measured: Percentage of functional ideas, novelty and variety of ideas (expert ratings, two evaluators)
649.method_detail: Between-subjects, four conditions with 10, 10, 11 and 12 participants
649.finding: No design fixation appeared with physical models, and building and testing raised the fraction of functional ideas, indicating that physical models supplement designers' mental models.

653.who: 34 Executive MBA students (25 men, 9 women; average age 38) in 8 design teams
653.task: Rated classmates on ease of creative ideas, were randomly teamed for a one-day design exercise, then rated teammate interactions
653.problem: Shopping bag for an open-air French market
653.prompt: Design a bag that eases grocery shopping at a typical open-air market, including customer needs visits, ideation and a final prototype
653.measured: Past and exercise creative-interaction ratings between pairs, source's average creative capability, team prototype votes
653.method_detail: Field experiment with two surveys around random team assignment (six teams of four, two of five)
653.finding: Past pairwise creative interactions did not predict creative interaction in the exercise; the best predictor was how strongly the source person triggered creative ideas in others generally.

654.who: 7 designers with product design experience beyond an undergraduate degree
654.task: Redesigned a tumbler in 60 minutes using affordance analysis and a feature repository, thinking aloud with tablet sketches, then a retrospective interview
654.prompt: Re-design a tumbler (portable coffee cup) using the given affordance analysis and repository
654.measured: Design process activity shares from coded think-aloud protocol (one designer detailed), use of repository features
654.method_detail: Illustrative test of a design-for-affordances framework; protocol coding shown for one designer
654.finding: Designers used repository features as clues in redesigning the tumbler, and the coded process for one designer was dominated by sketching, concept generation and browsing the repository.

655.who: 11 product development professionals (program managers, functional managers, architects, lead engineers) at 3 companies
655.task: Interviewed about platform-based product development practices in six case entities across three companies; interviews summarized and compared with a literature review
655.measured: Perceived enablers and barriers across platform life cycle stages and organizational factors
655.method_detail: Exploratory multi-entity case study of business-to-business products in Rochester, NY, plus literature review
655.finding: Key enablers were institutionalizing systems engineering, product roadmaps, an augmented phase-gate review and critical parameter characterization, with companies' platform experience ranging from success to disregard.

656.who: 48 freshman students, with 2 evaluators rating the concepts
656.task: Interacted 30 minutes with two basic alarm clocks, then generated three concepts each in modified 6-3-5; two evaluators rated concepts
656.prompt: Design the next-generation alarm clock for the current market as an employee at a design firm
656.measured: Inter-rater agreement and correlation for novelty, originality, quality and feasibility metrics at concept versus feature level and across scales
656.method_detail: Reliability analysis of existing ideation metrics on one concept generation session
656.finding: Inter-rater reliability of the novelty, quality and variety metrics was generally low, best at the feature level, and finer scales lowered agreement somewhat.

658.who: 5 male engineering graduates (3 PhD students, 2 with doctorates) with connectivity modelling experience
658.task: Disassembled a vacuum cleaner, then recorded component dependencies in a matrix, as 2 people on the whole or 3 on one module each
658.problem: Connectivity model of a vacuum cleaner
658.prompt: Identify interactions between component pairs in the matrix while examining the parts, with no time limit
