658.measured: Agreement between the whole-matrix and modularised connectivity models by component pair and dependency type; modelling effort
658.method_detail: Small two-group comparison of modelling approaches, plus mathematical effort models
658.finding: Models built by splitting the matrix among people matched the whole-matrix model for nearly all component pairs, differing mainly on spatial dependencies, while spreading the effort.

661.who: Over 500 engineering students and some practicing engineers (300 samples analyzed)
661.task: Took an eight-question divergent thinking test (alternative uses, synthesizing devices, unusual relations, conflict resolution, a design problem) in beta trials at several universities and companies
661.problem: Eight test questions on ideation, e.g. alternative uses of an artifact and a contest-style design problem
661.measured: Fluency, flexibility, originality, quality plus abstractability, afixability, detailability and decomplexability; factor analysis, norming and reliability
661.method_detail: Psychometric analysis of a standardized divergent thinking test, under 50 minutes
661.finding: Factor analysis of 23 test measures supported a four-factor structure and reasonable scaling, so the test is a usable instrument for ideation skill, though only intrinsic validation was done.

664.who: 84 participants: 24 product designers, 21 improvisational comedians, 26 MIT students, 13 others
664.task: Sketched as many innovative ideas as possible for each of three product themes in 12-minute individual brainstorms; 1767 ideas rated online by reviewers
664.prompt: Develop as many innovative concepts as you can around the given product theme, sketching each on its own sheet
664.measured: Reviewer ratings of creativity, novelty, usefulness, feasibility and sketch clarity; link between idea quantity and creativity
664.method_detail: Nominal brainstorm sessions in four participant groups, then online rating of ideas
664.finding: Creativity ratings tracked novelty but not usefulness, clearer sketches seemed more creative, and people who generated more ideas also scored higher on creativity and novelty.

666.who: 87 third-year students at a Tokyo technical junior college (43 Scenario Graph, 44 brainstorming)
666.task: Generated ideas alone for ten minutes using either the Scenario Graph mind-mapping method or plain brainstorming; four industry and academic evaluators rated the ideas
666.problem: New product or service for the future (open theme)
666.prompt: Think of new products or services you would like to have in the future
666.measured: Number of ideas, and rated novelty, feasibility, abstractness and related quality of ideas (0/1 judgments by four evaluators)
666.method_detail: Two-group comparison, assignment by odd or even student ID, Mann-Whitney tests
666.finding: Scenario Graph users did not produce more ideas than brainstormers, but their ideas were significantly more novel, feasible and abstract.

668.who: 4 people: 2 of the authors and 2 graduate students researching design theory
668.task: Each independently grouped 163 cards of biological transformation examples and tagged them with keywords, then discussed their strategies; a similarity algorithm compared the groupings
668.prompt: Group the cards by any attributes you find important and tag each with keywords, without using taxonomic classes
668.measured: Relatedness between participants' groups (similarity index), hierarchical, synonymous and causal relations among groups
668.method_detail: Card sorting and tagging task analysed with a new collective categorization algorithm
668.finding: The four participants categorized the examples quite differently, yet pooling their categories revealed meaningful hierarchical, synonymous and causal relations in biological information.

672.who: 121 senior mechanical engineering students at Texas A&M, in a capstone design course
672.task: Wrote or sketched ideas for 50 minutes, with or without a prompt to imagine how nature would solve it, before ideation training
672.problem: Corn shucking device or quiet personal alarm clock
672.prompt: Design a device that quickly and cheaply shucks corn, or an individual alarm clock that wakes the user without disturbing others
672.measured: Quantity of non-redundant ideas, quality, novelty and variety of solutions, rated by two trained raters
672.method_detail: Between-subjects, directed bioinspiration prompt versus control on two problems; the condition table counts do not sum to 121
672.finding: Simply telling designers to consider how nature would solve the problem gave no significant advantage in idea quantity, quality, novelty or variety.

674.who: 8 mechanical engineering faculty, then 11 tool sessions with faculty and graduate students
674.task: Faculty mapped a research project onto readiness-style scales; later faculty and students were guided through a new maturity-levels tool
674.problem: No design problem (rating academic research projects)
674.measured: Usability and interpretation of the maturity prompts, faculty concerns about scoring, fit across research types
674.method_detail: Iterative tool development with interviews and usability case studies
674.finding: Early scales felt like grades and confused researchers, while the revised Research Maturity Levels let faculty with varied research goals build a profile of their projects.

675.who: One design team (size not reported); Mechanical Turk workers rated appraisal wording
675.task: Team discussed carafe options while the transcript was coded for appraisals; online workers rated intensity, feeding a Markov preference model
675.problem: Choosing a coffeemaker carafe (glass, plastic, steel)
675.prompt: Choose a carafe and filter for a coffeemaker, discussing preferences with teammates until consensus
675.measured: Coded appraisals (27 statements, 72 semantic resources), intensity judgments, estimated probability of each alternative being chosen over time
675.method_detail: Reuses a prior team dataset to illustrate a language-based preference modeling method
675.finding: Linguistic appraisals could be converted into time-varying probabilities of which alternative a team would choose, illustrating the method on one discussion.

676.who: 50 mechanical engineering students (29 UTEP seniors, 21 University of Maryland graduate students)
676.task: Generated ideas for a redesign task with or without two 50-minute TRIZ lectures, then continued ideating for days within a two-hour limit
676.problem: LED traffic light that lets snow accumulate
676.prompt: Redesign a traffic light using LEDs so that snow no longer blocks vision, while keeping the LED energy savings
676.measured: Quantity, novelty and variety of ideas, judged by trained raters
676.method_detail: TRIZ training versus control, run at two universities with slightly different sequences
676.finding: TRIZ training improved the novelty and variety of concepts at both institutions, with matching results for seniors and graduate students.

678.who: 110 engineering students (23 at University of Sydney, 87 at Oregon State University)
678.task: Completed an online risk-attitude survey with a general risk test plus a new engineering-specific test of risk-averse and risk-seeking items across four risk-management domains
678.measured: Engineering domain-specific risk aversion and risk seeking, internal reliability (Cronbach alpha), factor structure of the four domains
678.method_detail: Test development and reliability study, E-DOSPERT instrument
678.finding: The new test was reliable overall and for risk identification and treatment, but factor analysis suggested four other domains describe engineers' risk attitudes better.

679.who: 254 senior mechanical engineering students at two universities (77 UMass Dartmouth, 177 UT Austin)
679.task: Interacted 20-30 minutes with similar products, then generated ideas for an hour in 6-3-5 or C-Sketch groups of about six
679.prompt: Design a product for a client in a simulated industrial task (alarm clock or litter grabber)
679.measured: Originality, number of innovation characteristics hit, and feasibility at feature level, initial ideas versus group ideas
679.method_detail: Secondary analysis of subject and control groups from an earlier study, 15 idea sets per group per product
679.finding: The rest of the group generally improved the originality and innovativeness of the initial ideas, while feasibility fell slightly but not significantly.

682.who: 8 expert mechanical designers from one company
682.task: Thought aloud for one hour while designing, with sketches recorded, then took a divergent thinking test; transcripts coded into problem maps
682.problem: Water sampling device for lakes, down to 500 m
682.prompt: Design a mechanical device used from a rowboat that descends to a set depth, returns with a 0.5-liter water sample and floats until picked up
682.measured: Problem map entities and relations over time, correlations with divergent thinking scores (fluency, flexibility, originality, quality)
682.method_detail: Exploratory think-aloud protocol analysis using the problem map model
682.finding: Designers who specified more behavior entities scored higher on creativity, fluency and quality, and more elaboration through parent-child links went with higher originality.

685.who: 145 senior engineering mechanics students in 21 capstone teams, US Air Force Academy, over three years
685.task: Capstone teams worked as a control year, then with a context-indicator method, then with the method plus feedback; 40 others applied it once
685.problem: Capstone design projects (micro-air vehicles, robotics, and others)
685.measured: Quality, novelty and feasibility of solutions, whether teams followed the indicated device type, survey opinions of the method
685.method_detail: Three-phase field study against a prior-year control, plus an auxiliary reliability exercise with 40 people
685.finding: Using the indicators method raised combined quality, novelty and feasibility by up to 44% over control when teams followed its indication, with smaller gains when they ignored it.

688.who: 28 experiment participants; ethnography of 2 Mennonite families and 3 experts (family size not reported)
688.task: Removed paint from balls using little water from a tap, 10 mL containers, containers earned by stepping, or a pulsed hose; plus interviews
688.problem: Product design principles for conservation; lab washing task
688.prompt: Remove the paint from two table tennis balls using as little water as possible
688.measured: Water used per condition (mL), observed behaviors; themes in Mennonite resource use
688.method_detail: Lead-user ethnography of two Mennonite households, then repeated-measures experiment (4th condition dropped after 3 subjects)
688.finding: Discretizing water into small units cut use sharply (about 22 mL versus 199 mL from a tap), and added physical effort made no significant further difference.

690.who: 30 undergraduate students with engineering design background, 10 per condition
690.task: Did a 10-minute questionnaire or collage prime (or none), generated toaster features 15 minutes, then 12 minutes on sustainability-signaling features
690.prompt: As a product designer, add or improve toaster features, then specifically create features that trigger customers to think of sustainability
690.measured: Number of features, judge-rated sustainability trigger of each feature, number and percentage of good features
690.method_detail: Between-subjects with questionnaire prime, collage prime and no-prime control
690.finding: Priming with a questionnaire or collage activity significantly increased the number and effectiveness of features that signal sustainability, with the collage prime slightly better.

693.who: 17 construction stakeholders (architects, builders, homeowners, insurers, producers) from several countries
693.task: Took part in phone, Skype or face-to-face qualitative interviews based on a 47-question guide; answers and a literature review shaped a design guide
693.problem: No design problem (guide for straw-built houses)
693.measured: Perceived barriers and incentives for straw construction, concerns specific to straw versus general to building
693.method_detail: Qualitative interview survey with practitioners and non-practitioners of straw building, plus literature review
693.finding: Straw building was not found to be more difficult or uncertain than conventional building; it is simply less familiar, so its issues are perceived as barriers.

698.who: 24 University of Toronto students (15 engineers, 9 non-engineers)
698.task: Designed a plant watering system after a fixating example, did 10 minutes of defixation with or without exercise, then generated more ideas
698.problem: Houseplant watering system giving 1/10 liter per week
698.prompt: Design a watering system for a houseplant that delivers one-tenth of a liter of water per week
698.measured: Fixation score of ideas (similarity to example, three judges), number of solutions, by physical activity condition and engineering education
698.method_detail: Random assignment to defixation with or without physical activity; tests a proposed long-term potentiation account of creativity
698.finding: Physical activity did not reduce fixation overall, but engineers who exercised produced more solutions after defixation, and non-engineers were less fixated than engineers.

701.who: About 40 innovation researchers, teachers and practitioners at an NSF conference (about 90% engineering professors)
701.task: Completed a web survey of demographic questions, seven-point Likert statements about innovation, and short-answer questions
701.measured: Agreement with innovation statements, correlations among responses, themes in short answers defining innovation terms
701.method_detail: Deductive and inductive analysis, including correlations across questions
701.finding: Experts saw brainstorming as useful but confusing, were split on whether analogies cause fixation, and agreed that innovation processes overcoming fixation and creativity training are possible.

706.who: 20 students aged 22-25 at one engineering school
706.task: Interactively picked preferred virtual table-glass shapes over up to 20 generations of a genetic algorithm in three tests: two goal-seeking tasks and one 'elegant' judgment
706.prompt: Select the glass shapes closest to a target shape, or most 'elegant', until satisfied with the product the algorithm converges on, then score it 0-10
706.measured: Convergence of the algorithm toward target shapes, score given to final product, clustering of users' final choices
706.method_detail: Simulated convergence tuning, then perceptive tests with a 20-person panel
706.finding: The interactive genetic algorithm converged within a user-tolerable number of generations on small problems and revealed shared and individual design trends for the 'elegant' glass shape.

707.who: 15 mechanical engineering students (6 in multi-product study, 9 in single-product study)
707.task: Disassembled consumer electromechanical products and built interaction matrices (HDDSM) of the components after training; second group modeled one product and answered a questionnaire
707.problem: Product architecture models of household electromechanical products
707.prompt: Examine a product, disassemble it, and record which components interact and how, following the HDDSM modeling process
707.measured: Inter-rater agreement (kappa) per interaction type between examiners, questionnaire feedback on the process
707.method_detail: Two repeatability studies comparing models by different examiners
707.finding: Agreement between examiners was high for concretely defined interactions and lower for vague or directional ones, so clearer definitions and non-directional interactions improve repeatability.

708.who: 64 university students (32 with design experience, 32 other majors)
708.task: Viewed 16 wheel rim renderings and rated each on semantic dimensions, Kansei attributes and overall liking
708.measured: Liking ratings, semantic-space and Kansei ratings; regression models predicting preference from design, Gestalt, semantic and Kansei variables
708.method_detail: Full factorial of 4 design variables at 2 levels; regression modeling
708.finding: Preference was predicted best by Gestalt variables combined with the meaning and emotion users attached to the rims, and Gestalt variables fit better than raw design variables.

718.who: 584 usable online survey respondents recruited via Mechanical Turk (about 100 per survey, six surveys)
718.task: Ranked four sketches of one object from least to most liked; each survey showed one object in either line or shaded styles
718.problem: Cube, Amoebe chair, cell phone (sketch styles)
718.prompt: Rank four drawings of the same object from the one you like least to the one you like most
718.measured: Rank preference for sketch finish and style, time taken to create each sketch
718.method_detail: Online between-subjects ranking surveys across 3 objects and 2 drawing families
718.finding: Respondents preferred clean, realistic hand sketches over rough ones and even over CAD renderings, which took much longer to make; object familiarity and complexity shaped responses.

719.who: 4 experienced software designers in 2 pairs from two companies
719.task: Pairs designed a traffic-simulation program for about two hours; researchers coded roughly 700 transcript utterances for cognitive activities
719.problem: Traffic flow simulation software for students
719.prompt: Design a traffic flow simulation program that students can use to explore traffic scenarios, given four broad requirements
719.measured: Cognitive activity codes (problem vs solution), breadth-first vs depth-first search, co-evolution of problem and solution, inter-coder kappa
719.method_detail: Transcript coding of two recorded sessions, compared with engineering design findings
719.finding: Software designers moved quickly to detailed design, co-evolved problem and solution, and worked mostly depth-first, similar to engineering designers in several respects.

721.who: 13 engineers from diverse departments at one aerospace company
721.task: Took part in semi-structured interviews about using a decision-mapping software tool, supplemented by collected example maps
721.measured: Successful mapping methods, common contexts of use, advantages over existing tools
721.method_detail: Semi-structured interviews plus documentary examples from long-term industrial use
721.finding: Engineers used maps mainly where several poorly defined options needed sorting, valuing clarification and collaboration more than record-keeping, which supports wider use of mapping tools.

726.who: 40 senior engineering students in 8 groups of 5 (34 finished)
726.task: Generated concepts individually, ranked them as a group informally, then a month later chose concepts with Pugh's Controlled Convergence or G-HEIM; interviews and surveys followed
726.problem: Sustainable playground for an impoverished country
726.prompt: Develop a playground concept for children in a developing country that is sustainable, meeting listed requirements
726.measured: Decision traps in group discussion, student perceptions of formal decision methods (interviews, surveys), group satisfaction with process and outcome
726.method_detail: Pilot study in a design methods course comparing informal vs two formal decision methods
726.finding: The pilot documented decision traps emerging in each group and student perceptions of formal methods, and identified framework and protocol changes for a larger repeat study.

727.who: 55 first-year engineering students in 4-member teams across 3 course sections
727.task: Teams dissected an electric toothbrush for two hours, then a week later each student sketched redesign ideas alone for 30 minutes; personality questionnaire taken beforehand
727.prompt: Redesign an electric toothbrush for increased portability, focusing on either the brush head or the body
727.measured: Novelty of features, designs and per participant (Shah metrics), number of ideas, exposure to parts during dissection, Five Factor personality traits
727.method_detail: Exploratory classroom experiment, ANCOVA on personality and dissection exposure
727.finding: Extraverted participants were more exposed to the body-design dissection activity and produced more novel ideas, so personality traits shape how dissection affects novelty.

728.who: 22 mechanical engineering capstone students in teams of two
728.task: Each team designed three assistive devices in 45-minute videotaped sessions, using brainstorming, morphological analysis, then TRIZ; protocols coded with the FBS scheme
728.problem: Assistive devices: window opener, door opener for stroke patients, wheelchair curb climber
728.prompt: Use the assigned concept generation technique to design an assistive device meeting stated requirements within 45 minutes
728.measured: Distribution of function, behavior and structure design issues (FBS coding) overall and by session half
728.method_detail: Protocol analysis of videoed sessions after technique instruction
728.finding: Students using morphological analysis or TRIZ spent less effort on structure and more on expected behavior than with brainstorming, suggesting structured methods encourage more abstract, expert-like thinking.

729.who: 40 engineering participants analysed (randomly assigned to function, interaction, pruned or no-model groups)
729.task: Received a problem statement, requirements and a seed model (or none), then sketched concepts alone; sketches scored for conformance to the model
729.prompt: Generate concepts for a device that folds burritos, meeting stated requirements, using the supplied model as a starting point
729.measured: Functional and other conformance of concept sketches to the supplied model, by treatment group
729.method_detail: Between-subjects with four treatments; 40 participants, 106 sketches
729.finding: Participants given a pruned function model conformed about 40% more in function use than those given a full function model, so level of functional detail affects concept generation.

734.who: 194 survey respondents (clients and consultants of design consultancies), plus 36 interviewees
734.task: Completed questionnaires about completed consulting projects, sampled via five consultancies and via patent records; earlier interviews and a pilot shaped the survey
734.measured: Project outcomes: commercialization and market success, client satisfaction, success dimensions, response bias between samples
734.method_detail: Random project sampling, benchmarking sample (156 responses) and patent-network sample (38 responses)
734.finding: Design consulting outcomes were generally good but varied widely across projects and consultancies, with commercialization and market success comparing favorably to in-house design results.

737.who: Engineers at one engine company (evaluator count not reported)
737.task: Evaluators scored a hypothetical design FMEA, then 38 real design FMEAs under a pooled-scoring method; predictions compared with failures seen two years later
737.problem: Design FMEA of engineering systems (no participant design task)
737.measured: Consistency and correlation of individual vs group risk scores, criticality and RPN prediction accuracy against later test results
737.method_detail: Analysis of scored industrial FMEAs and a long-term accuracy check
737.finding: Individual evaluators' scores correlated poorly with the group and with later failures, suggesting availability bias, so pooled scoring by a large diverse group is recommended.

739.who: 68 working engineers and designers in 13 graduate course teams
739.task: Over a semester, teams observed users, generated concepts and built working prototypes; time sheets, notebook sketches and prototype reports were analysed against final ranking
739.problem: Healthcare and healthy living products (team-defined user need)
739.prompt: Define a user need in the healthcare and healthy living theme through observation, generate concepts and build a working prototype with an $800 budget
739.measured: Amount of information generated (sketches, user groups, problems, concepts), timing of prototyping, team design outcome ranking by evaluators
739.method_detail: Correlational analysis of course data (512 notebook sheets, 721 sketches)
739.finding: Teams generating the most sketches and user groups did not do better; quality over quantity mattered, and starting prototyping early was associated with better outcomes.

741.who: 62 adults recruited from a university and surrounding area (31 per group)
741.task: Viewed cars and coffee carafes as either sketches and silhouettes or simple and realistic renderings while eye-tracked, answering opinion, evaluation and inference questions
741.problem: Cars (Audi TT variants) and coffee carafes as stimuli
741.measured: Preference and styling judgments, objective evaluations, inferences, consistency across representation types, eye gaze patterns
741.method_detail: Between-subjects survey with eye tracking; Taguchi-designed product variations
741.finding: Representation mattered: carafe sketches and car renderings gave consistent preferences, renderings elicited more consistent preferences generally, while inference questions were unaffected by representation.

743.who: 163 online survey respondents recruited via Mechanical Turk
743.task: Viewed four product sketches for three seconds each, described them in free text, then answered questions on material, feel, weight and use
743.problem: Four sketched mechanical products (e.g. hand-held eggbeater)
743.measured: What viewers recalled and inferred (name, function, shape, material, texture, efficiency), preference among drawings
743.method_detail: 20-minute online survey with free-text and multiple-choice items
743.finding: Viewers recalled tangible aspects such as material, shape and function more than an object's name, and preferred more informative drawings over merely attractive ones.

755.who: 72 university students (62 undergraduate, 10 graduate), 70 analysed; 24 per condition
755.task: Generated concepts with near, far or no patent analogies as stimuli, chosen from an LSA-based patent structure
755.problem: Low-cost portable device harvesting human-motion energy for rural communities
755.prompt: Design a low-cost, easy-to-make device for individuals and small households that collects energy from human motion to charge a battery for radios or lights
755.measured: Quality and novelty of concepts (mean and maximum) by analogy distance, validity of patent structure
755.method_detail: Between-subjects near vs far vs control; includes computational patent structuring
755.finding: Near analogies gave higher-quality output than far ones, while far analogies produced less novel best concepts, suggesting a sweet spot for analogical distance.

757.who: 31 senior mechanical engineering students (novices), compared with 31 engineering academics from an earlier study
757.task: Novices generated ideas for 40 minutes in control, fixation-example, or fixation-plus-alternate-representation groups; results compared to the earlier expert data
757.problem: Device to quickly shell peanuts without electricity for West Africa
757.prompt: Design a device to shell large quantities of peanuts quickly, cheaply and without electricity, for use in West African countries
757.measured: Non-redundant ideas per minute, example features reproduced per minute, effect of alternate problem representations
757.method_detail: Replication of an expert study with novices; random assignment to three groups
757.finding: Experts and novices fixated on example features equally, but experts produced more non-redundant ideas and only experts benefited from alternate problem representations.

758.who: Study 1: 30 engineering students (earlier data); Study 2: 16 university students
758.task: Study 1 coded group protocols from a biomimetic task; Study 2 did a card task and concept evaluation with or without a decision matrix
758.problem: Biomimetic wet scrubber redesign (Study 1); concept evaluation (Study 2)
758.prompt: Study 1: use a penguin thermoregulation analogy to improve a pollutant-removing scrubber; Study 2: evaluate a given belief or concept
758.measured: Confirmation and disconfirmation statements in protocols; choices in Wason card task and decision-matrix concept evaluation
758.method_detail: Protocol analysis plus a small controlled experiment
758.finding: Confirmation bias appeared during concept generation, leading designers to discount contradicting facts and fixate, and decision matrices reduced it during concept evaluation.

762.who: 26 engineering students (each used all three methods, 78 trials)
762.task: Dissected a hair dryer, power drill and NERF pistol, one per method, and drew a function tree using top-down, energy-flow or unstructured analysis
762.problem: Functional analysis of dissected products (hair dryer, drill, NERF pistol)
762.prompt: Dissect the product, work out how it functions using the assigned method, and diagram a function tree
762.measured: Number of functions, errors, levels of abstraction, unique subsystems and functions in the function tree
762.method_detail: Within-subject, three methods, after a sophomore course pilot
762.finding: No statistical or practical difference was found among the three functional analysis methods, suggesting formal methods may not help novices more than an unstructured approach.

765.who: 20 professional truck drivers from a driving school, aged 18 to 57
765.task: Rated 40 truck dashboard layouts in both a virtual reality experience and 2D visual images, then compared the two formats; holdout layouts tested model accuracy
765.problem: Truck dashboard control layout (positions and sizes of interface elements)
765.measured: Preference ratings, accuracy of utility models from experiential vs visual conjoint, user confidence and realism comparisons
765.method_detail: Fractional factorial conjoint survey in immersive VR versus visual conjoint
765.finding: VR-based preference ratings were consistent and gave accurate preference models for some users, differed from visual conjoint across the design space, and users judged the experiential format superior.

767.who: 100 mechanical engineering students from three university courses (55, 29, 16)
767.task: Read biology passages found with thesaurus keywords for 'separate' and marked whether each prompted any idea for the design problem
767.problem: Device to remove husk and silk from ears of corn
767.prompt: Judge whether each biology passage gives you any idea for a device that removes husk and silk from corn
767.measured: Number of passages prompting ideas, agreement among participants, passage and keyword characteristics, differences by course
767.method_detail: Online survey of biology corpus sentences containing thesaurus synonyms
767.finding: Participants rarely agreed on which passages gave ideas, passages were not chosen at random, and unhelpful passages were usually too technical or lacked biological system information.

768.who: 141 online participants across three studies (31, 30 and 80, no overlap)
768.task: Matched abstracted 3D car models to photos (Study I), rated emotional attributes of abstract and full car models (Studies II and III) in online surveys
768.problem: Car form (7 car models, 36 geometric abstractions)
768.measured: Brand recognition accuracy by abstraction level, ratings on 6 emotional attributes, correlation between responses to abstractions and full models
768.method_detail: Three online studies with Mechanical Turk participants plus a computational shape abstraction method
768.finding: Emotional responses to coarse debranded car abstractions strongly matched responses to final models, so aesthetic assessment can happen early, and some emotional attributes depend more on brand than shape.

769.who: 10 senior and master's mechanical engineering students in 5 pairs
769.task: Pairs collaboratively designed with pencil and paper on video, then each retrospectively explained their thinking while watching the video; coded for collaborative stimulation and novelty
769.problem: Secure storage for skateboards on campus
769.prompt: Develop a device that securely stores skateboards so students stop stacking them against classroom walls
769.measured: Types of collaborative stimulation (prompting, seeding, clarifying, correcting), novelty score of each concept
769.method_detail: Retrospective protocol analysis of five videoed sessions
769.finding: Concepts produced through seeding and correcting stimulation were more novel than concepts made without collaborative stimulation.

771.task: Spent 20 minutes visually inspecting and benchmarking, or dissecting, a milk frother, then generated ideas for a new design
771.prompt: Develop concepts for a new, innovative product that froths milk quickly and needs minimal instruction, covering form and function
771.measured: Novelty, variety, quality and quantity of ideas
771.method_detail: Between-subjects, visual inspection vs product dissection, ANOVA
771.finding: Students who dissected the frother produced more novel but lower-quality ideas than those who only inspected it.

772.who: 36 mechanical engineering students (17 in group A, 19 in group B)
772.task: Designed two products for 45 minutes each, once without and once with an inclusive-design diagram scheme, in counterbalanced order
772.problem: Inclusive food processor and inclusive refrigerator
772.prompt: Generate concepts for a food processor or refrigerator usable by people of all abilities, with the diagram and design rules in the experimental run
772.measured: Idea quality (4-point scale), inclusivity (new 4-point metric, inter-rater reliability), self-reported usefulness of the scheme
772.finding: The inclusive design representation scheme helped designers produce more inclusive ideas only to a limited extent, and effects differed between the two products.

773.who: 293 randomly selected participants from over 2000 (designers, engineers and students, ages 15-64)
773.task: Wrote as many alternative uses for a paperclip as they could in three minutes on an index card; responses coded by keyword and rarity
773.problem: Alternative uses for a paperclip (no design object)
773.prompt: List as many alternative uses for a paperclip as you can think of in three minutes
773.measured: Number of responses, novelty as infrequency of responses across the pool, novelty by response order
773.method_detail: Large-sample analysis of Alternative Uses Test responses
773.finding: People who gave more responses had more novel ones, later responses were more novel, and about nine ideas were listed on average before highly novel ones appeared.

782.task: Designed a cardboard tower in two rounds; one group built one first-round prototype, the other up to five
782.problem: Free-standing cardboard tower from one A4 sheet
782.prompt: Build the tallest free-standing structure possible from one A4 sheet of corrugated cardboard
782.measured: Height of preliminary and final prototypes, improvement between them, perceived difficulty and time pressure, satisfaction (surveys)
782.finding: Students who built five prototypes early felt more time pressure and less satisfied with early prototypes but improved significantly more between first and final prototype.

783.who: 67 mid-career professional graduate students in teams of 4 to 7
783.task: Over a semester-long course, students logged minutes per activity category every two weeks while building a proof-of-concept prototype; timing was correlated with team outcome
783.problem: Healthcare and healthy living proof-of-concept prototypes
783.prompt: Create a functioning proof-of-concept prototype in the healthcare and healthy living theme within an $800 budget
783.measured: Timing and total time of prototyping, benchmarking, user interaction and other activities (timesheets), design outcome from reviewer scores
783.method_detail: Correlational analysis of timesheets from a graduate design course
783.finding: Prototyping early, or repeating benchmarking and user interaction later, correlated with better design outcomes, whereas total time spent on these activities did not.

784.who: 83 adults from a university (72 with usable data)
784.task: Viewed car and electric bicycle images with varied feature designs and feature size changes on an eye tracker, rating preference and noticing size changes
784.problem: Cars and electric bicycles as visual stimuli
784.measured: Feature importance in preference, gaze data (fixation time, percentage time, count, time to first fixation), noticeability of size changes
784.method_detail: Eye-tracking survey with logistic models of gaze data
784.finding: Gaze measures were significantly correlated with feature importance, differed between noticeable and unnoticeable size changes, and logistic models of gaze data predicted both.

785.who: 4 expert product designers with at least 10 years of experience (a fifth was excluded)
785.task: Spent two hours arranging 45 patent cards on a wall into a structure for a design problem, then critiqued the algorithm's patent structure
785.problem: Device to collect energy from human motion for rural communities
785.prompt: Design a low-cost device for individuals and households in developing regions that harvests human-motion energy into a rechargeable battery
785.measured: Similarity of expert patent structures to the algorithm's structure, expert ratings and comments on cluster sensibility and distance from the problem
785.method_detail: Quantitative structure comparison plus qualitative expert feedback
785.finding: The computer-generated patent structure was sensible to experts and gave them common ground, while retaining some surprising groupings, supporting it as a basis for a design-by-analogy tool.

786.who: 4 graduate students (think-aloud) plus about 35 in each of 3 classes
786.task: Four students thought aloud on draft reasoning tests; class groups then took 40-minute test variants and gave feedback
786.problem: No design problem (reasoning test problems for deductive, inductive, analogical, abductive skills)
786.measured: Match between solution strategies and intended skills, correlations among problems, average performance, difficulty and clarity feedback, validity and reliability
786.method_detail: Think-aloud protocol study plus classroom test trials to revise a test
786.finding: Protocol and trial results were used to revise the alpha qualitative reasoning test into a beta version with problems matching intended skills and graded difficulty.

787.who: 40 participants: 34 novice users and 6 sound experts
787.task: Listened to 17 synthesized electric vehicle exterior sounds, gave word associations and rated each on pleasantness and appropriateness scales
787.problem: Artificial exterior sounds for electric vehicles
787.measured: Words used to describe sounds, ratings of pleasantness and appropriateness (ANOVA, conjoint analysis), opinion on adding sounds
787.method_detail: Word association plus semantic-scale rating experiment comparing novices and experts
787.finding: Novices described sounds by character and experts by composition, opinions varied widely between individuals, and most thought adding sound was needed, with novices favoring a combustion-engine-like sound.

788.who: 15 engineering students and researchers, mostly without design work experience
788.task: Sketched a teaching podium on a graphics tablet, rated mental effort, then explained their thinking in an interview
788.prompt: Design a movable, easily installed teaching podium for general classrooms seating at least 100 students, showing every step with sketches
788.measured: Kolmogorov complexity of design moves, design outcome quality, mental effort (RSME), derived cognitive efficiency
788.method_detail: Sketch and verbal protocol analysis with an information-theoretic measure
788.finding: Higher Kolmogorov complexity of designers' cognitive processes was negatively related to cognitive efficiency, meaning more cognitive actions went with lower efficiency.

789.who: 20 participants in a case study (people ranking aircraft cabin profiles)
789.task: Made 26 judgments of aircraft cabin interior design profiles; their rankings were compared with rankings from a nested utility copula model and an additive model
789.problem: Aircraft cabin interior design (27 attribute-level profiles)
789.measured: Kendall rank correlation between participant rankings and model-predicted rankings of cabin profiles
789.method_detail: Modeling method (nested utility copulas) demonstrated with a small participant survey
789.finding: The nested utility copula model produced rankings that agreed more with participants' own rankings than the additive independence model did, showing promise for aggregating user experience partworths.

790.who: 23 experienced designers and design managers from varied industries
790.task: Took part in 2-3 hour semi-structured interviews using an 87-question questionnaire about their company's design process and a reference project
790.measured: Design process stages and activities across industries, company and project context, fit of a literature-based transdisciplinary process framework
790.method_detail: Qualitative analysis at three levels: across organizations, within organizations, within one project
790.finding: Despite very different industries, products and backgrounds, the design processes shared common creative, iterative and evaluative stages, which could support collaboration across disciplines.

792.who: 40 engineering students (mostly senior mechanical) in 20 teams of two
792.task: Control teams watched videos while experimental teams applied a prototyping strategy method, then all built a coin-launching device from a kit
792.problem: Device to move a coin to a floor target without human energy at release
792.prompt: Build a prototype that moves a quarter from behind a line to a target on the floor, using the supplied materials, without human energy at release
792.measured: Prototype performance (coin reaching the target), self-assessed effectiveness, sufficient time and budget (Likert items)
792.method_detail: Two groups of ten teams; follow-up to an earlier classroom pre/post study
792.finding: All ten teams using the prototyping strategy method hit the target versus seven of nine control teams, though participants' self-rated effectiveness did not differ.

793.task: Completed a dissection activity varied by product, number of products, medium and visual representation, then sketched milk-frother ideas for 20 minutes and answered interview questions
793.prompt: Develop concepts for a new, innovative product that froths milk quickly and is usable with minimal instruction, covering form and function
793.measured: Novelty and variety of concepts, interview feedback on the dissection activity
793.method_detail: 2x2x2x2 factorial with ANOVA plus semi-structured interviews; very small sample
793.finding: Dissection structure, medium and number of products affected concept variety, while analogical distance and number of products affected novelty.

794.who: 194 practitioners (clients and consultants) surveyed about outsourced design projects
794.task: Answered an 8-page mailed questionnaire about a specific outsourced design project, rating success on measures from a seven-dimension typology; earlier interviews informed the typology
794.measured: Importance and ratings of success measures (client satisfaction, working relationship, project value, ROI, development problems), correlations among measures
794.method_detail: Benchmarking sample (82 clients, 74 consultants) and patent-network client sample (38)
794.finding: Practitioners valued working relationship quality, project value and client satisfaction over measures stressed in research, and client satisfaction looks like a promising summary measure of success.

800.who: 16 wheelchair users across three field trials (3, 5 and 8)
800.task: Used prototype lever-propelled wheelchair versions in field trials in East Africa, Guatemala and India, rated them against their own chairs, and some completed biomechanical tests
800.problem: Low-cost all-terrain lever-propelled wheelchair for developing countries
800.measured: Survey ratings (1-5) by terrain, requested design changes, speed, efficiency and peak propulsion force against conventional wheelchairs
800.method_detail: Three iterative user trials with stakeholder feedback between versions
800.finding: Stakeholder feedback drove a lighter, narrower, lower chair whose ratings improved each trial, and it was faster, more efficient and produced higher push force than conventional wheelchairs.

801.who: 4 professional designers of products for emerging markets, plus four product case studies
801.task: Designers were interviewed about practice; findings and literature formed a framework tested against case studies of phones, solar lamps, drip irrigation and cookstoves
801.problem: No design problem (existing products for emerging markets)
801.measured: Design strategies and guidelines for micro-enterprise products, product success in market, fit to the framework versus design-for-cost and business-opportunity strategies
801.method_detail: Literature review, 4 designer interviews and 4 cases following Yin's case method
801.finding: Successful emerging-market products served micro-entrepreneurs, leading to three guidelines: design for the entrepreneur's business plan, build reliable brand identity, and consider multi-functionality.

802.who: 22 adult subjects (11 per condition), more than half with a master's or doctorate
802.task: Chose toasters to consider and buy with or without sustainability-triggering features, emailed a purchasing agent, answered interview questions
802.problem: Bread toaster prototypes with sustainability-triggering features
802.measured: Consideration and purchase of toasters, mentions of sustainability in emails and information requests (coded), ratings and rankings
802.method_detail: Test vs control purchase experiment with coded qualitative data
802.finding: Exposure to sustainability-triggering features significantly increased mentions of sustainability as a purchase criterion, though consideration and purchase counts did not differ significantly.

804.who: 1200 US online participants recruited via Mechanical Turk
804.task: Trained on one sustainability aspect, then placed six French press products on a collage by sustainability and likeability and labeled them with provided features
804.measured: Placement on sustainability and likeability axes, selection of features perceived as sustainable, correlation between sustainability and liking
804.method_detail: Online collage activity, three versions (social, environmental, economic)
804.finding: Features perceived as sustainable were chosen more often for products placed high on sustainability, showing these features resonate with customers, while sustainability and liking were only weakly correlated.

805.who: DALL-E vs 8 novice designers; 12 experts rated outputs
805.task: DALL-E generated images from six text descriptions; novices designed for the same texts; experts rated creativity
805.problem: Six graphic or product design tasks from text descriptions (e.g. a t-shirt with a word on it)
805.prompt: Produce a design that matches each given textual description, using any familiar software
805.measured: Expert-rated creativity (novelty, feasibility, completeness) and exploratory creativity of text and images, machine vs human
805.method_detail: AI model compared with novice designers, expert online ratings
805.finding: Humans scored higher on overall creativity, while the machine scored higher on exploratory creativity, and humans' textual exploratory creativity exceeded their imagery.

808.who: 74 online workers recruited via Mechanical Turk
808.task: Washed simulated hands for 20 seconds at a web sink in three randomly ordered runs with different sink drain rates, adjusting water pressure
808.problem: Sink handwashing simulation with reduced waste outflow
808.prompt: Wash your hands at the simulated sink for 20 seconds to remove germs
808.measured: Water consumed, inflow rate settings, self-reported daily pro-environmental behavior
808.method_detail: Online within-subject simulation after a pilot with 35 students
808.finding: Participants used about 14% less water when slow drainage made the sink fill quickly, regardless of self-reported pro-environmental habits.

810.who: 19 novice mechanical engineering undergraduates (7 men, 12 women) in a remote course
810.task: Kept design notebooks and prototype learning logs during a 5-week user-centered project; sketches scored with a rubric
810.problem: Open-ended 5-week user-centered design project (topic not reported)
810.measured: Sketch quantity and quality (line smoothness, proportion, understandability), prototype reflections, design project outcome scores
810.method_detail: Correlational analysis of course sketches and prototype logs
810.finding: More sketches linked to better design outcomes, sketch quality alone did not, and novices' prototype reflections rarely focused consistently on users.

811.who: 10 participants: 4 design-team members and students, then 6 students
811.task: Built data representations in a 90-minute session; then two teams explored charging data with a physical toolkit or printed charts
811.problem: Making sense of quantitative data (electric vehicle charging data) for creative insight
811.prompt: Explore the given data set, in the toolkit or visualization condition, and generate insights
811.measured: Insights generated, engagement and understanding, pleasantness of process, reflection moments, interview feedback
811.method_detail: Two small creative sessions with observation and evaluation interviews; follow-up compared toolkit to visualization
811.finding: The physicalization toolkit gave more engaging, easily understood data exploration for non-experts and stimulated creative insights, with a mix of physicalization and visualization seeming most practical.

812.who: 3 independent raters scoring 3095 speculative technologies from a fiction database (no participants)
812.task: Raters judged with rubrics whether each technology from speculative fiction was later realized and when; agreement between raters was computed
812.problem: No design problem (speculative technologies in fiction)
812.measured: Realization status of technologies, time from speculation to realization, inter-rater agreement (Fleiss kappa)
812.method_detail: Database analysis with human raters; feasibility study of a rating method
812.finding: About 45% of 3095 speculated technologies were rated realized by at least one rater, taking roughly 45 years on average, with moderate rater agreement (kappa 0.57).

813.who: 42 mechanical engineering students (14 per tool group)
813.task: Sketched concepts for five minutes using pen, pencil or a tablet in response to an open prompt; sketches scored for quantity, quality, understandability and novelty
813.problem: Ways to experience photos in the home
813.prompt: Imagine working at a design firm hired by a client to develop concepts for ways to experience photos in the home
813.measured: Sketch quantity, quality (smoothness, proportion), understandability, concept novelty, sketching style, by tool and gender
813.method_detail: Between-subjects tool conditions after a pre-survey on sketching experience
813.finding: Sketch quantity did not differ by tool, but pencil drawings had higher quality than tablet and pen drawings, and tablet use was not linked to concept novelty.

815.who: Engineers at one turbomachinery company (number studied not reported)
815.task: Lead author observed 70 meetings and ran 52 interviews over two years, coded with grounded theory for object use
815.problem: No design problem (complex turbomachinery product development)
815.measured: Roles of objects in cross-boundary collaboration, outcomes such as co-discovery of risks and co-design of solutions
815.method_detail: 24-month focused ethnography with interviews and inductive coding
815.finding: Objects served three roles in cross-functional work: routinizing interaction, translating information, and motivating joint negotiation or discovery, the latter two leading to co-discovery and co-design.

816.who: 91 participants across three studies: 30 psychology students, 31 engineering students, 30 online workers
816.task: Did Stroop or finger-tapping conflict tasks at set conflict levels, then the Alternative Uses Test; run in person and online
816.prompt: List alternative uses for an object after completing the conflict-processing task
816.measured: Creative performance on the Alternative Uses Test by conflict level, differences in study environment, monitoring, instructions and participants
816.method_detail: Comparison of one in-person and two online iterations
816.finding: The online follow-ups did not replicate the in-person benefit of conflict processing, showing similar but non-significant trends, so in-person studies need careful adaptation for online use.

817.who: 42 hardware product design professionals (survey), 12 of whom were also interviewed
817.task: Online survey: grouped 13 sustainable design strategies by perceived control and impact, explained choices and suggested tool features; some then did 20-30 minute follow-up interviews
817.problem: No design problem (sustainable hardware product design practice)
817.measured: Perceived control and perceived impact over sustainability strategies, opportunity areas, desired tool functions
817.method_detail: Qualtrics survey (n=42) plus follow-up interviews (n=12), qualitative coding
817.finding: Designers feel least control and see little impact in manufacturing-related areas but high control and impact in practice and business-model areas, and want tools for transparency, prediction and knowledge sharing.

819.task: Trained a CNN plus hierarchy-based graph convolutional network on seen mechanical component categories and tested recognition of unseen categories against baseline models
819.measured: Top-k accuracy (k=1 to 10) for unseen categories, alone and combined with seen categories
819.method_detail: Benchmark comparison with Devise, ConSE and GCNZ baselines
819.finding: The proposed visual reasoning model beat the baselines at labeling unseen mechanical components, for example 16.5% top-1 accuracy on unseen categories versus 6.3% for the best baseline.

822.who: 107 first-year undergraduate students (35 baseline, 37 linking-statement, 35 negative-feature condition)
822.task: Received a design brief with example images, with or without instructions to use word-pair analogies, then sketched three ideas in 15 minutes
822.problem: Mobility device for low-income people with physical disabilities
822.prompt: Develop a device that improves mobility for low-income people with physical disabilities, drawing inspiration from the examples given
822.measured: Novelty and usefulness of 315 sketches rated by three expert judges (1-5 scales)
822.method_detail: Between-subjects, random assignment to three brief types, in an intro design course
822.finding: Briefs asking for textual analogies produced more novel ideas, while adding a step to name negative features of examples yielded more useful but less novel ideas.

823.who: Participants in a one-hour pilot session (number not reported)
823.task: Sketched a reconfigurable robot subsystem for 20 minutes without, then 20 minutes with, 44 mechanism design cards; gave feedback
823.problem: Shape-changing and locomotion units of a reconfigurable pavement-sweeping robot
823.prompt: Design the shape-changing and locomotion units for a reconfigurable pavement cleaning robot
823.measured: Concept quality (3-point feasibility and difficulty scale), concept novelty (share of dissimilar concepts), participant feedback on the cards
823.method_detail: Small within-subject pilot comparing sketches before and after using design cards
823.finding: Concepts made with the design cards were rated significantly higher in quality and novelty than those made without them.

825.who: 28 engineering students and research engineers (14 novice, 14 experienced in aerial robots)
825.task: After a one-hour lecture on design principles, generated ideas then evolved one for a familiar and a novel problem, using a principle list
825.problem: Aerial robots for sewer inspection (familiar) and tree resistograph measurement (novel)
825.prompt: Design a compact long-endurance aerial robot to inspect a sewer tunnel network, then a stable aerial robot to take resistograph tree-health measurements at height
825.measured: Originality of over 220 concepts (DTOAD 5-point scale), idea quantity, idea evolution
825.method_detail: Half-day workshop; comparison by expertise, problem novelty and idea evolution; no control without principles
825.finding: Originality was higher for the novel problem and for evolved ideas, while expertise level made no significant difference to idea quantity or originality.

826.task: After a TRIZ workshop, followed the TRIZ steps with no time limit on one design task while prefrontal brain activity was recorded
826.problem: Kitchen measuring tool for blind users
826.prompt: Use TRIZ to develop a conceptual solution for a kitchen measuring tool for blind people
826.measured: Prefrontal cortex activation (fNIRS) in each TRIZ step, by left, right and medial regions
826.method_detail: Neuroimaging (fNIRS) of one-group design task; comparison across TRIZ steps
826.finding: Left prefrontal activation was higher when defining the problem, right prefrontal during searching, and medial prefrontal during solution generation.

827.who: 4 undergraduate mechanical engineering students from a product design course
827.task: Built functional parts by mating 3D-scanned-style scrap casting pieces (sprues, gates, miscast parts) in Meshmixer under simple rules, then commented on their strategies
827.problem: Functional parts assembled from scrap foundry pieces
827.prompt: Design a functional part by combining scrap metal pieces from a foundry, mating them with enough contact area to weld and without modifying them
827.measured: Functional parts produced, strategies and rules used, participant comments, link between geometric variety of scrap and variety of functions
827.method_detail: Exploratory case study; scrap models simulated in CAD because foundry access was limited
827.finding: Students developed shared heuristics such as starting from the part with most mounting points, and scrap sets with greater geometric difference gave more varied functions.

830.who: 378 engineering students and/or working engineers online (49 pilot, 329 full study)
830.task: Did a gratitude, positive-emotion or neutral induction, then 3-5 minutes on an uses-for-a-spoon task and 15 minutes repurposing a wind-turbine blade
830.problem: Repurposing retired wind-turbine blades (plus alternate uses of a spoon)
830.prompt: Generate creative reuse concepts for a given section of a retired wind-turbine blade, avoiding common unsafe ideas
830.measured: Creativity of Alternate Uses Task and blade-repurposing responses scored by two blind raters, manipulation check, prosocial motivation
830.method_detail: Pre-registered online between-subjects study via Prolific, pilot plus full sample
830.finding: Gratitude did not change Alternate Uses Task scores in either sample, and only the pilot induction worked, so the blade-repurposing results give limited, tentative support for gratitude aiding creativity.

831.who: GPT-3 fine-tuned on 221 AskNature examples (no human participants); 10 engineers rated its concepts
831.task: Fine-tuned GPT-3 generators (three types) produced 50 bio-inspired concepts each for lightweight flying cars; machine classifiers screened them and the team rated selected concepts
831.problem: Lightweight flying car concepts inspired by nature
831.prompt: Input of application (flying car), benefit (lightweight) and a challenge statement about weight of a dual air-ground vehicle
831.measured: Share of concepts passing machine problem-solution and nature-solution checks, engineers' feasibility and novelty ratings (1-5)
831.method_detail: Case study of a government-funded project; 10 engineers rated chosen concepts
831.finding: The fine-tuned models produced readable bio-inspired concepts, with 40-86% passing machine checks depending on generator type, and one concept was chosen for embodiment design.

832.who: 28 fourth-year undergraduate engineering students (38 consented, 10 excluded as incomplete)
832.task: Online, did standard and scaled uses-for-objects tasks (3 min each), then repurposed wind-turbine blade sections (20 min), counterbalanced
832.prompt: Find creative reuses for hollow and solid sections of a retired wind-turbine blade, shown with human-scale figures
832.measured: Fluency and flexibility of uses, share of correctly scaled blade-reuse concepts
832.method_detail: Within-subject, counterbalanced order, online via Qualtrics and Zoom
832.finding: The scaled uses task lowered idea fluency and flexibility but significantly raised the number of correctly scaled blade-reuse concepts that followed.

833.who: 15 designers: 7 students and 8 industry professionals, all with 1+ year of CAD experience
833.task: Searched for inspirational 3D parts on a keyword, part and workspace search platform while thinking aloud (under 30 min), then was interviewed
833.prompt: Use the multi-modal search tool to find parts that inspire solutions for a multi-compartment disposal unit for household waste
833.measured: Search activities, behaviors (new vs continued search, expected vs unexpected result, accept vs reject) and pathways, compared by expertise and text vs non-text input
833.method_detail: Think-aloud protocol with screen recordings; Mann-Whitney comparisons of professionals and students
833.finding: Professionals and students used search types similarly, mostly keywords, but professionals found more results as expected and accepted more, while students ran more consecutive searches and met more unexpected results.

836.who: 155 engineering students in 33 teams at one Danish university, across three course sessions
836.task: Teams wrote a prototyping plan with minimal guidance, learned the Prototyping Planner, wrote a second plan with it, then compared both plans
836.problem: Teams' own product concepts (open topic, Covid-19 theme, or speakerphone)
836.prompt: Make a plan for prototyping and testing the product concept your team is developing in the course
836.measured: Questions answered in plans, clarity of testing purpose and plan structure (deductive coding), plan length, students' self-evaluation of supported vs unsupported plans
836.method_detail: Within-team before/after comparison in three course sessions (2019-2021), coded plans plus questionnaire
836.finding: With the Prototyping Planner every team chose a clear narrow purpose and planned execution, plan length rose 12%, and 81% of students judged supported plans better.

838.who: 4 high school engineering teachers in a 6-week professional learning program
838.task: Learned Structure-Function-Mechanism after a 20-minute training and did biological-system investigations and a bio-inspired design project; assignments, discussions and a focus group were analyzed
838.problem: Bio-inspired design projects (found-object and nature-walk investigations, thermal-regulation function)
838.prompt: Investigate a biological system, sketch and annotate how its features give rise to a function, and use it for a bio-inspired design
838.measured: Teachers' use of structure, function and mechanism categories in assignments and discussion; structural bias and fixation
838.method_detail: Remote summer professional learning in 2020; coding of assignments and video calls
838.finding: Teachers grasped structure easily but found the line between mechanism and function subjective in complex biological systems, and showed structural bias and fixation like novices.

839.who: 156 first-year mechanical engineering students at two North American universities
839.task: Grouped the elements of three products into subsystems from a function graph, component graph or function structure, with 45 minutes for the packet
839.problem: Clustering elements of a mixer, a hair dryer and a toilet into subsystems
839.prompt: As manager of a design team troubleshooting underperforming products, cluster each product's elements into subsystems, each element in one cluster only
839.measured: Number and content of clusters, how often element pairs were grouped, in relation to connective, physical and semantic distance
839.method_detail: Mixed between- and within-subjects design, 3 representation styles by 3 products
839.finding: Elements were more likely to be clustered when directly connected or physically close on the page, while semantic distance showed unclear effects, so layout shapes system understanding.

840.who: 28 undergraduate and graduate students from engineering, architecture, liberal arts and sciences (14 per group)
840.task: Brainstormed on two themes by writing lists or building mind-maps (about 20 min), then wrote design problem descriptions and needs, over Zoom
840.problem: Design opportunity statements for pollution and underwater camping
840.prompt: Explore the given theme and write design problem descriptions and needs statements for new products
840.measured: Design problem statement quality on a 4-point rubric (gap, needs, comprehensiveness, solution neutrality, creative scope), exploration behavior, user feedback
840.method_detail: Between-subjects (free writing vs mind-mapping), remote sessions with interviews
840.finding: Mind-mapping users explored problems more systematically and produced statements with a wider range of needs and more scope for creative outcomes than free writers.

841.who: 36 first-year-heavy undergraduate engineering students (random sample from an entry graphics course; 2 semesters)
841.task: Generated ideas for 45 minutes, then did sketching skill tasks and a self-efficacy survey; one group was told sketching would be evaluated
841.problem: Peanut sheller or corn shucker device
841.prompt: Design a device to shell many peanuts quickly without electrical outlets, or to remove husk and silk from lots of corn quickly with little kernel damage
841.measured: Idea quantity (non-redundant ideas by functional basis), sketch quality, drawing self-efficacy
841.method_detail: Two independent groups from different semesters (informed vs blind to sketch evaluation); preliminary analysis of first data collection
841.finding: Sketch quality and idea quantity were largely independent, and telling students their sketching would be evaluated had a negligible effect on idea generation productivity.

842.who: 21 mechanical engineering students analyzed (23 volunteered at UC Berkeley, 2 excluded for data errors)
842.task: Remotely searched a 3D-part platform by keyword, then part, then workspace (30 min total), saving 3+ inspiring parts each time, then rated features
842.prompt: Use the platform to search for and save 3D parts that inspire solutions to a multi-compartment disposal unit for household waste
842.measured: Search frequency, engagement with retrieved parts, coverage of the part dataset, strategies (open-ended), Likert ratings of feature usefulness and exploration breadth
842.method_detail: Fixed-order within-subject tasks using a new deep-learning search tool; interaction log analysis
842.finding: Search modality changed behavior, including search frequency, how people engaged with retrieved parts and how widely they covered the part space, with keyword search covering the most.

843.who: 23 graduate student new-product-development teams (107 members, summed from team sizes of 4 or 5)
843.task: Team emails over a semester were analyzed with semantic and social network analysis, then compared with team conflict from a survey
843.problem: Semester-long new product development projects (team-chosen user need and prototype)
843.measured: Content-based email interaction networks, four interaction patterns, team conflict level from feedback and peer-evaluation survey
843.method_detail: Archival email data from two semesters of a graduate NPD course; computational pattern analysis plus survey-based conflict measure
843.finding: Four network interaction patterns (central member, subgroup and aloof member, isolate member, pendant) identified high versus low-to-medium conflict teams with high accuracy.

844.who: 68 crowd participants (42 undergraduates, 16 graduate students, 10 others), after removing 1 of 69
844.task: Judged 40 triplets (which of two products is functionally closer to a third) using short purpose or detailed how-it-works descriptions
844.problem: No design problem (similarity of 20 consumer products)
844.prompt: Judge which product is more similar in function, not form, using either its overall purpose or how it works
844.measured: Human triplet similarity judgments at two abstraction levels, 2D embedding, agreement with six computed similarity measures on functional models
844.method_detail: Crowdsourced human ratings (2720 triplets) compared with computational measures of function models
844.finding: Cosine similarity matched human views of highly similar products at the detailed level, while network-based measures fit better at the purpose level, and existing measures missed the fuzzy similar versus somewhat similar line.

845.who: 100 mechanical engineering undergraduate and graduate students (50 per condition)
845.task: Over 30 truss problems picked a best next action, saw an AI suggestion, accepted or overrode it, got feedback, rated confidence
845.problem: Truss design actions to maximize strength-to-weight ratio
845.prompt: Pick the best next action on a given truss state, with an AI teammate suggesting an action each time
845.measured: Self-reported confidence in AI and in self per problem, acceptance of AI suggestions, modeled effect of experiences on confidence
845.method_detail: Online between-subjects: AI accuracy switched from 80% to 20% or from 20% to 80% after problem 20; confidence model fit to data
845.finding: Confidence in the AI dropped under poor but not good performance, self-confidence fell whenever accuracy changed, and the two confidences pushed acceptance of AI suggestions in opposite directions.

846.who: Simulated agents, plus 25 teams of 4 mechanical engineering graduate students surveyed (100 people)
846.task: Students completed team surveys during a semester-long company task; findings tailored a simulation of virtual vs face-to-face teams
846.problem: Semester-long company-set design task (students); simulated 2D solution landscape with 5 peaks (model)
846.measured: Self-efficacy, perceived influencers and degree of influence, trust, familiarity, communication, conflict resolution, task cohesion; simulated design outcome quality, exploration and solution variety
846.method_detail: MILANO agent-based model calibrated with questionnaire data from human teams (Mann-Whitney comparisons)
846.finding: Virtual teams showed higher self-efficacy and perceived influence, and simulations gave less exploration and more uniform member contribution than face-to-face, with outcomes depending on influencers and task complexity.

847.task: Held 30-minute video interviews on driving; users marked thoughts and feelings, designers guessed them for 10 clips; faces analyzed automatically
847.problem: User interviews about driving in difficult-vision conditions (for a driving-related product)
847.prompt: Semi-structured interviews on driving history, habits and hypothetical situations such as driving in heavy rain with poor visibility
847.measured: Facial expression mimicry and synchrony between user and designer, empathic accuracy of thoughts and emotional tone, user-reported tone
847.method_detail: Videotaped Zoom interviews with empathic accuracy task and facial expression recognition
847.finding: Users and designers mimicked each other's facial expressions, but users' faces did not match their stated tone and mimicry did not predict designers' understanding of users' thoughts.

849.who: 13 designers studying or working in Finland (8 women, 5 men)
849.task: Watched one 30-minute recorded driver interview, inferred the user's thoughts and emotional tone at marked moments, then had 15 minutes to write user need statements
849.problem: Identifying needs of a driver in low-visibility and crowded situations
849.prompt: Write user needs, in a set format, based on the interview video
849.measured: Empathic accuracy of mental contents and emotional tone, need quality (importance, satisfaction with current solutions), need depth and latency
849.method_detail: Single standard stimulus video; correlations between empathy scores and need scores; four raters
849.finding: Accuracy in reading emotional tone correlated with finding important unmet needs, but accuracy about users' thoughts did not, and need depth and latency were unrelated to empathy.

850.who: 14 three-person teams (42 students and practitioners) from the Stanford community, aged 20-54
850.task: Teams developed a fictitious device from a drawing for 30 minutes, getting a model at minute five; recordings were coded for blocking
850.prompt: Further develop the device shown in the engineering drawing, using the prototype model given after five minutes
850.measured: 104 blocks coded as adaptive, innovative or neither, subsequent idea generation, block sequence length and outcome
850.method_detail: Secondary analysis of video and transcripts with Interaction Dynamics Notation; two coders plus tiebreaker
850.finding: Blocks could be reliably coded as adaptive or innovative and sometimes led to new ideas, but neither style produced ideas more efficiently, and deflected blocks led to ideas most often.

851.who: 105 mechanical engineering students in 21 five-person teams (10 interacting, 11 nominal)
851.task: Online for 65 minutes, five-person teams built drone fleets and delivery plans for profit, facing a mid-session constraint shock
851.problem: Drone fleet design and delivery path planning
851.prompt: Within a budget, design drones and delivery routes to maximize profit, adapting to a hangar wall and no-flight area added midway
851.measured: Team profit, communication patterns, problem-solving actions, questionnaires on cognitive and workload burden
851.method_detail: Between-subjects: interacting vs nominal sub-teams, using the HyForm platform
851.finding: Nominal sub-structured teams earned more than interacting ones and communicated less, but their managers carried heavier cognitive and workload burden.

852.who: 42 second-year engineering students in 11 remote design teams
852.task: Worked remotely 14 weeks on a team project and posted biweekly reflections and a final essay, coded with grounded theory
852.problem: Self-chosen projects to help people stay healthy during the coronavirus pandemic
852.prompt: Design a way to help people stay healthy physically and/or mentally during the pandemic, with mechanical parts, basic analysis, and a CAD model
852.measured: Challenges, strategies and emotions (positive or negative) reported in reflections, remote vs non-remote challenges
852.method_detail: One course in fall 2020; grounded-theory coding of biweekly and final reflections
852.finding: Few challenges were purely remote after the first four weeks; remote format mostly aggravated existing team problems, while content comprehension was a common difficulty.

853.who: 98 first- and third-year engineering design students (re-analysis of an earlier study)
853.task: Took personality and creativity-preference surveys, generated ideas for 20 minutes, then anonymously marked teammates' ideas as consider or not
853.problem: UTI test strip tool, greenhouse grid tool, or pedestrian distraction accident reduction (three prompts)
853.prompt: Develop concepts for a new product addressing the assigned goal, for example reducing campus pedestrian accidents caused by mobile device distraction
853.measured: Hits, misses, false alarms and correct rejections of radical ideas, linked to Big Five personality, risk tolerance and motivation, idea novelty and goodness
853.method_detail: Secondary analysis of 2252 idea evaluations from a prior in-class study; regression on individual attributes
853.finding: Lower risk tolerance raised hits, higher neuroticism and motivation raised missed good ideas, and higher risk tolerance with lower motivation raised selection of weak radical ideas.

854.who: 20 undergraduate engineering students with 1+ year CAD experience (University of Toronto)
854.task: Online, did a solo baseline, then two 30-minute rounds adding mates to CAD parts in random teams of 1 to 4; surveyed after
854.problem: CAD assembly of low, medium and high complexity models
854.prompt: Add mates to pre-modeled parts to complete assemblies, starting with the least complex and ending with the most complex
854.measured: Productivity (mates added), audio communication, workflow and task allocation, survey-reported challenges
854.method_detail: Team size 1-4 (two teams per size per round) with multimodal analysis of audio, activity logs and surveys
854.finding: Teams finished assemblies in less calendar time than single users but used more person-hours because of coordination costs, and pairs showed an assembly bonus effect.

855.who: 1,254 people in 101 virtual robot-design competition teams (FIRST Robotics, typically high schoolers)
855.task: Teams spent 41 days designing a robot in the Onshape multi-user CAD platform; backend action logs and judges' scores were analyzed
855.problem: Robot design for real-world rescue problems (Robots to the Rescue 2020)
855.measured: Team size, CAD actions, synchronous collaboration occurrences, time commitment, judged design score (1-5 rubric criteria)
855.method_detail: Secondary analysis of competition logs with regression and mediation; teams of 4 to 32
855.finding: Larger teams scored higher and did more CAD actions, while more frequent synchronous collaboration, controlling for team size, went with worse scores.

856.who: 13 designers and 59 master's engineering students, plus one driver as target
856.task: Watched a driver interview, then guessed the driver's thoughts and feelings at paused moments in a shortened clip set, rating tone
856.problem: Understanding a driver's needs (road hazard detection device context)
856.prompt: Infer what the driver was thinking or feeling at each marked moment of the interview
856.measured: Empathic accuracy scores (rater similarity), internal consistency, variance, correlation of reduced entry sets with the full measure
856.method_detail: Measure-validation study; 10 random entries vs 5 design-related plus 5 random entries, online
856.finding: A 10-entry quick empathic accuracy measure correlated strongly with the full one, showed good reliability and variance, and cut inferring and rating time by at least half.

857.who: 148 first-year engineering students (121 men, 27 women) in 38 teams of 3-4
857.task: Over an 8-week project, teams (19 all-male, 19 mixed) took a psychological safety survey at five time points and rated peers at the end
857.problem: Course design challenge (specific problem not reported)
