857.measured: Team psychological safety (7-item survey, five time points), individual gender-to-gender peer ratings of psychological safety, team gender composition
857.method_detail: Field study in a first-year cornerstone design course; teams built as gender-homogeneous or heterogeneous with a psychological-safety intervention
857.finding: Team gender composition did not change psychological safety, but women felt safer with women than with men and rated safety with men lower than men rated safety with women.

858.who: 22 students (11 male, 11 female) in 6 remote summer-course design teams
858.task: In a remote course, teams chose design methods (90 selections) and justified them; goal alignment and awareness surveyed at midpoint and end
858.problem: Human-centered design projects on mobility and cybersecurity
858.measured: Decision-making strategy behind method selection (agent, outcome, process driven), team goal alignment, goal awareness, enjoyment, communication, fairness of workload
858.method_detail: Exploratory study, one remote summer 2020 course; qualitative coding with survey measures
858.finding: Teams with lower goal alignment tended to use agent-driven strategies and higher alignment went with process-driven ones, and falling awareness of teammates' goals shifted strategy mix, though results lacked consistent significance.

860.who: 11 professional engineering designers at one aerospace manufacturer
860.task: In a half-day additive manufacturing workshop, redesigned a part before and after instruction (two prompts, two groups), with pre/post surveys
860.problem: Redesign of 316 stainless steel parts for lower weight or cost
860.prompt: Redesign a stainless steel part to weigh less at similar cost, or to cost less to make, using any technique (second time, additive use optional)
860.measured: Manufacturing process selected, share of features suited to each manufacturing type (feature-based fixation score), rater agreement, survey feedback
860.method_detail: Exploratory workshop case study of manufacturing fixation; prompts counterbalanced across two groups
860.finding: The workshop moved process choice from machining to additive (1 to 8 people chose additive), but geometric feature choices did not change significantly, suggesting feature-level fixation is harder to shift.

861.who: 53 first-year engineering students in 15 teams of 3 or 4
861.task: Teams brainstormed together for about 12 minutes on a video-recorded concept generation session, followed by a psychological safety survey; turns and self-turns were counted
861.problem: Course project on health and well-being (diseases, pollution, traffic injuries)
861.prompt: Develop a product for ensuring healthy lives and well-being by addressing diseases, pollution and traffic injuries
861.measured: Number of turns and self-turns per person, individual and team psychological safety (7-item survey), gender
861.method_detail: Video of team concept generation in a first-year design course; turn-taking analysis and regression
861.finding: More turns and self-turns predicted higher individual psychological safety but not team-level safety, and gender did not affect turn-taking though men reported higher safety.

862.who: 57 professional engineers from two companies in 19 randomly formed teams of 3
862.task: Teams of three had 60 minutes to propose a concept and sketches on a whiteboard; videos were coded with the FBS ontology
862.problem: Next-generation personal assistant and entertainment system for 2025
862.prompt: Define what the 2025 personal assistant and entertainment system is, how it works and interacts with people, and what it offers users
862.measured: Coded design behaviors and interactions (FBS issues), differences between the two company cohorts via multiple factor and correspondence analysis
862.method_detail: Protocol analysis of videotaped team sessions outside the workplace; exploratory comparison of two cohorts
862.finding: Teams from the two companies showed some different behaviors alongside a common overall design approach, so pooling teams across organizations needs care.

863.who: 472 undergraduate engineering students (359 intro psychology, 113 capstone), 66% men, 34% women
863.task: In a lab, played four levels of a spacecraft layout game under instructions framing the goal as a robustness target or as maximizing
863.problem: Positioning spacecraft components in the Manned Mission: Mars game to maximize robustness
863.prompt: Move colored component blocks to reach a stated robustness score (60, 70, 80, 90 or 100%) or to maximize robustness
863.measured: Final robustness score on level 4, time on task, components moved, number of times the score was checked
863.method_detail: Between-subjects, random assignment to six framing conditions in a computer game; nine people who skipped level 4 excluded
863.finding: Requirement-style goals led people to persist longer and score better than value-driven maximize-the-merit framing, challenging theory that favors value-driven framing.

864.who: 52 fourth-year mechanical engineering students at one university
864.task: Online, sketched solutions to two problems for 30 minutes each, with requirements shown as embedded text, a list, or scrum stories
864.problem: Wheelchair-friendly convertible dorm desk and peach-picking device
864.prompt: Design a space-saving desk with two states for a student in a wheelchair, and a device to let a wheelchair user pick peaches
864.measured: Sketch quantity, requirement addressment, sketch detail, novelty and variety of solution fragments
864.method_detail: Mixed design with 12 counterbalanced packets, randomly assigned by ID digits
864.finding: Contextual scrum-story requirements raised novelty of solution fragments and requirements addressed without hurting sketch quantity, while sketch count was unrelated to requirements addressed.

865.who: 124 participants (44 women, 80 men; 92 first-year students, 32 older or graduates)
865.task: Did an 8-item lottery risk questionnaire, then 29 two-player design tasks against a computer partner, choosing designs and strategies
865.problem: Choosing wireless communication technology designs in a two-actor strategic game
865.prompt: Earn as many experimental currency units as possible by choosing designs and strategies given payoff tables for you and your partner
865.measured: Risk attitude (constant absolute risk aversion) from questionnaire and from observed choices, accuracy of predicting strategic decisions
865.method_detail: Secondary data from a multi-actor design experiment; model validation of the questionnaire
865.finding: A risk-neutral model predicted 62% of decisions and questionnaire-based risk attitudes barely helped (63%), while attitudes inferred from choices reached 78%, suggesting engineering risk attitude is contextual.

866.who: 213 first-year engineering students in 60 teams of 3-4 (plus 600 crowd raters)
866.task: Took the KAI inventory, joined homogeneous or heterogeneous teams, sketched ideas alone (15 min) then as a team; crowd workers rated 1,395 ideas
866.problem: Course projects on food insecurity, or healthy lives and well-being
866.prompt: Tackle food insecurity in developing countries, or ensure healthy lives and well-being through addressing diseases, pollution and traffic injuries
866.measured: Individual and team KAI scores, paradigm-relatedness of ideas rated by Mechanical Turk workers (7-11 per team)
866.method_detail: Field study over five semesters (4- and 8-week projects) with crowdsourced idea ratings
866.finding: Higher KAI (more innovative style) went with a greater chance of individual ideas being paradigm-breaking, and team KAI diversity with team ideas being paradigm-challenging; crowdsourced ratings were supported as a measure.

873.who: 28 undergraduate engineering students (24 men, 4 women) from an intro design course
873.task: Over Zoom, sketched solutions to two problems (10 min each, thinking aloud), one framed adaptively and one innovatively, with surveys and interviews
873.problem: Securing belongings in public, and opening a lidded food container one-handed
873.prompt: Design a way to secure belongings against theft quickly, or to open a lidded food container one-handed, framed as practical or radical
873.measured: KAI cognitive style, solution feasibility and paradigm-relatedness, think-aloud strategies and behaviors, survey and interview themes on coping
873.method_detail: Virtual controlled ideation study with think-aloud, surveys, interviews; regression plus qualitative coding
873.finding: Problem framing significantly predicted how paradigm-breaking solutions were, and participants showed similar strategies whether the frame matched their cognitive style or not.

874.who: 28 graduate mechanical engineering students (43 did the surveys, 32 the modeling task)
874.task: Completed four individual-difference surveys, then built a function structure model on paper from a design prompt while videotaped; videos coded for modeling activities
874.problem: Function structure model of a household recycling machine
874.prompt: Design an automatic household machine that sorts plastic bottles, glass, aluminum cans and tin cans, then compresses and stores each in separate containers
874.measured: Systemizing quotient, risk propensity, goal orientation, thinking style; modeling activity and element distribution; final model features; regression among them
874.method_detail: Exploratory protocol study with video coding in an advanced design methods course; regression of inputs, process and outputs
874.finding: Exploratory regressions pointed to possible links, such as goal orientation, thinking style and risk propensity with modeling process, which the authors turned into three hypotheses for future testing.

876.who: 57 analyzed participants (68 recruited) with engineering or design experience, students and professionals
876.task: Online, chose one of 21 gripper designs in 10 minutes with up to 5 tests, then answered a survey on reasoning
876.problem: Robotic gripper surface for a dishwashing robot
876.prompt: As a robotics engineer, choose which of 21 gripper surface and hardness combinations to produce, testing up to five to see grasp success rate
876.measured: Design actions (space explored, testing, manipulation strategy), reasoning factors rated in a survey, final design success rate, willingness to submit alternative
876.method_detail: Interactive Figma task logging actions plus post-task survey; participants grouped by outcome
876.finding: Testing strategies and choosing a design with observed top performance improved outcomes, but participants' stated reasoning factors did not predict their actions or results.

877.who: 16 Kenyan farmers and 19 market stakeholders interviewed; 11 farms toured
877.task: Toured farms, then interviewed farmers and stakeholders using four storyboards depicting an irrigation controller concept that sends SMS valve instructions
877.problem: Irrigation scheduling controller for medium-scale contract farmers in East Africa
877.prompt: React to storyboards of a solar drip irrigation system with a controller that sets schedules and its value to farmers
877.measured: Current irrigation practices and challenges, farmers' openness to adopting the controller, stakeholders' view of market viability
877.method_detail: Storyboard-based interviews and farm tours in Kenya, October 2021
877.finding: Lead-user farmers and most stakeholders responded positively, suggesting the controller could improve scheduling and be a viable product, though only storyboards rather than a prototype were tested.

879.who: 6 designers in 3 pairs (5 Master's students, 1 post-doc); 2 pairs used AI
879.task: Pairs spent about 50 minutes exploring the problem aloud, then wrote a framing; AI pairs used a text generator, baseline used web search
879.problem: Harassment of women in public spaces
879.prompt: Explore the problem of harassment of women in public spaces, note ideas and questions, and summarize your understanding of the problem in a short statement
879.measured: Patterns and content of designer conversation and designer-AI exchanges, problem interpretations, roles assigned to the AI
879.method_detail: Exploratory qualitative analysis of conversation transcripts, with one baseline pair and two AI pairs (InferKit)
879.finding: AI-generated text prompted designers toward more nuanced interpretations of the problem and new dimensions, and designers treated the AI as both partner and tool.

880.who: 15 households in three Himalayan villages in Uttarakhand, India (number of individual respondents not reported)
880.task: Researchers conducted semi-structured household interviews using an adapted energy assessment survey on fuel use, cooking and heating practices, and views on traditional stoves
880.problem: No design problem (household cooking and heating energy needs for cookstove design)
880.measured: Fuel availability and use, cooking routines, heating needs, perceived advantages and disadvantages of stoves, seasonal patterns
880.method_detail: Qualitative household survey in interview format, based on participatory design and Lean Research principles
880.finding: Households used traditional firewood stoves for cooking and winter heating, limited costly LPG use, and valued the stoves' culture and local materials, showing the need for community-based cookstove design.

882.who: 5 spatial computing professionals (4 in survey and interview, 3 in pre-test)
882.task: Pre-test interviews, then a 43-item survey and a 45-90 minute structured interview on whether and how ethics enters the design process
882.problem: No design problem (ethics in spatial computing design practice)
882.measured: How often time, budget, responsibility, stigma and familiarity affect ethics; diversity considerations; processes for integrating ethics and testing; interview themes
882.method_detail: Sequential mixed methods with pre-test, survey and interviews; very small expert sample used to build a framework
882.finding: Practitioners saw spatial computing artifacts as especially vulnerable to ethical harm, but had no processes unique to the field and no clear testing methods, which led to a proposed ethics framework.

884.who: 8 practicing software and graphic designers with 3-17 years of experience
884.task: After a lab session, did a roughly 30-minute semi-structured interview reflecting on an information-dimensions framework and their work
884.problem: No design problem (reflection on information use in design practice)
884.measured: How designers relate their practice to each information dimension of the Information Archetypes Framework, how they shift between dimensions, views on the framework
884.method_detail: Purposeful sampling; deductive content analysis and iterative thematic coding of eight transcripts
884.finding: Designers deliberately adapted how they handled information to the situation and moved between information dimensions through trajectories and loops.

885.who: 58 desktop 3D printer users (mostly 18-24 years old, 42 undergraduates, 54 in engineering)
885.task: Answered an online usability survey on difficulty and frequency of 3D printing issues; researchers also applied universal design analysis
885.problem: Redesigning print bed leveling of fused filament fabrication 3D printers for universal design
885.measured: Likert ratings of difficulty and frequency of printer issues (bed leveling, filament loading, adhesion, nozzle blocks), feature preferences, open comments
885.method_detail: Universal design analysis plus a usability survey; results used to set design specifications for bed leveling
885.finding: Users rated print bed leveling as the most challenging and frequent problem, so the authors derived universal design specifications to make bed leveling easier to see, reach and do accurately.

887.who: 6 upper-level mechanical engineering students (five fourth-year, one fifth-year) at a Midwestern public university
887.task: Shown three design process models in counterbalanced order, noted impressions, then answered semi-structured interview questions on each over Zoom
887.problem: No design problem (perceptions of design process models)
887.measured: Perceived usefulness of each process model, dimensions used to tell the models apart, views on iteration and level of detail
887.method_detail: Semi-structured Zoom interviews with thematic analysis; models were a socially engaged design model, a textbook engineering design process, and a spiral model
887.finding: Students judged the models along eight dimensions such as scope, stakeholders and novelty and differed in interpretation, suggesting students gain from multiple models, including ones that centre people and society.

888.who: 31 people interviewed (19 robot-vacuum non-users, 12 users), plus industry staff feedback
888.task: Phone interviews (1-2 hours) on product use, experience and purchase; answers were sorted into non-use reasons and customer attributes
888.problem: Customer attributes for robot vacuums (House of Quality)
888.measured: Types of non-use, reasons for non-use, customer attributes from users and non-users, industry feedback on usefulness of non-user attributes
888.method_detail: Small qualitative use case in late 2020 with a presentation to industry for feedback
888.finding: Non-users gave more extensive reasons than users' negative feedback and so yielded more attributes, which industry staff said mainly helped prioritize existing user attributes.

893.task: Rated workload after a baseline task, 10 minutes of sketching ideas, and 10 minutes building a low-fidelity prototype
893.problem: One-handed jar opener for rehabilitation clients
893.prompt: As an engineer, design and prototype with provided craft materials a way for rehabilitation patients to open a jar with one hand
893.measured: Cognitive load (NASA-TLX subscales) at baseline, ideation, prototyping; idea quantity, creativity, usefulness, uniqueness, elegance (two raters)
893.method_detail: Lab study, within-subject repeated workload surveys
893.finding: Cognitive load differed across design stages, and during ideation mental demand and effort correlated with idea uniqueness, usefulness and elegance, while load was unrelated to prototype quality.

894.who: 23 professional designers and engineers (varied roles, mean 3 to over 5 years experience)
894.task: Over 60 minutes, thinking aloud, grouped teardown notes and images, linked notes and groups, rated links, then took a survey
894.problem: Organizing knowledge from a teardown of smart sunglasses (Bose Tenor Frames)
894.prompt: Group teardown notes by function, behavior or structure, link related notes and groups, and rate link strength
894.measured: Grouping and linking behavior, perceived usefulness for learning and knowledge transfer, link types, graph structure of knowledge organization
894.method_detail: Remote think-aloud sessions on Mural with survey; 7 grouped by function, 8 by behavior, 8 by structure
894.finding: Designers found grouping better for learning and linking better for knowledge transfer, used links far more than nests, and links mostly flagged trade-offs, requirements and collaboration opportunities.

895.who: 156 first-year and early undergraduate engineering students at two universities
895.task: Clustered elements of three products into subsystems for troubleshooting in a 45-minute paper task, each product shown in a different representation
895.problem: Subsystem clustering of a hair dryer, food mixer and toilet
895.prompt: As a design team manager, cluster each product's elements into subsystems so your team can troubleshoot unexpected behavior
895.measured: Cluster count, cluster size, cluster content and element pairs clustered together, product recognition
895.method_detail: Mixed design: 3 representation modalities (component graph, function graph, function structure) by 3 products
895.finding: Representation modality affected clustering similarly at both universities but not consistently across products, so the specific system represented strongly shapes subsystem reasoning.

897.who: 2 employees of a retail company planning smart stores
897.task: Took part in three rounds of structured interviews over a week, plus review of internal planning documents
897.problem: No design problem (planning ambient intelligence for retail stores)
897.measured: Justifications for agency levels of ambient intelligence, harm-mitigation methods, link between agency level and unwanted outcomes
897.method_detail: Structured interviews and document review at one company
897.finding: The company was largely unaware of links between agency level and unintended harm, yet used a range of agency levels, justified by what is known and unknown about outcomes.

898.who: 200 undergraduate mechanical engineering students in 40 teams (engine task); NASA engineers across 6 studies (number not reported)
898.task: Students designed engine subsystems in distributed teams by text messages; NASA engineers designed spacecraft over 4-day studies; interactions and performance logged, then model fitted
898.problem: Automotive engine (5 subsystems) and spacecraft conceptual design
898.prompt: Students minimized engine mass while maximizing factor of safety; NASA teams met customer dry-mass requirements
898.measured: Timestamped interdisciplinary interactions, system performance (mass, safety factor), design interdependence
898.method_detail: Stochastic network-behavior model fitted by Bayesian inference to two existing datasets
898.finding: Student and NASA designers differed in how much they interacted but were similar in whom they chose, and interaction between loosely and tightly coupled subsystems helped performance.

901.who: High school students in a CAD solar design challenge (113 collected, 39 valid designs analyzed); no human subjects in the method itself
901.task: Students solved a two-day solar-panel design challenge in CAD software that logged actions; researchers embedded action logs and clustered designers
901.problem: Solarize Your School: rooftop solar panel design
901.prompt: Place solar panels on a 3D school model to produce at least 400,000 kWh per year with payback under ten years
901.measured: Design action preference, one-step sequences (Markov), contextual and long-term sequences (Doc2Vec, LSTM autoencoder), time gaps between actions; resulting clusters and design quality
901.method_detail: Embedding and X-means clustering applied to existing CAD log data
901.finding: Designers formed several behavioral clusters that differed depending on which behavior dimension was used, and different behavior patterns could produce similar design quality.

903.who: 306 US online participants recruited on Amazon Mechanical Turk (161 in Survey 1, 145 in Survey 2)
903.task: Viewed three images of an automated vehicle approaching a crosswalk at 20, 10 and 3 meters, then reported crossing decision, trust and perceived safety
903.problem: Pedestrian-automated vehicle interaction at a crosswalk (external display design)
903.measured: Crossing decision, trust in the automated vehicle, perceived safety
903.method_detail: Online survey experiment; early vs late eHMI message (within) and with vs without dynamic speed (between)
903.finding: Showing the vehicle's yielding message earlier raised crossing, trust and perceived safety; displaying dynamic speed raised trust and safety but did not change crossing decisions.

904.who: 7 engineering design faculty at US and European universities
904.task: Took part in 30 to 60 minute semi-structured Zoom interviews about their stakeholders and a hypothetical intelligent design assistant
904.prompt: Describe a hypothetical AI tool that would help your stakeholders in engineering design, and its challenges
904.measured: Human-centric requirements and challenges for human-AI interaction tools (thematic analysis)
904.method_detail: Semi-structured, recorded and transcribed; preliminary thematic analysis, no inter-rater reliability
904.finding: Requirements centered on understanding stakeholders' cognition and the engineering design context, pointing to the need for theory of mind in AI agents.

905.who: 71 US undergraduate and graduate students (38 AI-assisted, 33 solo; 70 analyzed)
905.task: Designed drones in an online platform across two 20-minute sessions, with or without an AI agent suggesting redesigns, plus mid- and post-task questionnaires
905.problem: Drones meeting range, velocity, payload and cost objectives (HyForm platform)
905.prompt: Complete as many of five increasingly demanding drone development objectives as possible, in order
905.measured: Drones submitted, design exploration, novelty, quality, search strategy (hidden Markov model), effort, mental workload (NASA-RTLX)
905.method_detail: Random assignment to AI-assisted vs solo; online platform logs
905.finding: AI assistance helped most on moderately complex objectives and less on highly complex ones, and AI-assisted designers explored more while solo designers optimized parameters.

908.who: 14 mechanical and aerospace engineering graduate students (7 per condition)
908.task: Spent 15 minutes exploring metamaterial designs with a design-space exploration tool, with learning tests before and after, under a learning goal or a performance goal
908.problem: Mechanical metamaterial (2D lattice unit cell) design
908.prompt: Learning group: learn as much as possible about the problem; performance group: maximize stiffness and minimize volume fraction
908.measured: Learning test score change (pretest vs posttest), design performance (hypervolume of designs generated)
908.finding: Subjects given a learning goal scored higher on learning tests, while those given a performance goal produced better designs, suggesting a trade-off between the two goals.

910.who: 8 academic researchers as expert users (interviews) plus 48 survey respondents (students and researchers), summed
910.task: Experts used a keyword-network discovery tool in their own research for 4 weeks with interviews; others tried the tool and rated stimulated creativity in an online questionnaire
910.problem: Evaluation of B-Link, a creative knowledge discovery web tool
910.measured: Novel items found, inspiration, and ratings of relevance, interestingness, novelty, inspiration, usefulness (5-point), usability, usage logs
910.method_detail: Longitudinal interviews, questionnaire survey and usage logs (modified MILCs evaluation)
910.finding: All eight experts found novel items, and survey ratings on all five creativity metrics were positive, suggesting the tool aids creative knowledge discovery.

911.who: 46 upper-level engineering students generating ideas; 3 raters (2 graduate students, 1 professor) scored them
911.task: Listed solutions to three everyday problems, 5 minutes each, in an online survey; raters ranked and scored sample ideas to tune a weighted quality metric
911.problem: Three everyday problems (e.g., waking someone up reliably)
911.prompt: List as many ideas as you can for ways to solve a stated everyday problem, such as waking a person whose alarm clock fails
911.measured: Idea effectiveness and feasibility (1-5), weighted-sum quality, interrater reliability (Kendall's W), match with raters' intuitive rankings (Kendall's Tau)
911.method_detail: Metric development with idea set from an online ideation survey; rater calibration and rank comparison
911.finding: A weighted sum of effectiveness and feasibility, with weights tuned per problem, matched raters' intuitive quality rankings and was reliably rated, showing promise as an efficient quality metric.

914.who: 115 students in a creativity class (8 graduate, 107 undergraduate); 3 incomplete tests dropped
914.task: Took three creativity tests (RAT, AUT, TTCT), listed bicycle accessory ideas for 10 minutes, and rated familiarity with and interest in bicycles
914.prompt: Write down as many ideas for creative bicycle accessory products as you can in 10 minutes
914.measured: RAT, AUT and TTCT scores; number of ideas rated creative by three bicycle industry experts; familiarity and interest (1-5)
914.method_detail: Correlational classroom study with moderation regression
914.finding: Only the Alternative Uses Test predicted expert-rated creative ideas, and interest strengthened while product familiarity weakened the link between divergent-thinking scores and creative ideas.

915.who: 3 product design teams at 3 companies (consumer electronics, footwear, medical devices; number of people not reported)
915.task: Researchers observed one team per company for about 10 months (200+ hours) with field notes, recordings and artifacts, then mapped the design methods used early on
915.problem: New physical products (consumer electronics, footwear, medical device)
915.measured: Design methods and tools used in planning and concept development, evolutionary vs revolutionary nature of products
915.method_detail: Ethnographically informed fieldwork with grounded theory analysis
915.finding: All three teams relied heavily on benchmarking and reverse engineering for concept generation, and all produced evolutionary rather than revolutionary products.

917.who: 74 mechanical engineering students in a senior bioinspired design elective (32 in one semester, 42 in the next)
917.task: Learned five bioinspired design methods as course modules, each followed by a homework design problem solved with that method, plus self-efficacy surveys and feedback
917.problem: Five problems (e.g., quiet portable alarm clock, blind cup, towel ironing, coconut harvesting, peach pitting)
917.prompt: Generate solutions to each module's design problem using that module's bioinspired method (directed, case study, AskNature, BioTRIZ, functional modeling)
917.measured: Idea quality and quantity, creativity and effectiveness of solutions, design self-efficacy, motivation, outcome expectancy, anxiety, student feedback
917.method_detail: Course-embedded study across two semesters; methods in fixed order, compared via problem-equivalency adjustment
917.finding: Each method yielded many effective, creative ideas, and the course raised students' design confidence and outcome expectancy and lowered anxiety while motivation stayed high.

919.who: 11 raters (1 PhD, 1 Master's engineering student, 9 psychology undergraduates) for polygons; raters for sketches not fully reported
919.task: Raters answered triplet questions on which of two items looked more similar to a third, for 10 colored polygons and 10 milk frother sketches; maps were learned from answers
919.problem: Judging similarity of colored polygons and milk frother sketches
919.prompt: For each triplet, choose which of two designs is more similar to the reference design, and explain why
919.measured: Self-consistency and transitivity violations, 2D idea maps, map-derived novelty versus raters' own novelty rankings, criteria raters cited
919.method_detail: Two case studies; triplet embedding (GNMDS) with rater explanations
919.finding: Idea maps from simple similarity comparisons revealed which attributes each rater used, and distance on the map gave a usable estimate of idea novelty.

922.who: 29 sophomore mechanical engineering students (ideators); paired student raters scored ideas
922.task: Sketched and described as many solutions as possible in 20 minutes; 104 ideas were scored with three existing and one new variety metric
922.problem: Personal transport on snow for people without ski skills
922.prompt: Design a way for people lacking skiing or snowboarding experience to move themselves on snow, with direction and braking control, learnable quickly
922.measured: Variety scores from four metrics (Nelson/Shah, Linsey bins, new quality-based metric), correlations among them, ease of use
922.method_detail: Secondary analysis comparing metrics on 104 ideas; interrater reliability by Cronbach alpha
922.finding: The four variety metrics correlated at varying levels, so they are related but not interchangeable, and each offers a distinct view of variety suited to different uses.

923.who: 152 undergraduate engineering and industrial design students at two universities (87 teaming, 44 framing, 21 heuristics); 8 student raters
923.task: Each student generated ideas for 20 minutes without an intervention, then 20 minutes on a new problem with one intervention (paired teaming, problem framing, or design heuristic cards); 966 ideas rated for quality
923.problem: Open-ended design problems (specific problems not reported here)
923.prompt: Generate as many design ideas as possible, sketching and describing each on its own sheet
923.measured: Idea quality via six rated metrics (applicability, effectiveness, implicational explicitness, clarity, acceptability, implementability); cognitive style (KAI), academic standing
923.method_detail: Within-subject neutral vs intervention sessions; secondary analysis of three prior studies
923.finding: Idea quality differed significantly with the teaming and problem framing interventions compared with neutral ideation, but not with design heuristics.

924.who: 61 participants in a graduate product development course (52 graduate students, 4 visitors, others unspecified)
924.task: Listed paperclip uses for 2 minutes, then either classified their ideas or reviewed them to combine, then listed new uses in a second round
924.prompt: List as many ways of using a paperclip as possible, then list as many new ways as possible
924.measured: Idea quantity, novelty, number and novelty of unique ideas after the intervention
924.method_detail: Two groups randomized by form (classify vs combine), paper-based alternate uses test with intervention between rounds
924.finding: Both classifying and combining raised idea novelty, classifying more so, and classifying also produced more unique ideas than combining.

925.who: 37 engineering students working in design teams
925.task: Completed a personality survey, sketched milk frother ideas for 20 minutes, then rated every teammate's ideas as consider or not consider
925.prompt: Develop concepts for a new, easy-to-use product that froths milk quickly, covering both form and function
925.measured: Ownership bias (share of own vs teammates' ideas selected), Big Five personality traits, gender
925.method_detail: Lab study with personality survey one week before the design session
925.finding: Male students selected more of their own ideas than female students, and agreeableness and neuroticism affected how many ideas were selected, showing ownership bias in concept selection.

926.who: 30 adult volunteers (researchers, fellows, graduate students) in Germany; 37 recruited
926.task: Online: proposed at least three uses for each of 12 IKEA product photos shown upright or rotated, then completed a pattern-meanings test and a need-for-closure scale
926.problem: Alternative uses of 12 IKEA objects (Alternative Uses Test)
926.prompt: Propose at least three uses for each pictured object
926.measured: Tendency to reorient objects, alternative-uses creativity, Wallach-Kogan pattern meanings score, Need for Closure subscales
926.method_detail: Online study with objects shown at 0, 90 or 180 degrees across three groups; correlational analysis
926.finding: Tendency to reorient objects correlated strongly with several creativity measures and with the predictability subscale of need for closure.

927.who: 55 graduate students in two German university courses (29 and 26); computer method has no human subjects
927.task: Wrote reuse concepts for four wind-turbine blade parts shown in CAD views with a human scale, compared with concepts derived from visually similar images
927.problem: Alternative uses for retired wind-turbine blade parts
927.prompt: Identify how to reuse each shown part, maximizing reuse, cutting only if needed; second group barred from turbine or aircraft uses
927.measured: Reuse concepts' scale relative to the blade, prohibited reuses, feasibility (human-rated)
927.method_detail: Two paper concept-generation activities compared with image-recognition-based visual similarity method
927.finding: Visual similarity produced fewer concepts that were too small for the blade's scale than human concept generation, though feasibility depended on the photo chosen.

928.who: 381 online raters recruited on Amazon Mechanical Turk (190 saw sketches, 191 text only)
928.task: Rated seven product ideas for the same problem on a 10-point scale, shown with text plus sketches or text only
928.measured: Perceived idea value (novelty, valuableness, feasibility ratings) and its dependence on sketch quality
928.method_detail: Online between-groups survey, sketches vs text-only
928.finding: When sketches were shown, ratings of an idea's value were strongly influenced by sketch quality, and ratings differed somewhat from those given for text alone.

929.who: 25 graduate students in an advanced product design course
929.task: Formulated each of two design problems in a web-based problem map tool, then sketched concepts; ideation scored by independent judges and predicted from map variables
929.problem: Basketball return device (shot buddy) and an autonomous surveillance device challenge
929.measured: Problem-map entity counts and structure; ideation variety, average and maximum quality, average and maximum novelty; regression predictions
929.method_detail: Correlation and regression of problem formulation data against ideation scores; model trained on problem 1, tested on problem 2
929.finding: Problem formulation patterns correlated with ideation outcomes, and models built on the first problem predicted variety and quality for the second problem better than novelty.

930.who: 80 LeTourneau engineering volunteers analyzed (40 freshmen, 40 upperclassmen; text also mentions 41 upperclassmen)
930.task: Online, typed ideas for text-based divergent thinking items in about 30 minutes, including an unusual-uses item and an umbrella problem; ideas sorted into category trees
930.problem: Unusual-uses item and an everyday umbrella problem (keeping person and backpack dry)
930.prompt: List unusual uses for an object; list as many ways as possible to keep a person and backpack dry in rain
930.method_detail: Online between-group comparison of freshmen and upperclassmen, mixed-design ANOVA
930.finding: Originality did not differ significantly between freshmen and upperclassmen, and both groups produced their most original ideas on the generally familiar task.

931.task: Online, typed ideas for three everyday problems, 5 minutes each; ideas mapped to genealogy trees to score variety, novelty and quality
931.problem: Three everyday problems (alarm clock, hot apartment, wet backpack in rain)
931.prompt: List as many ideas as you can to solve each person's stated everyday problem
931.measured: Rate of variety (broad-search and detail-search counts), novelty, quality, quantity
931.method_detail: Correlational analysis of an online problem-solving survey
931.finding: A broad-search style correlated positively with idea novelty and a detail-search style with idea quality, with idea quantity a possible confound.

932.who: Crowd ideators: over 2,000 mid-career professionals at a workshop plus Mechanical Turk workers (counts not given); human raters scored 50 concepts per case
932.task: Crowds wrote design concepts in four ideation cases (over 4,000 concepts); an unsupervised language-processing method filtered, categorized and scored them, checked against human ratings
932.problem: Four crowdsourced ideation cases (specific prompts not reported)
932.measured: Machine novelty and level-of-detail scores vs human ratings (agreement), saturation of ideas, dominance of top-ranked ideas vs human, random and control selections, later industry appearance
932.method_detail: Method evaluation on four crowdsourced concept sets with human inter-rater checks
932.finding: The automated novelty and detail metrics agreed with human ratings, and ideas it ranked highest were selected as dominant over human-picked, random and control ideas.

933.who: 460 participants, from design and engineering professionals to college students; 89 of them also took a drawing test
933.task: Listed alternative uses for a paperclip in three minutes on a notecard; a subset also made objects from nine triangles in three minutes
933.problem: Alternative uses of a paperclip; drawing objects from triangles (ATTA)
933.prompt: List as many alternative uses for a paperclip as you can think of in three minutes
933.measured: Quantity, originality (rarity across pool), elaboration (words per response, extra drawing details), fluency
933.method_detail: Correlational analysis of existing Alternative Uses Test and Abbreviated Torrance Test data
933.finding: Later responses were more original than early ones, and people who wrote longer or more elaborate responses had lower originality and fluency under the time limit.

934.who: 105 second-year engineering students in 21 teams of 4-6
934.task: Individually generated concepts for a spherical rolling robot using provided patents as stimuli during a course project; 138 patent-inspired concepts analyzed
934.prompt: Conceive a working spherical rolling robot for a self-chosen application, generating multiple alternative concepts individually using patent stimuli
934.measured: Analogical distance of patents (technology class knowledge distance), novelty and quality of concepts, frequency of stimuli use
934.method_detail: Course project data; most-cited and random patent sets from 121 patent classes
934.finding: Closer stimuli were used more often and led to higher quality concepts, while more distant stimuli led to more novel concepts.

935.task: In the scanner, pressed a button for each new solution to 12 open-ended problems during 2 minutes each, seeing near words, far words, or problem words as stimuli
935.problem: 12 open-ended design problems (e.g., travel exercise device, milk frother, time measurement)
935.prompt: Develop as many solutions as you can to each problem within the time limit
935.measured: Idea fluency by stimulus condition, brain activation during ideation (fMRI), timing of stimulus use
935.method_detail: fMRI within-subject design: near, far and control word conditions, 4 problems each, counterbalanced
935.finding: Any inspirational words raised idea fluency, and successful use of stimuli produced a distinct brain activation pattern called inspired internal search, triggered more often by nearer stimuli.

936.who: Mechanical Turk workers (10 responses per query) and 4 expert raters judged variety; milk frother ideas came from 141 prior students
936.task: Raters chose which of two sets of polygons or milk frother sketches was more varied; new variety metric tested against these judgments
936.problem: Variety of sets of polygons and of milk frother sketches
936.prompt: Judge which of two idea sets has higher variety (or can't decide)
936.measured: Alignment of Herfindahl-based, tree-based (SVS, NM) variety metrics with human pairwise ratings, sensitivity, greedy optimization
936.method_detail: Metric development with two human-rated datasets (crowd for polygons, 4 experts for sketches)
936.finding: The Herfindahl index variety metric aligned with human ratings more than existing tree-based metrics, was more sensitive, and can be optimized efficiently.

939.who: 352 first-year undergraduate students at one university, in 16 classes
939.task: In a design course ideation session, sketched concepts after receiving a brief with a different mix of four extra information types
939.prompt: As a product team member, develop a concept for a new, easy-to-use device that extracts juice from fresh oranges at home, avoiding blender-type solutions
939.measured: Concept novelty, appropriateness and usability of sketches
939.method_detail: 2^4 full factorial design (numbers, video example, physical example, context), one condition per class
939.finding: Plain briefs gave high novelty but low appropriateness and usability, video examples raised appropriateness and usability but lowered novelty, and physical plus context briefs balanced novelty and usability.

940.who: 184 undergraduate engineering students at one university (some completed more than one form over three years)
940.task: Online, typed ideas for three engineering ideation problems per form, 5 minutes each; ideas scored with two rarity-based novelty metrics and by rated novelty, effectiveness and feasibility
940.problem: Nine engineering design ideation problems across three forms
940.prompt: List as many ideas as possible for each everyday problem
940.measured: Shah and Johnson rarity novelty, perceived novelty ratings, effectiveness and feasibility ratings, convergent and discriminant validity correlations
940.method_detail: Secondary correlational analysis of data from a longitudinal study and an initial study
940.finding: Rarity-based novelty and perceived novelty ratings showed only moderate convergent validity, so they should be treated as distinct measures, with the Shah metric the better rarity option.

941.who: 10 mechanical engineering graduate students specializing in design
941.task: Identified functions for a design brief, then generated concepts without a time limit, then explained their concepts in recorded interviews; interviews were coded
941.prompt: Identify the high-level actions of the device, then generate conceptual solutions for the towel-folding problem
941.measured: Internal knowledge queries (objectives, thought process, direction of reasoning, behavior type), single vs compound analogy, similarity types used (function, flow, form)
941.method_detail: Design task plus follow-up interview, qualitative coding by two raters
941.finding: Function, flow and form similarity all appeared when designers formed analogies, with little difference between single and compound analogies, and flow behavior was a common abstract similarity.

942.who: 14 teams of 3 (42 people): students, design instructors and practitioners aged 20 to 54
942.task: Teams spent 30 minutes developing a fictitious device from an engineering drawing, given a prototype at minute five; interactions coded from video and members' cognitive style measured
942.prompt: Further develop the device shown in an engineering drawing
942.measured: Cognitive style (KAI scores), team interaction behaviors (Interaction Dynamics Notation), idea utterances and interaction sequences
942.method_detail: Secondary analysis of a team concept generation video dataset; correlation and sequence analysis
942.finding: Individual cognitive style correlated with specific interaction behaviors and idea utterances, and certain interaction sequences raised the chance that a team produced an idea.

943.task: Dissected an assigned product for 30 minutes wearing eye-tracking glasses, then sketched milk frother ideas for 20 minutes, then explained inspirations in an interview
943.problem: Milk frother, after dissecting a nerf gun, tape dispenser, hand mixer or toothbrush
943.prompt: Create several product solutions for the frothing task, drawing each idea on its own sheet
943.measured: Unique reuses of interior and exterior parts (design fixation), eye fixation duration on parts, idea creativity
943.method_detail: 2x2 design (analogical distance by product complexity) with eye tracking and post-task interview
943.finding: Reusing parts from the dissected product was positively related to creativity of ideas, and eye fixations did not predict reuse, suggesting reuse was deliberate rather than unconscious.

944.who: 66 recruited university students (60 analyzed) in engineering, fine arts, computer science and social sciences
944.task: Sketched solutions for 10 minutes, then received a near, far, or no inspirational stimulus chosen by semantic analysis of their current ideas, then continued ideating
944.problem: Reducing accidents from people walking while texting
944.prompt: Think of solutions to minimize accidents from people walking and texting on a cell phone
944.measured: Feasibility, usefulness and novelty of intermediate and final solutions, semantic distance of stimuli, innovativeness of stimuli
944.method_detail: Lab study with adaptive stimuli (latent semantic analysis); near, far, control conditions
944.finding: Semantic analysis could select near and far stimuli in real time, and a stimulus's overall innovativeness shaped final design innovativeness more than its distance from the designer's work.

945.who: 21 adults at one university (engineering and technology; 15 male, 6 female)
945.task: Did no warm-up, 8 minutes of lines and circles, or art activities to reduce sketch inhibition, then sketched ideas for 15 minutes with EEG and skin response recorded
945.problem: Devices to help student athletes with leg injuries get around campus
945.prompt: Generate as many ideas as possible for devices that make it easier for student athletes with leg injuries to move around campus
945.measured: EEG cognitive states, galvanic skin response, NASA-TLX, attitudes toward sketching, number of ideas and other performance metrics
945.method_detail: Lab study, 3 warm-up conditions, psychophysiological sensing
945.finding: Warm-ups reduced stress, especially for those familiar with the problem, and art warm-ups raised engagement for younger participants, but warm-ups did not change number of ideas or other performance.

946.who: 90 engineering students who generated 938 milk frother ideas (prior experiment); 3 quasi-expert raters scored a subset
946.task: Ideas were rated by three raters for a subset; a machine learning model trained on idea descriptions and those ratings predicted creativity of the remaining ideas
946.problem: Milk frother (ideas from an earlier dissection study)
946.prompt: Generate ideas for a novel, innovative device for frothing milk in a short time
946.measured: Rater uniqueness, usefulness and overall creativity (6-point, alpha 0.85); machine learning prediction accuracy, sensitivity and correlation with ratings
946.method_detail: Random forest and other classifiers trained on human ratings of a subset of existing ideas
946.finding: A random forest model trained on a small human-rated subset predicted idea creativity with fairly high accuracy and sensitivity, correlating well for uniqueness and usefulness but not overall creativity.

947.task: Freely browsed 8 clickable pieces of causal or effectual design information on a web interface, then generated ideas; interactions logged and ideas rated
947.prompt: Develop concepts for a new, innovative product that froths milk quickly and is usable with minimal instruction
947.measured: Use of causal vs effectual information, idea novelty and quality
947.method_detail: Lab pilot study with interaction logging
947.finding: Novice designers used causal information more than effectual, and those using more causal information produced more novel but lower-quality ideas on average.

948.who: 50 junior and senior mechanical engineering students in a theory of machines class
948.task: For each target electromechanical product, picked from five source products those useful as analogies for designing it, and named the similarity dimensions behind each pick
948.problem: Hypothetical design of electromechanical products (analogy selection)
948.prompt: Imagine designing the shown product and choose which of five other products would be useful recommendations, saying how they are similar
948.measured: Selected source products, similarity dimensions cited (function, form, energy flow, material flow, motion)
948.method_detail: Exploratory user study with paper product choices
948.finding: Participants chose reference products by similarity on several dimensions, with function most dominant, followed by energy, motion, material and form.

949.who: 53 mostly mechanical engineering students in two courses (32 in Study 1, 21 in Study 2), summed
949.task: Study 1: sketched solutions for 50 minutes to one of two problems using the directed bioinspired method. Study 2: solved two problems on separate days (35 minutes each), then listed existing solutions and biological analogies
949.problem: Alarm clock, corn husking, blind cup, peanut sheller
949.prompt: Sketch as many solutions as possible, one per page, regardless of feasibility (Study 1 using nature as inspiration where possible)
949.measured: Idea quantity, quality, novelty, variety; familiarity with and knowledge of the problems (existing solutions and analogies listed)
949.method_detail: Study 1 between-subjects (17 alarm, 15 corn); Study 2 within-subjects with survey, run as course assignments
949.finding: Design problems produced different metric profiles, and participants' familiarity and knowledge of a problem influenced those metrics, with hints that method and problem interact.

950.who: 84 workshop participants (36 visual impairment, 28 hearing impairment, 20 aging); 81 analyzed
950.task: After a briefing and a simulated extreme-user experience, listed issues and solutions for the target population on questionnaires before and after, plus self-efficacy ratings
950.problem: Needs of people with visual impairment, hearing impairment, and the elderly
950.prompt: List as many issues as possible, in order of importance, for the target population, and give solutions to them
950.measured: Creativity of listed ideas, empathy (self-efficacy ratings), effect of gender, age and personal connection to the target group
950.method_detail: Three empathy simulation workshops combined for analysis
950.finding: Personal connection to the simulated population significantly affected how much the simulation boosted creativity and empathy, while gender showed no significant effect.

952.who: 25 design students (24 senior undergraduates, 1 graduate) in 6 teams of 4-5 in a healthcare design course
952.task: Teams built activity diagrams, derived needs, then used simulated extreme user perspectives to identify latent needs and generate concepts for a medical device project
952.problem: Six medical devices (guidewire safety, biopsy needle stabilizer, shoulder dislocation aid, guidewire threading, neonatal monitor, blood pressure measurement)
952.measured: Latent needs identified, a latency metric for needs, concepts generated
952.method_detail: Course-embedded multi-week study with control and extreme-user phases
952.finding: The extreme user approach helped teams identify latent needs for all six devices, and the proposed latency metric looks useful for judging how latent a need is.

953.who: 52 engineering juniors and seniors at one university
953.task: Online, typed alternate uses for three household objects (3 minutes each) and ideas for three engineering problems, then fluency and flexibility compared between the two tests
953.problem: Alternate uses of shoe, bedsheet, paperclip; three open-ended engineering ideation problems
953.prompt: List as many alternate uses as you can for the object; list as many ideas as you can for each engineering problem
953.measured: Fluency (quantity) and flexibility (variety) on a spontaneous flexibility test and an engineering ideation test
953.finding: Both fluency and flexibility were strongly correlated between the alternate uses test and the engineering ideation test, suggesting the two tests together better measure spontaneous flexibility.

954.who: 229 engineering students who completed sessions (190 freshmen and sophomores between-subjects, 39 seniors within-subjects), summed
954.task: Between-subjects: sketched solutions for 48 minutes to one of four problems. Within-subjects: seniors did two 50-minute ideation sessions, peanut sheller then corn husker, two days apart
954.problem: Peanut shelling, corn husking, coconut harvesting, personal alarm clock
954.prompt: Generate as many solutions as possible to the given problem, with five customer requirements, as sketches with descriptions
954.measured: Idea quantity, quality, novelty, variety and completeness; perceived difficulty and problem familiarity
954.method_detail: Large between-subjects test of four problems plus smaller within-subjects test of two problems
954.finding: Peanut and corn problems behaved similarly and alarm and coconut problems behaved similarly, but individuals could still score differently across similar problems.

955.task: Given a prepopulated morphological chart in one of five function orders, generated twenty integrated design concepts by combining means, judged on cost, reliability and ease of use
955.problem: Automatic clothes ironing device and automatic household recycling sorter
955.prompt: Generate twenty promising integrated design concepts from the given morphological chart, evaluated on usage cost, reliability and ease of use
955.measured: Frequency of means selected, chart coverage, sequence of exploration, effect of function order
955.method_detail: Two problems by five function orderings (priority, reverse, input-output, output-input, random)
955.finding: Students focused on the first columns regardless of order, and listing functions from most to least important gave a higher chance and more uniform exploration of the design space.

956.who: 15 healthy adults recruited from a research institute participant pool (analyzed); mean age 25.5
956.task: Named alternative uses aloud for 12 object images (each shown 2 minutes in four views) while eye movements were tracked
956.problem: Alternative Uses Test with 12 objects (e.g., paperclip, chair, tire)
956.prompt: Name as many alternative uses as possible, different from normal use and from each other, for each pictured object
956.measured: Eye fixation on object views and blank space before and during naming, new instances and new categories of uses
956.method_detail: Lab eye-tracking study with randomized object order
956.finding: Naming new uses and categories correlated more with looking at multiple views than a single view, and new-category uses followed more looking at blank space.

957.who: 69 industry professionals from 52 companies in Mexico and Singapore
957.task: Generated ideas for 15 minutes, then two days later again after training in WordTree, SCAMPER or no method, and self-rated 11 psychological and contextual factors
957.problem: A service design problem (same in both phases)
957.prompt: Generate solution ideas to the service design problem in two ideation sessions
957.measured: Self-rated entertainment, motivation, inspiration, easiness, interest, commitment, concentration, success, time pressure; idea fluency, novelty, fixation
957.method_detail: Two-phase field experiment with three conditions: control, WordTree, SCAMPER
957.finding: Few self-rated factors predicted outcomes: motivation and problem easiness predicted novelty with WordTree, time pressure predicted fluency without a method, and none affected fixation.

959.who: 37 undergraduate engineering design students aged 20-26 (20 in Treatment Group 1, 17 in Group 2)
959.task: Mapped a syringe's user activities, then used empathy tools (eye mask, one-hand band, low-dexterity glove, hearing emulator) either guided by a systematic framework or unguided, to list needs and redesign
959.prompt: Redesign a medication syringe, identifying design needs while emulating visual, hearing, dexterity or single-hand impairment
959.measured: Latent design needs identified, need statements, effect of guided vs unguided empathy tool use
959.method_detail: Pilot study with control and treatment phases and two treatment groups
959.finding: A simple systematic way of choosing empathy tools captured a wider range of latent needs than unguided, instinct-based tool choice.

963.who: 10 expert systems engineers and managers on the JPL A-Team (avg. 16 years engineering experience)
963.task: Took part in one-hour semi-structured interviews stating the rules of thumb they use in early space mission design, then rated each one in a follow-up survey
963.measured: Heuristics extracted (context-action form) and classified; survey ratings of source, applicability by concept maturity, frequency of use, reliability, tendency to evolve
963.method_detail: Semi-structured interviews with post-interview survey; 5 by phone, 5 in person
963.finding: 101 heuristics were extracted and classified, and participants' ratings of how often a heuristic is used, how reliable it is and how much it evolves were statistically correlated.

964.who: 7 professionals at one small electromechanical company: 4 R&D team members and 3 executives
964.task: R&D team sketched ideas in a two-day design thinking workshop, then sorted and rated all ideas; executives separately screened the anonymized ideas by survey; interviews on project risk
964.problem: Redesign of existing products for a younger target audience (details withheld, proprietary)
964.measured: Categorization of ideas (primary, secondary, do not fund), perceived riskiness, originality and feasibility of 37 ideas, interview themes on risk
964.method_detail: In-situ shadowing of one company team with workshop, surveys and interviews
964.finding: Both groups moved forward ideas with high market potential and avoided risk, but only executives favored high-feasibility ideas, while idea generators showed no preference on originality or feasibility.

967.who: 619 crowd raters on Amazon Mechanical Turk (983 recruited, filtered)
967.task: Rated how well boat sketches would float and move in a 2D environment, then classified sketches as human or computer made; some sketches carried labels
967.problem: 2D boat sketches (50 human-drawn, 50 generated by a deep learning model)
967.prompt: Judge each boat sketch on how well it would float, how well it would move when pushed, and whether a person or computer drew it
967.measured: Perceived functionality (7-point scale for floating and moving), effect of human/computer labels, accuracy of human vs computer classification
967.method_detail: Crowdsourced between-subjects questionnaire, 25 versions of 8 sketches each
967.finding: Raters judged computer-generated sketches as more functional than human ones, labels did not change this, and raters could not tell the two kinds apart better than chance.

970.who: 5 robotics graduate students with at least 2 years of robot design experience
970.task: Were interviewed about their design approach, then worked 45 minutes on a design problem while thinking aloud on video; coders extracted and classified heuristics from recordings
970.prompt: Design a wearable third-arm robot that assists with an everyday cooperative task you define, meeting requirements on payload, speed, maneuverability and sensing
970.measured: Heuristics extracted from video and audio (coder agreement 77.8%), classification by design phase, field of engineering and action intent (kappa about 0.71)
970.method_detail: Preliminary think-aloud design session with grounded-theory taxonomy of heuristics
970.finding: A preliminary extraction method yielded a set of robotics design heuristics and a taxonomy by design phase, engineering field and action intent, though extraction proved difficult.

971.who: 45 design professionals from two companies (15 automotive parts, 30 media hardware/software)
971.task: Sketched milk-frother concepts individually for 20 minutes, then each rated every teammate's ideas and their own as consider or do not consider; team picked a final idea
971.prompt: Develop concepts for a new, innovative product that froths milk quickly with minimal instruction
971.measured: Ownership bias in selection, idea goodness (team agreement on future value), expert-rated creativity (uniqueness, usefulness)
971.method_detail: Two identical on-site design workshops, logistic regression on selection of ideas
971.finding: Professionals showed ownership bias only for ideas their teammates judged low in goodness, creativity did not change this, and they favored ideas high in usefulness but low in uniqueness.

972.who: 4 professional software designers with 3-8 years of experience
972.task: Practiced grouping SET cards, read 16 information sheets, generated concepts for a design challenge, sorted the information aloud, then were interviewed; 2-3 hour individual sessions
972.problem: Product or system to reduce distraction-related pedestrian accidents
972.prompt: Develop concepts for a new, innovative product or system that cuts pedestrian accidents caused by mobile phone distraction
972.measured: How designers grouped and structured information (card sorting, information sorting), reasons for grouping, interview themes on information use
972.method_detail: Think-aloud sessions with qualitative coding and post-task interview
972.finding: Designers grouped information differently, but all judged it by relevance to constraints, resources or user requirements, and experience and tools helped them turn information into insight.

975.who: 10 academic microfluidics engineers (professors, researchers, postdocs, graduate students) at two universities
975.task: Took part in 30-90 minute semi-structured interviews about how they developed one microfluidic device, focusing on problem definition and idea generation
975.problem: No design problem (recalled microfluidic device projects)
975.measured: Divergence in problem versus solution exploration, contextual factors in academia, coded themes with frequency counts
975.method_detail: Semi-structured interviews with inductive coding, snowball sampling
975.finding: Engineers started from an existing solution and searched for problems it fit, showing little divergence in solutions but much in problems, unlike standard design process models.

977.who: About 25 sophomore design teams (headcount not reported); 78 industry engineers
977.task: Student teams drew function diagrams by an assigned method before concepts; 78 engineers' design reports checked for decomposition and grades
977.problem: Student project: device improving life of a disabled person; engineers: low-cost clothes washer for developing countries
977.prompt: Students designed an assistive device for a disabled person; engineers designed an extreme low-cost clothes washing device for developing countries
977.measured: Mapping of function diagram to final concept, detail of function diagrams, use and structure of functional decomposition, report grades
977.method_detail: Part 1 treatment by lab section in a course; part 2 correlational analysis of graded reports
977.finding: Top-down and energy-flow methods outperformed enumeration for students, while among professionals using functional decomposition did not correlate with design grades, suggesting it helps communication more than outcome.

979.who: 11 managers, architects and simulation experts at one carmaker; meeting attendees not counted
979.task: Researchers observed 5 decision meetings (40 decisions), ran 60-minute semi-structured interviews, and analyzed company process documents
979.problem: Vehicle platform development, design issue resolution supported by simulation
979.measured: Types of decision problems, decision-making process, challenges with modeling and simulation use, escalation of decisions
979.method_detail: Meeting observation, interviews and document analysis with qualitative coding; findings validated with company experts
979.finding: Design decisions were escalated upward as complexity, uncertainty and impact grew, and limited knowledge of simulation limits, ambiguity and uncertainty caused postponed decisions and iterations.

984.who: Simulated deep Q-learning agents in teams of 3-6 (no human participants)
984.task: Trained independent deep Q-learning agents to push a box, then tested networks across team sizes of 3-6 and 10-50% action noise
984.problem: Box-pushing task for self-organizing robot teams
984.prompt: Not applicable, agents learned to cooperatively push a box past an obstacle to a goal without central control
984.measured: Learning stability (cumulative reward convergence), scalability across team sizes, robustness to random action noise
984.method_detail: Simulation in pygame with multi-agent reinforcement learning
984.finding: Networks trained with larger teams generalized to different team sizes, but those trained with smaller teams did not scale up, so training should use team sizes at least as large as the target.

986.who: 54 senior undergraduate and graduate engineering students
986.task: Designed a connected cooling system in 30 minutes with 50 actions, interacting with teammates every 10 actions, every 5, or never
986.problem: Internet-connected cooling system for a 13-room house
986.prompt: Design a system of connected products that minimizes peak temperature (ideally under 24 C) and total cost (ideally under $20,000), within 50 design actions each
986.measured: Best team solution quality (peak temperature, cost), interaction frequency, post-survey perceptions such as personal satisfaction
986.method_detail: Three interaction-frequency conditions testing a computationally derived prediction
986.finding: Teams that did not interact and picked their best member's solution did best, as the computational model predicted, so interacting teams were inferior on this problem.

990.who: 40 university students (mechanical engineering and marketing) in 7 entrepreneurial teams
990.task: Teams interviewed over 100 people, generated over 100 ideas, prototyped and tested, and pitched in a semester course; members took the Big Five personality test
990.problem: Team-chosen ventures, e.g. gardener produce exchange, deaf-psychologist communication, campus transportation
990.prompt: Each team picked a need in one topic area (e.g. health, environment, transportation) and developed a technology-based product through design thinking
990.measured: Team average personality (TOP) and personality variability (TPD) on Big Five, instructor ranking of team performance (best versus worst)
990.method_detail: Course-based field study with cluster analysis of personality against team ranking
990.finding: Best-performing teams tended to have high variability in neuroticism and extraversion and average extraversion and agreeableness, suggesting member personalities affect team performance.

992.who: 21 university students aged 20-29 (11 with assistant, 10 without)
992.task: Sorted cards in the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task while also doing a speed-and-accuracy key-press task, with or without a Wizard-of-Oz voice assistant giving suggestions
992.problem: No design problem (card sorting task with simulated cognitive assistant)
992.prompt: Not applicable, participants sorted 31 cards by an inferred rule and could ask the assistant for help
992.measured: Card sorting accuracy, secondary task reaction time and accuracy, NASA-TLX workload and frustration, number of help requests
992.method_detail: Between-subjects lab study with random assignment
992.finding: Participants with the assistant performed better and felt less frustrated, but their mental workload was not significantly different from the control group.

994.who: 90 junior mechanical engineering students in 3-4 person teams (94 took the MBTI)
994.task: Did 10-minute ideation sessions in class, using individual or group brainstorming or mind mapping with a different prompt each week; team personality computed from MBTI
994.problem: Four short concept prompts, e.g. zoo-goer interaction with animals, supplies to remote areas, crop gathering, passenger travel
994.prompt: Generate concepts for a stated need, such as letting zoo visitors interact with animals or helping a farmer gather crops
994.measured: Quantity, quality and variety of ideas; team average MBTI personality and variance
994.method_detail: Pilot study, four lab sections each using a different ideation method per week; no statistical tests yet
994.finding: Teams with average personality near the extremes of Thinking-Feeling looked more creative, and neutral Introversion-Extraversion teams did best with brainstorming for quantity and mind mapping for quality.

995.who: 22 academic and industry experts in 7 teams of 2-3 at a conference
995.task: Analyzed an elevator system's design structure matrices with chosen software tools over about two hours plus an evening, then gave 10-minute recommendations and feedback
995.problem: Reducing risks from long lifecycle and lead time of an elevator system
995.prompt: Analyze the elevator DSMs and suggest architecture or other improvements to predict and prepare for late changes and long lead times
995.measured: Variety and usefulness of team recommendations, tools and DSM versions used, participant feedback
995.method_detail: Hackathon-style design sprint with an industry case; analysis of presentation videos and feedback session
995.finding: The sprint produced seven different sets of insights quickly from non-experts, useful for further analysis, though lack of detailed system knowledge limited depth.

999.who: Simulated heterogeneous agents pushing a box (no human participants)
999.task: Agents in a box-pushing simulation, some less competent, used a beta-distribution trust model or none, 100 runs per setting
999.problem: Box-pushing task for self-organizing agents with mixed competence
999.prompt: Not applicable, agents pushed a box toward a goal while avoiding an obstacle without central control
999.measured: Success rate (runs reaching goal without hitting obstacle), time duration to finish, with and without trust model
999.method_detail: Agent-based simulation with two-sample t tests across 100 runs per setting
999.finding: Adding a trust model raised success rate, especially with many incompetent agents, but task time first increased then decreased depending on how many agents were incompetent.

1002.who: 19 first-year engineering students in 5 teams of 3-4
1002.task: Wore sociometric badges in two class design sessions while video recorded; badge speech data compared with two raters' video coding
1002.problem: First-year course design project (specific problem not reported)
1002.measured: Badge accuracy and precision of speaking time versus video coding at 1-second resolution, speech dominance and turn-taking
1002.method_detail: Validation of wearable sensors against video coding in a course setting (inter-rater alpha 0.81)
1002.finding: Badges captured total speaking time accurately but missed precise speaking moments and often overestimated them, so they suit high-level participation measures but not fine turn-taking.

1003.who: 20 design automation experts (10 mechanical engineers, 10 architects) from industry, academia and research labs
1003.task: Planned aloud in 20-90 minute interviews how they would solve a bus stop problem and a roof sub-problem with computers; transcripts coded
1003.problem: Passively cooled open-air bus shelter for a tropical climate
1003.prompt: Plan your process for designing a passively comfortable open-air bus stop, then for designing its roof shape in a windy tropical setting
1003.measured: Over 1,300 coded statements (function, behavior, structure), 45 computational strategies, 10 challenges, phases and transition probabilities
1003.method_detail: Think-aloud interviews with function-behavior-structure coding (inter-rater agreement 76-80%)
1003.finding: Design automation followed four phases (discovery, evaluation, extrapolation, interpolation) with evaluation usually preceding extrapolation, and slow simulations and model preparation were key challenges.

1004.who: 30 graduate-level engineering design students (20 completed both sessions)
1004.task: Drew functional mental models of a hair dryer, clothes dryer and vacuum cleaner before and after three weeks of lectures and homework on functional modeling
1004.problem: Functional models of three household products
1004.prompt: Show the function and components of each outlined household product, following a worked toilet example
1004.measured: Mental model rubric scores for each product, before versus after instruction
1004.method_detail: Pre/post in-class intervention with blinded rubric scoring
1004.finding: Mental model scores improved after functional modeling instruction, significantly for clothes dryer and vacuum, while the hair dryer likely showed a ceiling effect.

1008.who: 34 startup representatives (mostly founders) from European and American incubator and accelerator programs
1008.task: Completed an online survey on funding, how often they used seven prototyping best practices, purposes of their prototypes, and how difficult typical startup tasks were
1008.problem: No design problem (startups' own product development)
1008.measured: Funding sources and sufficiency, frequency of prototyping best practices, prototype purposes (exploring, evaluating, communicating), perceived difficulty of startup tasks, risk-taking
1008.method_detail: K-means cluster analysis of survey responses into three startup groups
1008.finding: Startups with the most funding used prototyping best practices more often and reported less difficulty with startup tasks than other startups.

1010.who: 61 postgraduate students and professionals in Australia (38 male, 23 female, aged 18-65)
1010.task: Viewed images of 8 everyday artifacts for 10 seconds each while eye gaze was tracked, then picked and explained how they would use each object
1010.problem: Recognizing intended affordances of 8 artifacts (e.g. ashtray, cake server, corkscrew, caliper)
1010.prompt: Look at the object and say what you would most likely do with it, why, and what came to mind
1010.measured: Gaze data (areas of interest), correct identification of intended affordance, mention of function or semantic category
1010.method_detail: Screen-based eye-tracking experiment with logistic regression; 4 warm-up artifacts discarded
1010.finding: Gaze measures did not predict identifying the intended affordance, but mentioning the artifact's function or category strongly related to it, suggesting analogical priming rather than affordance perception.

1011.who: 85 first-year mechanical engineering students (40 in teams, 45 individuals)
1011.task: Solved a design problem in 30 minutes by sketching, as a team of five, alone in silence, or alone thinking aloud; constraints added at 10 and 20 minutes
1011.prompt: Design a low-cost, easy-to-make device that removes peanut shells, usable without electricity in developing countries and handling large quantities with little damage
1011.measured: Design quality and novelty of the final design, compared between real teams, nominal teams of five individuals, and speaking versus silent individuals
1011.method_detail: Three conditions run in class; nominal teams built from random groups of individuals
1011.finding: Individuals (nominal teams) produced higher-quality designs than collaborating teams, and thinking aloud did not hurt individuals' performance.

1012.who: 44 pre-first-year engineering students (35 male, 9 female) in 12 four-person teams
1012.task: Worked in teams on a four-week course design project and filled in a seven-item psychological safety survey at six time points, plus open-ended questions
1012.problem: Food insecurity problem in developing countries
1012.prompt: Choose or define a food insecurity or agricultural problem in developing countries and design a solution to reduce its burden on vulnerable populations
1012.measured: Team psychological safety (Edmondson 7-item scale) over time, reliability of the measure, open-ended reasons for changes
1012.method_detail: Longitudinal field study across two sections of a summer course
1012.finding: Psychological safety stabilized only after idea generation began, trajectories varied widely across teams, and dips often occurred during concept generation and selection.
