1014.who: 50 senior mechanical engineering students at one university
1014.task: In a 50-minute class, sketched the modified unit cell after applying two design guidelines in sequence, six packets of cases each, on two starting cell shapes
1014.problem: Unit cells for a flexible shear band of a non-pneumatic tire
1014.prompt: Apply the given guidelines in sequence to the initial unit cells to increase shear flexibility, and draw the resulting shape
1014.measured: Similarity and clustering of modified unit cells across 12 guideline sequences, novelty of results, subjectivity of guidelines
1014.method_detail: User study with packets randomized across 12 sequences, 300 responses over two initial cells
1014.finding: Guidelines can be applied in sequence, but order changes the resulting cells, especially when the subjective curved-beam guideline is used, which gave more novel results.

1015.who: Simulated designer agents in two-actor games (no human participants)
1015.task: Two simulated designers explored coupled design value spaces (10,000 random seeds), then their resulting values fed a strategy game analyzed for Nash equilibria
1015.problem: Synthetic two-actor design value spaces (Red and Blue scenarios)
1015.prompt: Not applicable, agents explored a shared value space and then chose cooperation or defection strategies
1015.measured: Frequency of converged design decisions, value asymmetry, Nash equilibria across Harmony/Concord and Prisoner's Dilemma strategy games
1015.method_detail: Multi-agent simulation of a bi-level collective design model, to generate hypotheses for later human studies
1015.finding: Agents often converged on symmetric design outcomes rather than global maxima, and the structure of value spaces shaped strategy dynamics, suggesting problem structure can align or misalign actors.

1018.who: 46 design professionals (R&D engineers, advanced engineers, managers) at one global manufacturer
1018.task: Completed an online survey on background, perceptions of risk in the company, creative risk-taking preferences, personality, and lottery questions
1018.problem: No design problem (survey about attitudes in the fuzzy front end)
1018.measured: Preferences for Creativity Scale risk-taking, financial risk aversion from lotteries, education, years of experience, job type
1018.method_detail: Preliminary online survey at one company
1018.finding: Education level and years of experience related to willingness to take risks on creative ideas, and R&D staff and managers were more financially risk averse than other engineers.

1019.who: 10 stakeholders in one cookstove project: 6 students, 3 NGO employees, 1 community partner
1019.task: Took part in 30-90 minute semi-structured interviews about the participatory co-design of an improved cookstove; transcripts coded against Lead User Theory
1019.problem: Improved cookstove for a village in Gujarat, India
1019.measured: Lead user characteristics (ahead of trend, expected benefit, technical expertise, prototyping access) and other user traits linked to co-design success
1019.method_detail: Interviews with thematic coding by three coders, following Yin's case study method
1019.finding: Technical expertise and high expected benefit mattered, being ahead of trend did not, and design communication skill and access to community preferences should extend the lead user concept.

1020.who: 21 factory workers, founders, faculty and students in Nigeria
1020.task: Researcher did in-person interviews and participant observation at two factories and two universities over summer 2018
1020.problem: No design problem (team coordination in manufacturing)
1020.measured: Obstacles to coordination between less-skilled and highly-skilled workers, effects on accountability, predictability and common understanding
1020.method_detail: Ethnographic fieldwork with semi-structured interviews, notes and thematic coding
1020.finding: Resource scarcity hindered coordination through unclear roles, poor attitudes toward work, under- and overuse of employees, and worker demoralization, weakening accountability, predictability and common understanding.

1021.task: Performed design tasks of varying difficulty (choosing the best solution, or sketching one) on a touchpad while EEG was recorded, then rated each task's hardness
1021.problem: Short design problems of varying hardness (details not reported)
1021.measured: Transient microstate percentage of EEG signals compared with self-rated task hardness, eyes-closed baseline
1021.method_detail: EEG microstate segmentation analysis of data from earlier lab experiments
1021.finding: The proposed transient microstate percentage was low at rest and higher for harder-rated tasks, suggesting it can index perceived hardness of design problems.

1022.who: 60 MIT students (30 female, 30 male; undergraduates, master's, PhD)
1022.task: Each designed two 2D truss structures in 15-minute problems, using a design-only, design-plus-analysis, or design-plus-analysis-plus-optimization tool, after tutorials and surveys
1022.problem: 2D linear truss for a bridge and for a windblown road sign (cantilever)
1022.prompt: Design a truss for a bridge or a windblown sign, shown by a brief statement and illustration, with lowest material cost for a feasible structure
1022.measured: Cost of best design (material volume), speed of improvement, design complexity (number of members), efficiency across tool levels
1022.method_detail: Within-subjects study, 12 problem and tool order permutations, 5 participants each
1022.finding: More integrated tools gave better designs faster, and the fully integrated tool with optimization let half of designers reach costs that other tools' users never achieved.

1023.who: Undergraduate engineering students (number not reported), a 4-year-old lead user, daycare toddlers
1023.task: Students designed toys for the lead user and prototyped three; the lead user and daycare children played with them while observers counted behaviors
1023.problem: Toys encouraging two-handed play for a child with hemiplegic cerebral palsy
1023.prompt: Design toys that suit the extraordinary motor needs of one child with cerebral palsy, encouraging two-handed play and being rewarding to use
1023.measured: Play duration, number of intended functions accomplished, children achieving solutions, using a modified Early Problem Solving Indicator observation
1023.method_detail: Lead user design with prototype testing at a daycare center
1023.finding: The lead user did 6 of 9 intended functions, and daycare children played longer and also found the toys challenging, suggesting designs for one extreme user can suit a broader group.

1024.who: Simulated agents with varied cognitive styles (no human participants)
1024.task: Teams of simulated agents (8 for beam, 33 for race car) worked 100-step simulations with different cognitive styles, sub-team assignments and problem decompositions
1024.problem: Cantilever beam design and SAE race car design (56 variables)
1024.prompt: Not applicable, agents searched a decomposed design space to optimize a global objective
1024.measured: Team performance on the objective function by cognitive style (KAI), role-style alignment, effect of problem decomposition
1024.method_detail: Agent-based model (KABOOM) of cognitive style, not validated with human data
1024.finding: Effects of cognitive style depended on the problem: style did not matter for the beam but more innovative teams did better on the car, and aligning styles with roles helped.

1025.who: Simulated annealing teams (no humans); compared with 16 human teams of 3
1025.task: Configured simulated teams to replicate a human truss design study (three problem statements over six 4-minute sessions), then removed model features from 100 teams to see which mattered
1025.problem: Truss structure design with changing problem statements
1025.prompt: Not applicable, simulated teams minimized truss mass under safety factor constraints; the original human problem required a safety factor of 1.25 with lowest mass
1025.measured: Simulated versus human team performance correlation, effect of removing each cognitive feature on final performance
1025.method_detail: Agent-based model (CISAT) validated against previously published human team data
1025.finding: Simulated team results correlated strongly with the human study, and self-bias and organic interaction timing were the features most important to team success.

1026.who: 30 designers in 10 groups of 3 (secondary data; 222 individual tasks analyzed)
1026.task: Reanalyzed logs of individuals solving a context-free parameter design task by moving sliders on coupled or uncoupled problems
1026.problem: Abstract parameter design (linear system with 2-6 variables)
1026.measured: Number of actions, productivity, performance, error, with gender and problem complexity as predictors
1026.method_detail: Secondary analysis of computer action logs from an earlier experiment, with regression
1026.finding: Designer behavior (actions, performance, error) could be predicted from problem complexity and gender, and more actions went with higher error and lower performance.

1028.who: 10 employees of one large power tool company (engineers, designers, project managers, a vice president)
1028.task: Took part in 30-60 minute semi-structured interviews run by five teams of two interviewers about requirements; transcripts and documents analyzed
1028.problem: No design problem (use of requirements in product development)
1028.measured: Presence of a requirements culture (shared communication, artifacts, norms and values), differences across departments, engagement with requirements
1028.method_detail: Semi-structured interviews with snowball sampling at one company site; abstract says ten interviews, only nine transcripts listed
1028.finding: The company had a clear requirement culture, consistent transfer of requirements between departments was necessary, and engagement was higher among those involved early in product development.

1031.who: 1 team of 4 graduate students; 3 raters coded video
1031.task: Team built a function structure model together in about 53 minutes while on video; raters coded functional leadership behaviors from 10-minute segments
1031.problem: Function structure for an automatic household recycling sorter
1031.prompt: Design an automatic household recycling machine that sorts bottles, glass, aluminum and tin cans, compresses and stores them, aiming for about 15 seconds per item
1031.measured: Leadership functions coded (task, relational, transition and action phases), intra-rater and inter-rater agreement (percent agreement, Cohen's kappa)
1031.method_detail: Protocol study piloting a leadership coding protocol on one team video
1031.finding: The leadership protocol showed high intra-rater agreement and acceptable inter-rater reliability, and clarifying leader and follower behaviors should improve agreement further.

1033.who: 201 Amazon Mechanical Turk respondents (100 plus 101 in two rounds)
1033.task: Rated how likely each product concept would persuade them to adopt a behavior, gave reasons, and split 10 points across egoistic, sociocultural and altruistic motives
1033.problem: Concepts to promote reusable shopping bags and taking stairs instead of elevators
1033.prompt: Judge how likely each concept would persuade you to perform the behavior, then rate how relevant each motive type is to you
1033.measured: Concept ratings on a 4-point scale, self-assessed motive type, relatedness of concepts targeting the same motive, match between dominant motive and preferred concept
1033.method_detail: Two online survey iterations plus categorization of news comments to explore the motive model
1033.finding: The three-motive model described public comments, but preferences for matching concepts deviated from predictions mostly because respondents perceived concepts in unexpected ways, so concepts needed revision.

1034.who: Senior mechanical engineering students (170 designer-study and 22 protocol-study models; headcount not reported)
1034.task: Completed function structures from seed models using forward, backward or nucleation chaining at 10, 40 or 80 percent, on paper in class or on video
1034.problem: Function structures for two electromechanical design problems
1034.measured: Functions and flows added to the seed model, quality score of final model, comparison between designer and protocol studies
1034.method_detail: Mixed factorial design run as a class designer study and a smaller protocol study
1034.finding: Models from the protocol and designer studies did not differ significantly, and nucleation seeds led to more functions and flows added, with small differences in quality scores.

1035.who: 19 first-year engineering students analyzed (30 consented) in 7 teams
1035.task: Generated ideas individually with design heuristic cards, later sorted teammates' ideas into consider or do not consider, and completed creativity preference and cognitive style questionnaires
1035.measured: Preferences for Creativity Scale, Kirton adaption-innovation score, expert-rated creativity, quality and originality of 116 ideas generated and selected
1035.method_detail: Exploratory correlational study within an 8-week course project
1035.finding: Creativity preferences (team centrality, risk tolerance) predicted how creative the ideas students selected were but not how creative their own ideas were, and cognitive style had small effects.

1036.who: 680 users of the Local Motors online co-innovation community (behavior data mined, no direct contact)
1036.task: Researchers mined 9,571 participation records from one vehicle project, defined four behavior properties and inferred user motivations from actual behavior
1036.prompt: Not applicable, users voluntarily contributed to an online vehicle design project
1036.measured: User participation behaviors and their properties, six inferred motivations (status, individuality, monetary rewards, social relations, interest and curiosity, enjoyment)
1036.method_detail: Netnography with web mining, based on expectancy theory
1036.finding: Six motivations were identified, with most users driven by interest and curiosity, many by social relations and monetary rewards, and few by status or individuality.

1037.who: 22 MIT students and postdocs with mechanical design experience
1037.task: Solved five parameter design tasks in a software interface by adjusting input sliders and pressing calculate until all constraints were met; action logs analyzed and compared with simulated annealing
1037.problem: Two-pass seawater reverse osmosis desalination plant design (2x2 up to 10x5 variables)
1037.prompt: Set flow and equipment parameters of a seawater reverse osmosis plant so that all output constraints are satisfied
1037.measured: Distance to target, step size and problem progress per iteration, performance ranking, match to simulated annealing behavior
1037.method_detail: Lab task with action-log analysis and end interview, compared to an algorithm
1037.finding: Top-performing subjects behaved like a well-tuned simulated annealing algorithm, while the worst performers used a roughly random search.

1038.task: Researchers observed each team for 8-10 months (55-87 hours each), ran interviews and focus groups, and collected documents and artifacts; coded with grounded theory
1038.problem: Audio board, kid's winter boots and surgical device 2.0 development projects
1038.prompt: Not applicable, teams carried on their own product development
1038.measured: Definition of a prototype and the roles prototypes play in company product development
1038.method_detail: Qualitative fieldwork (grounded theory with ethnographic observation) across three companies
1038.finding: A prototype is a physical embodiment of critical design elements, and prototypes played three roles: enabling communication, informing decisions, and aiding learning.

1039.who: 20 university students (15 undergraduate, 5 graduate) in IT-related majors
1039.task: Programmed a simulated smart lock to a schedule and went through 5 scenarios, checking whether the door locked, in two sessions with different agent gender and location
1039.problem: Smart lock home automation simulation (no design object)
1039.prompt: Program the smart lock according to the provided schedule, then handle five everyday scenarios and optionally check the lock status
1039.measured: Explicit trust behavior (observable actions such as checking and correcting), implicit trust (reaction time), effect of stereotype congruence
1039.method_detail: 2x2 between-subjects design (agent gender by home or office location) with counterbalanced second run
1039.finding: Users showed more explicit trust in stereotype-congruent systems, but implicit measures such as reaction time showed no such difference.

1040.who: 10 designers: 3 undergraduates, 2 design consultants, 5 professional designers (ages 21-54)
1040.task: Took part in 30-55 minute semi-structured interviews describing a recent user-centered design project and situations of perspective taking, concern and distress
1040.problem: No design problem (recalled user-centered design projects)
1040.measured: Antecedents and outcomes of cognitive and affective empathy toward users, coded themes
1040.method_detail: Retrospective semi-structured interviews with thematic analysis; data saturation not reached
1040.finding: Cognitive empathy improved accuracy of user understanding and led to design changes, while affective empathy increased acknowledgement of user problems and motivation to help users.

1042.who: 228 third-year mechanical engineering students in 75 teams (text also says 70)
1042.task: Teams chose a concept then sketched their current prototype concept at three times over 8 weeks and submitted a final prototype; sketches and prototypes scored with ideation metrics
1042.prompt: Design an educational activity that uses 3D printing to create a novel, engaging hands-on classroom experience, packaged easily and costing under $50
1042.measured: Originality, effectiveness, implementability and applicability scores over time, metric reliability and discriminatory power
1042.method_detail: Within-subjects pilot study in a semester course; rating of concepts at four time points
1042.finding: Implementability and applicability could not be applied after the second time point, and originality and effectiveness gave limited insight, so new prototype metrics are needed.

1043.task: Built a function structure model on a whiteboard while videotaped, after a pre-survey and before a post-survey; videos coded for pauses and what was added after them
1043.problem: Function structure for an automatic clothes ironing device or an automatic recycling sorter
1043.prompt: Design an automatic machine (hotel clothes ironer, or household recycling sorter) and model it as a function structure; roughly 5 minutes per garment or 15 seconds per item desired
1043.measured: Pause time and frequency, pauses by quarter of the session, pause length groups, model elements added, edited or deleted after pauses
1043.method_detail: Protocol study with video coding of pauses; groups too small for significance tests
1043.finding: Participants spent about 38% of modeling time paused, mostly added elements, deleted after longer pauses and edited after shorter ones, and paused more before adding flows.

1044.who: 35 graduate students in 9 teams of 3-4 from two Clemson University groups
1044.task: Teams jointly built a function structure model on video; videos coded for leadership functions by individual and by time period
1044.problem: Function structure for an automatic household recycling machine
1044.prompt: Design an automatic household recycling machine that sorts bottles, glass, aluminum and tin cans, compresses and stores them, aiming for about 15 seconds per item
1044.measured: Leadership function occurrences (transition, action, relational), distribution across members, emergence of leaders over quintiles, leader-follower networks
1044.method_detail: Protocol study applying a leadership coding protocol to team videos; abstract calls participants undergraduates but text describes graduate students
1044.finding: Teams had no formal leaders, most leadership behavior was transition and action functions, early top leaders usually stayed on top, and leadership was shared across members.

1045.who: 27 practicing design professionals (2-45 years of experience, mean 20)
1045.task: Completed an online survey about preferences for creative ideas, concept selection practices, and familiarity with and usefulness of 11 formal selection methods
1045.problem: No design problem (survey on concept selection practice)
1045.measured: Preference for creativity, selection practices, familiarity and perceived utility of formal concept selection methods, factors limiting their use
1045.method_detail: Exploratory online survey, 59 questions of which 39 are reported
1045.finding: Designers personally preferred creative ideas but felt their organizations did not, and they relied on informal selection (reviews, client opinion, personal preference) rather than formal methods they barely knew.

1046.who: 9 junior mechanical engineering students (7 male, 2 female) for the chunking study
1046.task: Sketched a design concept on a tablet with software that color-coded pen-stroke clusters by pauses, then labeled objects in the sketch; a second part develops information metrics
1046.prompt: Design a device that cooks burger patties consistently and automatically, given that a person inserts each new patty
1046.measured: Cognitive chunks detected from pen strokes and pauses (cluster size per object), entity-relation model and four information content metrics of sketches
1046.method_detail: Protocol study with automated chunk detection, plus method development and verification of metrics
1046.finding: Most objects were drawn in a single cluster, supporting chunking during sketching, and these chunks allowed information content of sketches to be computed with an entity-relation model.

1047.who: 12 graduate engineering students (data from 2 removed for poor signal)
1047.task: Generated solutions to three tasks, one each with brainstorming, morphological analysis and TRIZ, while a near-infrared brain sensor on the prefrontal cortex recorded blood oxygenation
1047.problem: Window raising aid for the elderly, alarm clock for the hearing impaired, kitchen measuring tool for the blind
1047.prompt: Design an aid for the stated user group in each of three tasks, describing designs in words or figures
1047.measured: Oxygenated hemoglobin (BOLD) response across 20 time segments, left and right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activation, brain network density and centrality
1047.method_detail: Within-subjects lab study with fNIRS neuroimaging; technique order fixed to task order
1047.finding: Brainstorming evoked a high left DLPFC response early that was not sustained, while morphological analysis and TRIZ gave repeated high responses and denser brain network coordination.

1048.who: 18 undergraduate students from varied majors (IT, general engineering, business, criminology)
1048.task: Read 8 information pieces about the problem, typed as many ideas as they wanted, then freely recalled the information pieces from memory
1048.problem: Reducing pedestrian accidents caused by phone distraction on campus
1048.prompt: Develop new, innovative ideas that reduce pedestrian accidents caused by distraction from mobile devices
1048.measured: Time on each information piece, linguistic properties (LIWC cognitive-process scores) of generated ideas and recalled information, correlations between them
1048.method_detail: Exploratory online study with no comparison groups; Spearman correlations of text features
1048.finding: Memory use during idea generation showed both semantic and linguistic components, with language features of recalled information pieces relating to those of the ideas generated.

1050.who: 4 US engineers working at a Rwandan waste-to-fuel manufacturing company
1050.task: Researcher observed the plant for 10 days, then interviewed each engineer for about an hour about prototyping purposes, methods and constraints
1050.prompt: Interview questions on how they define prototyping, a recent prototype and its process, materials, iterations and lessons learned
1050.measured: Purpose of prototyping, prototype characteristics and methods, resource constraints and their effect on design outcomes (coded themes)
1050.method_detail: Site visit plus semi-structured phone interviews, one coder
1050.finding: Engineers prototyped to build high-fidelity functional models through simple iteration and physical builds, held back by variable inputs, limited manufacturing access and weak modeling predictions.

1051.who: 5 female students using an academic makerspace
1051.task: Took part in a series of three 90-minute in-depth interviews about their making history and experience; second interviews of two students coded
1051.prompt: Open-ended interview questions about life history of making, current makerspace experience, and what making means to them
1051.measured: How learning occurs, design skills learned, life skills learned (coding scheme from open and axial coding)
1051.method_detail: Phenomenological interviewing with grounded-theory style coding; preliminary analysis of about ten percent of data
1051.finding: A preliminary coding scheme shows these women learn both design skills and life skills in the makerspace, and describes the ways that learning happens.

1052.who: 27 engineering students in 9 teams (3 teams each of 1, 3, 5)
1052.task: Teams of different size solved a design problem while protocols were recorded; talk was coded for micro- and macro-strategies and solutions scored
1052.problem: Machine to separate recycled glass, aluminum, paper and plastic into crates
1052.prompt: Design a machine that tells apart glass, aluminum, paper and plastic and sorts each into a separate crate
1052.measured: Micro-strategies (e.g. proposing, analyzing solutions), macro-strategies such as backtracking, final design score on constraints, manufacturability, feasibility, cost
1052.method_detail: Exploratory protocol study with team size as the condition
1052.finding: Larger teams analyzed more and proposed less, teams of three scored best on final designs, and teams of five backtracked most often.

1053.who: 11 industry practitioners (engineers and designers) from engineering firms and design studios in Central Europe
1053.task: Took part in 90 to 180 minute semi-structured interviews on how they find, select, adapt and assess design methods and share experience
1053.prompt: Interview questions on company, personal background, a typical design project, and use and selection of design methods
1053.measured: How practitioners search for, select, assess and share experiences about design methods
1053.method_detail: Semi-structured interviews in German, in person or by phone, over five months
1053.finding: Practitioners find, select and assess methods in similar ways, judge efficacy as the key criterion, and want context-specific exchange of experience with peers.

1055.who: 18 mechanical engineers aged 25-40 analyzed (26 recorded, 8 excluded for EEG or video problems)
1055.task: Wore a 14-channel EEG headset for five tasks: furniture problem-solving, basic and open layout design, then sketching an entertainment system
1055.problem: Furniture layout in a room, and a future personal entertainment system
1055.prompt: Place furniture pieces under stated requirements, then arrange a room freely, then sketch an outline of a future personal entertainment system
1055.measured: EEG task-related power and transformed power per electrode, time-related activation and associated Brodmann areas, task duration
1055.method_detail: Within-subject EEG study extending an earlier fMRI task set
1055.finding: Brain activation was higher when designing than when problem-solving, with time-related neural responses linked to cognitive functions of particular Brodmann areas.

1056.who: 130 sophomore mechanical engineering students (45, 40 and 45 per treatment)
1056.task: After a tutorial and quiz, converted 8 raw lawn-mower customer need statements into requirement statements using an assigned method in a 50-55 minute class
1056.prompt: Turn a set of raw customer statements about a lawn mower into customer requirement statements using the assigned derivation method
1056.measured: Eight metrics on derived requirements, including number, completion time, relevance, clarity and specificity
1056.method_detail: Pilot study with random assignment to a traditional or one of two affordance-modeling methods
1056.finding: No requirement derivation method was dominant among novice students, although the three methods differed on most of the evaluation metrics.

1057.who: Leaders of 26 nuclear reactor design projects (36 interviews; number of individual people not reported)
1057.task: Took part in open-ended interviews (23 by phone, 13 in person) about their reactor design project, decisions and the principles guiding them
1057.prompt: Open-ended interview questions on project motivation, choice of reactor technology and size, safety and cost decisions, and commercialization
1057.measured: Explicit (self-aware) and implicit (naive) design principles found by grounded-theory coding of interviews
1057.method_detail: Cross-sectional stratified sample of projects by reactor technology and organization; coded in Atlas.ti
1057.finding: Designers state a few principles explicitly and implicitly follow others that recur across projects, and the ability to articulate principles grows with the number of prior designs in the domain.

1059.who: 56 Imperial College students (20, 20, 8, 8 across four groups)
1059.task: Held an 8 pound card, chose a mug price, paid after a slider stroke and/or visual reminder, then answered a questionnaire
1059.problem: Tangible interaction for cashless payment (prototype card slider with display)
1059.measured: Mug valuation, ownership of card balance, ownership of purchased item, payment aversion (7-point questionnaire), open comments
1059.method_detail: 2x2 between-subjects test of a prototype built with a proposed tangibility framework; follow-up discussion
1059.finding: The tangible interaction increased psychological ownership of digital money, but its effect on payment aversion and spending behavior was inconclusive.

1063.who: 24 engineering students (20 undergraduate, 4 graduate) in 12 pairs
1063.task: Pairs built two mind-maps of 10 minutes each on a shared web canvas without talking, then answered questionnaires; sessions video and data logged
1063.problem: Mind-mapping on solar energy and on space travel
1063.prompt: Brainstorm the uses, benefits, limitations and solutions around solar energy, and the needs, difficulties, ideas and solutions for space travel
1063.measured: Expert-rated quantity, variety, novelty and quality of maps, map growth over time, participation, exploration patterns, pauses, self-reported knowledge and collaboration
1063.method_detail: Inter-rater outcome ratings plus video protocol analysis of the process
1063.finding: Partners acted as a catalyst for exploring ideas, with patterns and pauses in exploration varying by topic and phase, pointing to needs for computer-supported mind-mapping.

1067.who: 42 experienced designers in 14 teams of three, plus corpus of research meetings
1067.task: Teams redesigned a non-functional hand-held material-sensing device in 30-minute videotaped meetings; transcripts analyzed for language style matching over time and teams ranked by experts
1067.problem: Redesign of a hand-held device said to identify material properties
1067.prompt: Redesign a hand-held device that could identify the material properties of nearby items, using supplied drawings and prototypes of varying coarseness
1067.measured: Style Entrainment Signal measures from transcripts, expert team rankings on how much the design changed and how relevant it was
1067.method_detail: Secondary analysis of existing meeting transcripts with an automated language measure
1067.finding: Teams whose conversation showed a forward-moving pattern of language-style anti-entrainment produced better-rated designs, and better teams also converged in language as meetings progressed.

1071.who: 104 adult participants of varied gender, age, marital status and driving experience
1071.task: Completed an online survey of 36 ranking, rating and short-answer questions with images and text about perceived injury probability and severity for vehicle designs
1071.measured: Perceived probability and seriousness of injury, ranking of design factors (shape, size, structure, color, mass, component quality, speed) by personal characteristics
1071.method_detail: Factor analysis and breakdown by personality, gender, driving experience, age, marital status
1071.finding: Perceived vehicle safety varied with personal traits and experience, with shape the most influential feature for everyone and experienced drivers weighing speed and specific components more.

1072.who: 96 mid-career graduate students (62 in 2013, 34 in 2014) in 18 teams
1072.task: Teams chose a concept, built a prototype on an $800 budget and filed seven requirement documents; judges ranked products
1072.problem: Student-chosen product opportunities (e.g. backpack converting to laptop desk)
1072.prompt: Identify a product opportunity, then design and deliver a working prototype
1072.measured: Number and change rate of requirements, requirement priority and risk over time, product success ranking by judges
1072.method_detail: Quantitative analysis of team requirement documents over two course years; top versus bottom teams compared
1072.finding: A falling risk level of requirements, especially high-priority ones, predicted project success, while the number and change rate of requirements related less clearly.

1073.who: 15 respondents to an online conjoint survey (potential users of a child-tracking wearable)
1073.task: Chose between text scenario cards describing user experiences of a child-tracking wearable in two online choice tests (6 and 8 comparison sets)
1073.problem: Flexible wearable for parent-child communication and tracking
1073.measured: Utility values (part-worths) for alert type, location tracking display, and optional communication and reminder experiences
1073.method_detail: Scenario-based choice conjoint analysis within a product development case study, complementing interviews
1073.finding: Respondents preferred sound or vibration alerts and map-based tracking and valued alerting the child, while a passive reminder was clearly disliked and dropped from the product.

1075.who: 48 participants (44 analyzed; mostly Stanford affiliates, 32 women and 12 men among those analyzed)
1075.task: Viewed emotion-evoking images, then asked a mock-up Amazon Echo ten questions, rated each response's competence and expectation, and reported trust afterward
1075.problem: Interaction with a voice assistant (Amazon Echo mock-up)
1075.prompt: Ask the device a set of ten given questions in random order and listen to its responses
1075.measured: Perceived competence of each response, whether expectations were met, trust-related statements and trust propensity after interaction
1075.method_detail: Between-subjects priming (positive, neutral, negative images) with Wizard-of-Oz recorded responses
1075.finding: Affective priming did not change overall trust, though effects of primes and perceived competence on trust appeared only for participants whose expectations were met.

1076.who: 253 public participants recruited via a survey panel (60% male)
1076.task: Watched a tutorial, then reshaped seed 3D models of two products in a web tool, tagged the shapes, and gave design-process and usability feedback
1076.problem: Computer mouse, bicycle seat, pen holder, cola bottle
1076.measured: User-created virtual prototypes (shape clusters), tags describing shapes, self-reported design process and interface usability
1076.method_detail: Online crowdsourcing study with 506 user-made prototypes analyzed by shape clustering and tag semantics
1076.finding: Web-based co-creation captured varied form and function requirements from customers and surfaced innovative concepts and links between user perception and product shape.

1077.who: Research team coders plus 3 engineering graduate students (total not reported)
1077.task: Built a customer-need ontology from design textbook categories and tested it in five coding trials of 40 to 75 customer needs, reconciling disagreements
1077.problem: Categorizing customer needs for everyday products (toy, camera, coffee maker, car door, restaurant)
1077.measured: Inter-rater reliability of each of five taxonomies across trials
1077.method_detail: Iterative ontology development with inter-rater reliability testing across 11 iterations
1077.finding: The final ontology has five taxonomies (Who, What, Message, Innovative, Recipient); expert coders reached up to substantial agreement and new coders reached fair to moderate agreement.

1078.who: 217 engineering undergraduates (freshmen and seniors; 80+36 with example, 53+48 without)
1078.task: Sketched garbage-collection concepts for 10 minutes, either after handling an example grabber product (modified 6-3-5 in nominal groups) or without one, working alone
1078.problem: Next-generation litter or trash collection system
1078.prompt: Design a next-generation litter collection system (with an example product) or trash collection system (without one)
1078.measured: Concept originality (0-10 coded scale), fixation on the example, curriculum level (freshman vs senior)
1078.method_detail: Between-groups comparison in class sessions across two years; coder kappa 0.79
1078.finding: Seniors produced more original concepts than freshmen, those given an example showed more fixation, and with an example higher fixation went with lower originality, especially for seniors.

1079.who: 9 MIT mechanical engineering students with CAD experience (3 solo, 3 pairs)
1079.task: Made as many of 42 given edits to a toy-car CAD model as possible in 60 minutes, alone or in pairs, while faces were recorded
1079.problem: Editing a toy car CAD model
1079.prompt: Carry out a list of 42 edits to a toy car model, such as adding a chamfer to wheel edges or setting the wheel diameter to 30 mm
1079.measured: Facial emotion detections (e.g. joy, fear, contempt), CAD activity events preceding emotions, frequency and logistic regression links
1079.method_detail: Small-sample comparison of single versus paired working styles with automated facial emotion detection
1079.finding: Paired designers showed more emotion than solo designers, and emotions were partly predictable from preceding CAD activities such as graphics-area work for solo users and chat or menu use for pairs.

1081.who: 8 university students (5 undergraduate, 3 graduate; 7 male, 1 female)
1081.task: Did risk and trust surveys, then in one session programmed a simulated smart lock across scenarios, chose whether to check it, rated trust
1081.prompt: Program the smart lock to a given weekly schedule and decide in each scenario whether to check the door, imagining use in a dorm or a research office
1081.measured: Perceived trustworthiness, checking behavior, risk and ambiguity aversion, propensity to trust machines, follow-up interview answers
1081.method_detail: Pilot 2x2 study of agent location (home/office) and voice gender (female/male) with qualitative questions
1081.finding: Users trusted stereotype-congruent agents more, meaning a male voice in the office and a female voice at home, while location and gender alone had no significant effect.

1082.who: 40 participants with CAD course experience (31 males, 9 females, aged 19-33)
1082.task: Did a spatial cognition test, then reviewed gearbox assemblies for errors in four display environments and with different controllers, answering multiple-choice questions
1082.problem: Finding errors in gearbox assembly models
1082.prompt: Decide whether CAD errors are present in the assembly and, if so, where they are located
1082.measured: Accuracy in identifying assembly errors (misalignment, collision, ergonomic), spatial cognition score, experience survey
1082.method_detail: Two within-subject experiments: output display immersion (2D, 3D CAD, two VR modes) and input controller type
1082.finding: Head-mounted VR improved error identification over 2D representations of the design, and the keyboard and mouse controller setup was clearly less suited to virtual design review.

1083.who: Engineering students from one lab in teams of 2-3 (7 unique users; total not reported)
1083.task: Built cardboard towers in 10-minute rounds, logged each design with the ARCHIE photo-and-questionnaire device, tested the tower with a weight, then redesigned and logged again
1083.problem: Cardboard tower holding maximum weight at its highest point
1083.prompt: Build a cardboard tower that supports the most weight at its top
1083.measured: Requirements listed, prototype goals chosen, feasibility and user feedback on the data-collection device across 9 logged designs
1083.method_detail: Pilot test of a newly built automated data-collection device in a contrived design activity
1083.finding: ARCHIE captured designers' requirements, prototype goals and design changes between iterations without researcher intervention, showing it is feasible for logging prototyping in design projects.

1086.who: One 4-person multidisciplinary design team (the authors took part), with two supporting industry projects
1086.task: Team built over 200 prototypes in 6 months for a bank fintech product; researchers analyzed cost, time and information gained for 50 concepts
1086.problem: Fintech product-service helping young people adopt digital payments
1086.prompt: A bank asked the team to create an innovative product-service to move the young generation onto digital payment
1086.measured: Prototype cost, time, fidelity and design information value per prototyping effort, plots of value against fidelity
1086.method_detail: Participatory inductive study of one driving industry project, compared with two supporting projects
1086.finding: Higher fidelity did not bring more value, so heuristics follow: raise prototype dimensionality, test core concepts with cheap low-fidelity models, and use DIY methods.

1087.who: 167 students in an introductory machine design class
1087.task: Picked which of four alternative designs was most similar to a baseline in up to five shaft-design scenarios, as extra-credit items in the final exam
1087.prompt: Choose which of four alternatives is most similar to the baseline design, judged on a given output parameter
1087.measured: Share of knowledge-based versus feature-based similarity answers, relation to final exam score on fatigue theory
1087.method_detail: Probabilistic similarity model tested with simulations and an exam-embedded student experiment
1087.finding: The knowledge-based measure reproduced known features of similarity such as context dependence and directionality, and students with higher exam scores leaned more on knowledge than on surface features, though marginally.

1088.who: 25 adults: 11 with upper-limb disabilities, 14 without (tested with and without a suit)
1088.task: Used kitchen product pairs while thinking aloud and on video, and did a nine-hole peg test; non-disabled people repeated tasks wearing a disability simulation suit
1088.problem: Kitchen tools (can openers, garlic presses, jar openers, ice trays), inclusive vs ordinary versions
1088.prompt: Use each product and voice thoughts and experiences, with a researcher only asking for clarification
1088.measured: Customer need statements and overlap between groups, nine-hole peg test times, need weights and frequencies
1088.method_detail: Validation of a disability simulation suit against people with disabilities, via protocol analysis
1088.finding: Suit wearers produced a comparable set of customer needs to people with disabilities, but the suit slowed hand dexterity more than actual disabilities did.

1091.who: 315 Mechanical Turk workers (kept if they recognized car brands at 30% or more)
1091.task: Ranked car-face images on one styling attribute and named brands, morphed a 3D car with sliders, then ranked and identified morphed designs
1091.problem: Front styling of Audi, BMW, Cadillac and Lexus midsize cars
1091.prompt: Morph a 3D vehicle model to maximize one styling attribute such as aggressive or sporty, after ranking vehicle images on that attribute
1091.measured: Brand recognition of original and morphed designs, ten styling attributes (e.g. powerful, sporty, innovative), design freedom distance
1091.method_detail: Crowdsourced online experiment feeding logit and Markov-chain models of brand recognition
1091.finding: Brand recognition depends strongly on the manufacturer, and predictive models can measure the tradeoff between design freedom and brand recognition to guide styling decisions.

1092.who: 46 first-year engineering design undergraduates (21 female, 25 male)
1092.task: Rated self-efficacy, brainstormed 10 minutes, built a wood or cardboard tower in 45 minutes logging tool use, then justified choices in open questions
1092.problem: Tall, strong, attractive tower holding weight at its top
1092.prompt: Design a tower as tall and attractive as possible that holds the most weight at its highest point, using wood or cardboard
1092.measured: Tool and material choices, tower performance, engineering design and tinkering self-efficacy, tool familiarity, coded justifications of decisions
1092.method_detail: Controlled in-class building task with quantitative analysis plus qualitative coding of reflections
1092.finding: Tool familiarity and self-efficacy shaped material choice and tower performance, and students justified poor decisions by blaming outside factors or using passive language.

1094.who: 108 university participants (72 in round one, 36 in round two), mostly students
1094.task: Compared pairs of cars and electric bicycles with shared and unique features as text, images or both, sequential or side by side, with eye tracking
1094.problem: Choosing between competing cars and electric bicycles
1094.prompt: Indicate preference for product Y over product X on an 8-level scale, then rate satisfaction and goodness of each
1094.measured: Preference ratings, satisfaction with choice, goodness ratings, gaze attention to shared versus unique attributes
1094.method_detail: Six between-subject conditions (text, image, image-with-text; sequential or side-by-side) with eye tracking
1094.finding: Shared text attributes cancel as predicted only in limited cases, shared image features instead reinforce impressions, and differences between products draw more gaze than commonalities.

1097.who: 72 first-year engineering students (23 sketch, 25 cardboard, 24 CAD condition)
1097.task: Completed a lottery risk survey, then viewed 9 milk-frother prototypes at one fidelity and rated likelihood to advance, risk, uniqueness and usefulness
1097.prompt: As an engineer on a team redesigning a milk frother usable with minimal instruction, decide which of 9 ideas to present to the board
1097.measured: Financial risk aversion, likelihood to move forward, perceived risk, perceived uniqueness and usefulness, expert-rated uniqueness and usefulness
1097.method_detail: Online between-subjects survey, random assignment to prototype fidelity
1097.finding: Students favored concepts with medium uniqueness and high usefulness; prototype fidelity and individual risk aversion did not predict choice, though more useful concepts seemed less risky.

1098.who: 92 online survey respondents (42 female, 50 male, licensed drivers recruited via Mechanical Turk)
1098.task: Answered driving-style questions, rated how effective three dashboard displays would be at encouraging smooth driving, rated any existing display, and completed an inclination questionnaire
1098.problem: Dashboard eco-driving display (coffee cup, wrecking ball, dial gauge)
1098.measured: Perceived effectiveness of each display, driving style, driver inclination toward efficient driving, demographics, existing display use
1098.method_detail: Online survey with regression models controlling for seven driver measures
1098.finding: Drivers significantly preferred the animated coffee-cup display over the other two displays as a way to encourage smoother driving, after controlling for demographics.

1099.who: 44 university students aged 21-29 (target segment of young adults), a 7-person verification round included
1099.task: Each viewed 3 physical prototypes of an alarm device with stated price and battery life, and rated each one's desirability from 1 to 5
1099.problem: Anti-theft alarm device for a hardware startup
1099.prompt: Rate how desirable each presented alarm prototype is, for varied size, weight, battery life and price
1099.measured: Perceived desirability (5-point scale) as a function of four design parameters, response-surface model fit (R2 0.69) and prediction accuracy
1099.method_detail: Design of Experiments with response surface model, built in a startup case study, plus a verification experiment
1099.finding: A response-surface model from the user tests identified the main drivers of alarm desirability and their interactions, and predicted ratings for new prototypes in a verification test.

1100.who: 5 Danish residents of similar age and lifestyle (6 screened into the field study)
1100.task: Kept a two-week journal of every electric-kettle use (purpose, situation, water heated and used), after a home pre-interview and followed by a post-interview
1100.measured: Volume of excess water heated by usage purpose, effect of minimum fill marker, purchase considerations, reasons for keeping or discarding leftover water
1100.method_detail: Two-week self-reported field journal with pre- and post-interviews
1100.finding: Excess water heated depended on usage purpose and urgency, the fill marker had no effect, and sustainability concerns did not shape kettle choice or use.

1101.who: 377 freshman engineering students in nine course sections (322 finished all surveys)
1101.task: Took two spatial visualization tests at start, after six weeks of sketching, and after CAD; sections learned perspective or traditional sketching
1101.measured: Spatial visualization scores (Purdue PSVT:R rotations test and Mental Rotation Test) at three time points, by course version and initial low scorers
1101.method_detail: Repeated-measures comparison of an industrial design sketching approach with a traditional one
1101.finding: Spatial visualization improved over the semester, mostly after the sketching portion rather than CAD, and perspective sketching raised scores as much as traditional methods.

1102.who: 122 mechanical engineering students: 98 third-year (3 conditions) and 24 graduate students
1102.task: Experiment 1: redesigned a toaster sustainably in 30 minutes with no aid, guidelines or GREEn Quiz; experiment 2: graduate pairs redesigned concepts with the quiz
1102.problem: Sustainable toaster redesign, and redesign of graduate course product concepts
1102.prompt: Redesign an existing consumer toaster to be more sustainable (experiment 1); redesign your team's product concept using the quiz (experiment 2)
1102.measured: Number of concepts, design decisions and sustainable design decisions (by category), novelty against status-quo decisions, self-rated solution quality
1102.method_detail: Experiment 1 between-groups with 3 conditions; experiment 2 before and after use of the quiz
1102.finding: Designers using the GREEn Quiz made more sustainable design decisions, in both novice and graduate groups, though novices produced fewer concepts.

1104.who: 52 adults recruited near Stanford (26 per group; 44 aged 18-29, 33 women)
1104.task: Washed three sets of sticky dishes at a custom faucet; a hidden operator adjusted flow for one group in the middle phase
1104.problem: Dishwashing with an apparently autonomous water-saving faucet
1104.prompt: Wash each set of dirty dishes using the faucet; the test group was told it would now work as a smart faucet
1104.measured: Water used per phase, handle touches, satisfaction with the faucet, dishwashing habits
1104.method_detail: Between-subjects, three phases (baseline, treatment, post-treatment) with Wizard-of-Oz control
1104.finding: Smart-faucet users cut water use by 26.5 percent during treatment and kept a slight saving afterward on a normal faucet, suggesting brief product-based training can persist.

1106.who: 113 capstone engineering students in 32 teams (course records and reports as data)
1106.task: Researchers extracted topics from transcript course descriptions and final reports, then compared three topic models and five regression methods predicting project grades
1106.measured: Prediction error of topic models (pLSI, LDA, NMF) and regressors (linear, tree, k-nearest neighbors, SVR, neural network) for project performance
1106.method_detail: Secondary analysis of one semester of capstone course data; no tasks done by participants
1106.finding: Representing both prior coursework and project outputs as topic distributions and using support vector regression gave the most accurate mapping from competency to design performance.

1109.who: 30 adults of varied background from a university research participant pool
1109.task: Saw sketches of four eco-feedback products (quantitative or figurative) in usage scenarios and reported expected feelings and actions, plus attitude and mood surveys
1109.problem: Eco-feedback products: electricity meter, light switch, water faucet, washing machine
1109.prompt: Imagine using each product in a scenario with a convenience tradeoff, report likelihood of conserving, and report emotions in conserving and wasteful scenarios
1109.measured: Emotions (descriptor ratings), certainty of taking conservation action, aesthetics, usefulness and quality ratings, pro-environmental attitude (NEP), current mood (PANAS)
1109.method_detail: In-lab study, between groups for quantitative versus figurative designs, with interviews
1109.finding: Taking immediate conservation action went with negative emotions such as guilt, design evaluations went with positive emotions, and figurative designs stirred stronger emotions in younger than older participants.

1110.who: 27 designers from 22 organizations engaged in open source projects (developers, engineers, managers, marketers)
1110.task: Took part in one-hour semi-structured interviews on how they gather information and design with open source communities; transcripts coded for information dimensions and archetypes
1110.prompt: Interview questions on context, knowledge, expertise, inspiration and constraints in information gathering and design
1110.measured: Five information dimensions (source, abstraction, generality, etc.) and combinations forming information archetypes
1110.method_detail: Part of a seven-year field study; qualitative theory-building coding
1110.finding: Interviews confirmed two earlier information archetypes in open source design and revealed new ones tied to coordination, extending the Information Archetypes Framework.

1111.who: 73 mostly graduate engineering students recruited at a design conference and at Stanford
1111.task: Did a 12-minute collage prime or reading task (or none), ideated 8 minutes, watched a sustainability video, ideated again, then evaluated own and others' ideas
1111.prompt: Imagine working at an appliance company and generate ideas for a sustainable washing machine, covering water and energy use, manufacturing and user appeal
1111.measured: Ideas judged by novice users on user desirability, cost and environmental pillars, ownership bias in evaluating own versus others' ideas
1111.method_detail: Five conditions: three collage primes (desirability, cost, environment), reading activity, control
1111.finding: Collage priming helped produce more environmentally friendly ideas but not social or economic ones and beat reading little, and the cost-themed collage best reduced ownership bias toward others' ideas.

1112.who: 20 attendees from five companies and two universities at an industry-academia roundtable
1112.task: Companies presented their lean product development experience, then three groups of 5-6 brainstormed and clustered challenges and opportunities in affinity diagrams
1112.prompt: Questions on pressing product development challenges, barriers to adopting lean, and the most impactful projects to pursue in the next 6-12 months
1112.measured: Successes and challenges of lean product development, affinity-clustered themes, research roadmap
1112.method_detail: One-day roundtable with presentations and facilitated brainstorming
1112.finding: Firms reported successes but common challenges in nomenclature, visual management and metrics, knowledge repositories and lean training, leading to a five-area research roadmap.

1119.who: 41 fourth-year engineering students (21 in experiment 1, 20 in experiment 2; 17 analyzed)
1119.task: Chose or rated relevance of biological phenomena for four design problems, described in full or with nouns replaced by broader terms
1119.problem: Biomimetic selection for fuel cells, drag reduction, clean clothes and recycling problems
1119.prompt: Pick which of two biological phenomena is more useful for the problem (experiment 1), or rate each phenomenon's relevance from 0 to 10 (experiment 2)
1119.measured: Choice of relevant versus irrelevant phenomenon, relevance ratings, types of reasoning, correct completion
1119.method_detail: Two between-subjects experiments, control versus abstraction condition
1119.finding: Abstracting biological descriptions did not give the expected benefits; novices still linked non-abstracted words to problems and found abstract descriptions harder to understand.

1120.who: Students in a Georgia Tech bio-inspired design course, 2011-2012 (34 in 2012; 2011 not reported)
1120.task: Used the Four-Box method (function, operating environment, constraints, performance criteria) to specify problems and compare biological analogues; assignments coded and 2012 final reflections analyzed
1120.prompt: Each team picked its own design problem and wrote problem definitions in the four-box format
1120.measured: Accuracy of 73 student problem definitions against researcher coding, positive and negative student comments on usefulness and usability
1120.method_detail: Classroom implementation of a new method, with assignment coding (kappa 0.778) and reflection analysis
1120.finding: Students were about 86 percent accurate with the Four-Box method after brief instruction and mostly commented positively, suggesting it is both useful and usable.

1122.task: Rated product forms, then made form-function-price choices for three products, first without and then with environmental impact values for each configuration
1122.problem: Single-use spoons, reusable water bottles and home washing machines
1122.measured: Utility of form, function and price attribute levels before and after environmental impact information, individual versus group-level preference, model validation (hit rate, likelihood ratio)
1122.method_detail: Within-subject conjoint analysis with ratings and discrete choice (logit and Bradley-Terry-Luce models)
1122.finding: With environmental impact shown, people valued product form less and function more, a trend seen at both group and individual level, with large individual differences.

1123.who: 34 students, researchers and staff from one university in a living laboratory kitchen
1123.task: Cooked two packets of instant noodles as usual, were interviewed, saw an energy bill and tried to cut energy use, cooked again, were interviewed again
1123.problem: Everyday cooking activity (instant noodles) as target for sustainable behavior design
1123.prompt: Prepare two packets of instant noodles using the full 800 ml of water, first as usual and then trying to use less energy
1123.measured: Energy consumed per activity, time-stamped activities from video, interview reasons, deviations from the minimum energy as failure modes
1123.method_detail: Living-lab observation with energy metering and interviews; first 14 participants shaped a process template
1123.finding: Comparing actual to minimum energy use gave six overconsumption failure modes and four user groups, which a matrix sorted into those suited to behavioral nudges and those needing product redesign.

1128.who: 33 third-year industrial technology students (28 to 33 valid rubrics per exam)
1128.task: In three pilot exams modeled a part and assembled a pulley in SolidWorks, then self-scored with a quality rubric that the teacher scored separately
1128.problem: CAD models of a pipe cover and a pulley assembly with drawings
1128.prompt: Model the shown cover (then apply listed modifications), and assemble the pulley and extract drawings, then self-evaluate against a rubric
1128.measured: Gap between student self-evaluation and teacher evaluation on rubric assertions about model validity, completeness, consistency, conciseness, clarity
1128.method_detail: Three pilot experiments without a control group, single teacher rater
1128.finding: Rubrics conveyed some CAD quality criteria, but complex ideas such as design intent and repetition patterns stayed poorly understood, and weaker students also self-assessed poorly.

1129.who: 104 freshman engineering students with SolidWorks experience (52 control, 52 annotated-model group)
1129.task: Made sequential alterations to a parametric CAD part and chose a solution to a design challenge, with or without 3D annotations
1129.problem: Altering and reusing a parametric CAD model
1129.prompt: Modify an existing model to meet new requirements so it can be reused in another product, one alteration at a time
1129.measured: Modeling approach chosen (e.g. mirror versus remodel) and task performance with versus without annotations
1129.method_detail: Two studies in a computer lab, random assignment to annotated or non-annotated model
1129.finding: Models carrying 3D design-intent annotations led to significantly better choices and performance in alteration tasks than non-annotated models.

1130.who: 11 graduate engineering students and 1 instructor; three authors rated the assertions
1130.task: Played the two-player BioP-C game on a cell-division abstract for an hour, producing 183 assertions; 70 sampled and rated for correctness, plus enjoyment
1130.problem: Describing the biological phenomenon of cell division through a game
1130.prompt: Keymaster picks a word from a shared passage and the Codebreaker guesses it, with the Keymaster describing each guess's relation to the keyword
1130.measured: Absolute and relative correctness of assertions (1-5 ratings), links between correctness and game-session data, perceived fun
1130.method_detail: Classroom deployment of a human-computation game, expert correctness ratings and user experience evaluation
1130.finding: Player assertions were significantly more correct than random but well below the ideal, correctness rose with source passage length, and several game changes were identified to improve fun.

1131.who: 155 students: 91 freshmen at one university, 64 senior mechanical engineers at another
1131.task: After minimal training, rated originality of features in concept sketches for a new alarm; compared with trained expert ratings
1131.problem: Next-generation alarm or new way to wake the user (sketches rated, not designed)
1131.prompt: Rate each concept sketch feature's originality on a five-point scale from common to exceptional
1131.measured: Agreement of novice raters with expert originality ratings, inter-rater agreement among novices, composite crowd ratings
1131.method_detail: Two pilot phases; second phase added sample-problem training
1131.finding: Novice raters chosen by high mutual agreement, especially after training with example problems, produced composite originality ratings that nearly matched experts.

1132.who: 10 senior and master's mechanical engineering students in 5 pairs (one pair analyzed)
1132.task: Pairs designed collaboratively on video, then verbalized thoughts retrospectively while watching; thoughts coded as intuitive (Type 1) or analytical (Type 2)
1132.problem: Secure storage for skateboards on campus
1132.prompt: Develop a device that securely stores skateboards so students stop stacking them against classroom walls
1132.measured: Share of Type 1 versus Type 2 thinking per idea, idea novelty, evolution of thought type over the session
1132.method_detail: Exploratory pilot using retrospective protocol analysis of one pair for about 22 minutes
1132.finding: Ideas with more intuitive Type 1 thinking were more novel up to a threshold, with an even mix of Type 1 and Type 2 maximizing novelty.

1133.who: 66 undergraduate, graduate and affiliated researchers from engineering departments (33 women, 33 men)
1133.task: Worked alone 30 minutes building a ball-lifting mechanism with no sketching, 5 minutes of sketching first, or free sketching, in erector set or foam core
1133.problem: Mechanism to lift a ping-pong ball as high as possible
1133.prompt: Build a mechanism that displaces a ping-pong ball vertically as high as possible, powered by a 500 g weight, with the given tools and materials
1133.measured: Maximum ball displacement, sketch types, completeness, proficiency and sketch-prototype match, debrief survey
1133.method_detail: 2x3 design: building material by sketching condition, unequal group sizes
1133.finding: Ball height did not differ whether people sketched or built directly, suggesting quick prototypes explore a simple design space as well as sketches do.

1134.who: 31 PhD and postdoctoral engineering and physics students (complete data from 25)
1134.task: Watched short tutorials then did 15-minute rounds of brainstorming, mind-mapping and C-Sketch in a five-day challenge; personality type and self-efficacy surveyed
1134.problem: Low-cost atomic force microscope for Chinese high schools
1134.prompt: Within a week conceive a design and build a working prototype of a low-cost AFM suited to high-school science teaching
1134.measured: Idea quality, quantity, novelty and variety per method, personality type (Myers-Briggs) and Six Thinking Hats preferences, self-efficacy
1134.method_detail: Correlational study of ideation outcomes by personality type within an international summer-school challenge
1134.finding: Personality types differed significantly in ideation results across methods, in ways that fit type theory, suggesting methods or method sequences tailored to personality.

1135.who: 47 sophomore mechanical engineering students in five randomly assigned groups
1135.task: Individually generated concepts for 20 minutes (text or sketch) after receiving a problem plus a set of requirements, or none
1135.prompt: Design a device that makes burritos for 100 alumni guests during halftime at a department tailgate party
1135.measured: Quantity and quality of concepts generated under five requirement conditions (none, functional, non-functional, mixed random, mixed prioritized)
1135.method_detail: In-class between-subjects study, 8 requirements per treatment group
1135.finding: Non-functional requirements led to more and better concepts than functional requirements, and no requirements produced more concepts than functional ones.

1138.who: 12 aerospace subsystem designers and integrators (interviews); simulated two-subsystem optimization
1138.task: Interviewees discussed how they integrate their subsystem with others; researchers then simulated sequential optimization with no, constant or decreasing bias in shared information
1138.problem: Subsystem integration and negotiation in complex system design (interviews); simulated optimization problems
1138.prompt: Interview question was how they manage integration of their subsystem with other subsystems; no design brief for simulations
1138.measured: Interview themes on negotiation and conservative margins; simulated number of iterations to converge and Pareto optimality of system solutions
1138.method_detail: One-hour unrecorded interviews followed by multidisciplinary optimization simulations of three bias conditions
1138.finding: Practitioners described padding shared estimates as a negotiation hedge, and simulations showed a constant bias hurt system-level optimality while a decreasing bias needed more iterations.

1139.who: 61 engineering and science students (31 in first study, 30 in second) plus computational agents
1139.task: Used a slider interface to evaluate ten designs within four minutes on each of three optimization tasks; later followed an imposed search strategy while agents tested strategies
1139.problem: Abstract nonlinear optimization tasks derived from myosin-based nanosystem design, with variables renamed generically
1139.prompt: Search the design inputs to maximize a goal output while meeting one or two constraints, using ten evaluations in four minutes
1139.measured: Best design found relative to global optimum, search patterns of best and worst users, agent strategy performance, correct use of learned knowledge
1139.method_detail: Two human cognitive studies (31 and 30 participants) with an agent-based simulation step between them
1139.finding: Univariate searches followed by greedy local search worked best for agents, and users instructed to follow this strategy performed significantly better than users with no strategy.

1141.who: 45 senior mechanical engineering students (14, 15 and 16 per group)
1141.task: Worked individually: either elicited requirements (10 min) then generated concepts (20 min), or received ten requirements and generated concepts (20 min)
1141.problem: Device for wheelchair users to pick peaches
1141.prompt: Design a manually operated device that lets a person in a wheelchair pick peaches from a tree into a basket without damaging or dropping the fruit
1141.measured: Number of given and unique requirements addressed by the concepts generated
1141.method_detail: In-class between-subjects study with three groups: no, partial (5 given) and full (10 given) requirements
1141.finding: Eliciting requirements before ideation gave no benefit; the group handed all ten requirements addressed as many or more requirements, and the partial-elicitation group addressed the fewest.

1142.who: 19 first-year engineering students (18 analyzed) in 4-member teams
1142.task: Completed a lottery risk and ambiguity survey, then a week later sketched milk-frother ideas for 20 minutes and sorted a teammate's ideas into consider or do not consider
1142.prompt: Develop new, easy-to-use product concepts that froth milk quickly, covering both form and function
1142.measured: Risk and ambiguity aversion (lottery survey), creativity of ideas generated and of ideas selected
1142.method_detail: Pilot-scale lab study with survey one week before the design session
1142.finding: More risk-averse students generated and chose less creative ideas, and being good at generating creative ideas did not predict choosing them.

1143.who: 272 undergraduates from a university psychology subject pool (220 played the game, 52 took the survey)
1143.task: Played a roughly 30-minute Mars-mission design game, or answered a matching survey, deciding whether to keep developing their own design when a superior alternative appeared
1143.problem: Crew habitation module for a manned Mars mission
1143.prompt: Take the role of an engineer designing a Mars habitation module, then decide whether to continue your own design or adopt a better existing alternative
1143.measured: Share of participants continuing with their own design (sunk cost effect) across control, implicit-alternative and explicit-alternative treatments; game versus survey differences
1143.method_detail: Between-subjects lab study comparing a serious game to a survey; game had three treatments, survey two
1143.finding: Players of the game showed the sunk cost effect despite treatment, while survey respondents in the control did not, suggesting games can induce behavior unlike real-world engineers.

1146.who: 3 mechanical engineering students at different levels (1 freshman, 2 PhD)
1146.task: Individually developed nail-removal concepts for 45 minutes with prototyping materials, tools and consumer products on the table; sessions filmed with four cameras and coded for actions on objects
1146.problem: Nail remover for a confined space
1146.prompt: Develop several concepts for a device that removes a nail along its own axis without damaging the surrounding wood
1146.measured: Coded actions and objects handled over time, recurring action-sequence patterns, use of materials by position, inter-rater agreement
1146.method_detail: Video protocol analysis with a new action-entity coding scheme
1146.finding: The most common action patterns suggested participants learned from or found inspiration in physical objects they handled, and the coding protocol could document these interactions.

1147.who: 12 tractor users (8 farmers, 4 manufacturer employees); follow-up with 8 participants (overlap not stated)
1147.task: Operated a tractor through set tasks while software analyzed recorded operations; follow-up added a slope task and interviews
1147.problem: No design problem (operation of an existing tractor)
1147.measured: Safety and effectiveness gaps detected between designer assumptions and user operations, causes of gaps classified by human error type
1147.method_detail: Proposed a gap model and analysis program, tested on observed tractor use plus post-hoc interviews
1147.finding: The gap analysis program detected potential unsafe operations, mostly in clutch release and reverser lever use, and interviews classified their causes to suggest measures.

1148.who: 48 senior engineering students in 16 teams of three
1148.task: Teams designed truss bridges in a software tool over six 4-minute periods, with two unexpected changes to the problem statement; half the teams also got extra load scenarios
1148.prompt: Design a bridge spanning a river that carries a mid-span load with safety factor above 1.25 and low mass; later also survive losing a support, then avoid a restricted zone
1148.measured: Design quality, mass, complexity (members, joints), distance between successive designs and exploration of the design space, high versus low performing teams
1148.method_detail: Lab session of about one hour; simple versus extended scenario condition; logged software actions
1148.finding: High-performing teams chose simpler designs and explored small regions thoroughly, while low-performing teams used complex designs with little targeted exploration; extra scenarios did not help resilience.

1149.who: 661 fourth-year mechanical and manufacturing engineering students in 120 capstone teams over five years
1149.task: Completed a Myers-Briggs personality form, then worked in 4-6 person teams on sponsored year-long capstone projects graded by advisors
1149.measured: Cognitive factor scores from Wilde's Teamology model (eight factors), adjusted team course grades, team GPA percentile, group size
1149.method_detail: Correlational analysis with stepwise regression across five cohorts
1149.finding: Wilde's model explained about 10% of variance in team outcomes, with Imagination, Community and Evaluation factors significantly associated with better results.

1150.who: 18 professional designers (6 each in graphic, industrial, web design; 9 experts, 9 novices)
1150.task: Searched the web and ideated for 90 minutes, saving examples in a digital notebook, then took a semi-structured interview and a familiarity survey on collected examples
1150.problem: Recycled-material product (industrial), UNICEF campus campaign (graphic), NPR.org homepage redesign (web)
1150.prompt: Collect inspiring examples online and brainstorm initial ideas for a domain-specific brief, such as a consumer product from discarded materials, a charity ad campaign or a new radio-station homepage
1150.measured: When and how examples were searched, example characteristics (similarity to task, familiarity to designer), differences by domain and expertise
1150.method_detail: Lab sessions with logged searches, plus interviews and surveys; expert-novice and cross-domain comparison
1150.finding: Search strategies and example use differed by design domain, and experts mostly sought highly familiar or similar examples, which risks missing the benefits of more diverse ones.

1151.who: 25 engineers at a medical ultrasound company (9 in screening survey, 16 in validation survey)
1151.task: Compared 3D models of transducer handle variants with a baseline and rated style similarity on a 1-7 scale, for linear and curved designs
1151.prompt: Rate how similar the style of each candidate handle model is to the baseline model, from very similar to very different
1151.measured: Perceived style similarity ratings across six shape parameters (fractional factorial screening) and three parameters (full factorial validation)
1151.method_detail: Survey-format factorial experiment using shape-grammar generated variants; about 20 minutes per screening survey
1151.finding: Strain relief angle was the dominant shape parameter shaping perceived style similarity, while indentation offset and side curve angle had little effect, and the validation survey confirmed the screening.

1152.task: Took part in semi-structured interviews about early-stage concept work in front-end departments and pre-development
1152.measured: Challenges of the fuzzy front end, internal selling of concepts, fit of the academic definition to automotive practice
1152.finding: The main challenge is selling concepts internally, notably conveying value and cost, and the academic go/no-go view of the fuzzy front end misses transformational work where only execution is uncertain.

1154.who: 63 engineering students aged 18-23 (31 viewed one medication brand, 32 the other)
1154.task: Completed a 17-minute online survey: health literacy test, choosing the right medication from four package variants per question, and ratings of five package designs
1154.problem: Over-the-counter cold medication packaging (two brands, five package designs)
1154.prompt: Select the medicine that best relieves a stated symptom from four labels; then rate how useful each package design was
1154.measured: Health literacy, selection accuracy, selection time, package commonality metrics, usefulness ratings of designs
1154.method_detail: Online mixed within-between design; abstract says 64 participants but methods give 63
1154.finding: Product family commonality affected selection time and preferences, and larger font gave the fastest selection, yet participants preferred designs other than those that helped most.

1156.who: 1 undergraduate design team of 4 mechanical engineering seniors
1156.task: Sketched on tablets with a collaborative sketching tool for a 65-minute in-class ideation session, then kept using it for 18 days; video, server logs, survey and interview
1156.problem: Action toy for a toy design course project
1156.prompt: Generate toy ideas from given requirements, discuss and extend the best ones, then select and refine a final concept
1156.measured: Types of sketch creation and modification, lateral and vertical idea transformations between members, team feedback on the tool
1156.method_detail: 19-day longitudinal study embedded in a course project
