1156.finding: The team's sketching showed lateral and vertical transformations between members, indicating shared exploration of the design space, and the tool also worked as a research instrument.

1157.who: 7 capstone teams of 6-8 (6 analyzed); volunteer teams of 2-4 (counts not reported)
1157.task: After a 15-minute lecture, each person generated ideas for 15 minutes from analogy prompt words, then teams spent 30 minutes or more combining ideas on a mind-map
1157.problem: Team capstone projects (UAVs, heavy-lift system, bridge corrosion monitor, etc.); volunteers: separating a 3D-printed part from its print bed
1157.prompt: Use words lexically distant from a key function word to inspire solution principles; volunteers were asked to devise automatic removal of a printed part from the substrate
1157.measured: Quantity and uniqueness of concepts generated, loss of ideas from individual to team phase, effect of lexical distance of prompt words
1157.method_detail: Two studies of a new analogy-seeded mind-map method: in-class capstone teams and a volunteer session
1157.finding: Teams produced many analogical concepts, averaging 65 per team in the volunteer study, but up to 55% of individual ideas were lost at the team stage and the effect of word distance stayed unclear.

1159.who: 10 engineering designers (7 undergraduates, 3 graduate students or practitioners)
1159.task: Completed an online survey rating 27 existing concept sketches: picked five adjectives per concept, then rated novelty and feasibility on 0-100 sliders
1159.problem: Three tasks whose concepts were rated: milk frother, electric toothbrush power mechanism, device reducing walking-and-texting accidents
1159.measured: Semantic-similarity novelty and feasibility scores from word choices (SCAT), perceived novelty and feasibility, comparison with Shah novelty and Linsey quality measures, number of raters needed
1159.method_detail: 81-question online rating survey testing a new evaluation method against established metrics
1159.finding: Word-based novelty ratings approximated relative novelty measures with about seven raters though weakly (r = 0.35), while word-based feasibility did not predict quality and slider-perceived ratings worked better.

1160.who: 200 online crowd workers in the US (83 men, 117 women)
1160.task: Rated how much they liked each of 16 two-dimensional wheel rim concept images on a 7-point scale, in random order, with an attention check
1160.problem: Automotive wheel rim designs (Y-, fan-, V- and chamfer-spoke styles)
1160.prompt: Rate whether you like each wheel rim preliminary design concept, from not at all to strongly
1160.measured: Preference ratings for designs with low versus high quantified Gestalt, within style to hold complexity constant
1160.method_detail: Online repeated-measures survey, 2 (Gestalt) x 4 (style) x 2 (version) design
1160.finding: Designs with higher quantified Gestalt were preferred over lower-Gestalt versions, while designs with different geometry but the same Gestalt were not rated significantly differently.

1161.who: 25 people (11 with upper-extremity disabilities, 14 able-bodied who also wore a disability simulation suit)
1161.task: Used kitchen products in pairs (inclusive and standard) while talking through their experience on video; able-bodied group repeated it wearing a suit, and most did a 9-hole peg dexterity test
1161.problem: Kitchen products (can openers, jar openers, garlic presses, ice cube trays)
1161.prompt: Use each product and think aloud about your experience with it
1161.measured: Customer needs mentioned (frequency and weight), similarity of needs with and without the suit, peg-test dexterity times
1161.method_detail: Think-aloud interviews coded into customer needs, plus a quantitative dexterity test; 23 of 25 did the peg test
1161.finding: Needs from people with disabilities showed early signs of a common high-frequency, high-weight module, but the suit slowed able-bodied participants more than disability did, so the dexterity hypothesis was rejected.

1162.who: 227 US online survey respondents (194 used in analysis)
1162.task: Answered an online survey of about 15 minutes choosing preferred solar panel appearance from image pairs, first on blank backgrounds, then installed on roofs, plus design selection
1162.problem: Residential solar panel appearance (cell color, cell shape, wire pattern, frame)
1162.prompt: Choose the solar panel you prefer based only on appearance, then choose a preferred combination for panels on house roofs
1162.measured: Part-worth preferences for four appearance attributes via choice-based conjoint, consistency of preference between standalone and in-context images
1162.method_detail: Choice-based visual conjoint analysis on Mechanical Turk; 33 responses rejected as low quality
1162.finding: Preferences shifted significantly when panels were shown on roofs rather than standalone, so context of presentation changes stated appearance preferences.

1163.who: 40 people: 15 Bolivian amputees, 14 US veterans hospital users, 11 student designers
1163.task: Students had a 30-minute training and wore a mock prosthetic limb, interviewed before, between and after; others interviewed once
1163.problem: Volume-adjustable socket for lower-limb prosthetics in developing countries
1163.measured: Customer needs identified by each group, share of lead-user and typical-user needs matched, number of latent needs
1163.method_detail: Needs analysis interviews across three sites with an empathic training and simulation intervention for the student group
1163.finding: The empathic lead user group identified 95% of both lead-user and typical-user needs, and adding them doubled the latent needs beyond the 5 found by lead users alone.

1167.who: Deep learning models (no human participants), trained on Quick, Draw! sketches
1167.task: Trained a deep clustering model on 48x48 sketch images and compared its clustering accuracy with sketch-rnn, sketch-pix2seq and k-means on three five-category sets
1167.problem: No design problem (sketch similarity for visual analogy support)
1167.measured: Unsupervised clustering accuracy, robustness across runs, qualitative visualization of latent shape similarity
1167.method_detail: 15,000 sketches per category; three datasets of varying category similarity (vehicles, mixed, unrelated)
1167.finding: The proposed deep clustering model grouped sketches more accurately and robustly than baselines on most datasets, suggesting it can surface visually similar sketches to prompt analogies.

1169.who: 104 third- and fourth-year mechanical engineering students (38, 33 and 33 per condition)
1169.task: Individually, in three 10-minute steps, listed requirements, sketched a solution and identified sketch features, in one of three step orders
1169.problem: Mechanism for wheelchair users to reach books on a high shelf
1169.prompt: Develop a device that lets people in wheelchairs take books from shelves 6 feet or higher, safely, conveniently and without damaging books, simple enough to install on existing shelves
1169.measured: Variety, typology and novelty of the requirements elicited
1169.method_detail: In-class between-subjects study with random packet assignment: requirements-sketch-identify, sketch-identify-requirements, sketch-requirements-identify
1169.finding: Sketching before listing requirements improved the typology and novelty of requirements but not their variety, with the largest gain when features were identified in the sketch before writing requirements.

1171.who: 2 expert and several student raters (number not reported) rating 932 ideas; 4 experts in concept mapping
1171.task: Rated novelty and quality of existing milk-frother ideas with a social-science method and engineering feature-tree methods; four experts pinned 10 sketches by similarity while thinking aloud
1171.problem: Milk frother ideas (932 concepts from an earlier study)
1171.measured: Novelty and quality ratings by consensual assessment and by feature-tree methods, agreement between expert and quasi-expert raters, coded factors raters used for novelty
1171.method_detail: Quantitative comparison of rating methods plus think-aloud concept-mapping with content analysis (kappa 0.88)
1171.finding: Both approaches gave similar quality ratings, but expert consensual and feature-tree novelty ratings were negatively related, and quasi-experts agreed with experts on novelty but not quality.

1172.task: Did easy and hard versions of a Stroop task and a finger-tapping task, with a 2-minute Alternative Uses Test before and after each, in a 30-40 minute session
1172.problem: No design problem (Alternative Uses Test with everyday objects)
1172.prompt: Type as many creative uses as possible for an everyday object such as a brick or bottle in two minutes
1172.measured: Fluency (number of uses) and flexibility (number of use categories) on the Alternative Uses Test
1172.method_detail: Within-subjects 2 (task) x 3 (difficulty) lab study with counterbalanced task and object order
1172.finding: Harder versions of both tasks increased the number of alternative uses, and the Stroop task raised category flexibility more, making it the better candidate for a behavioral creativity intervention.

1173.who: 50 junior mechanical engineering undergraduates (41 men, 9 women)
1173.task: Each person completed two worksheets: marked which of five source products were useful analogies for a target product and wrote why, in up to 50 minutes (7-23 used)
1173.problem: Choosing analogy sources for five target products (electric kettle, glue gun, hairdryer, drill gun, blender)
1173.prompt: Given a product to be designed and five other products, mark those that would be useful sources of analogy and explain in plain words why
1173.measured: Dimensions of similarity coded from written reasons (working principle, structure, human interaction, function, energy and material flow, etc.), 2,440 dimension instances
1173.method_detail: Human-subject worksheet study with five instrument variants and coded written responses
1173.finding: Analogy choices were driven by at least six dimensions, with working principle, structure and human interaction stronger than function, which was previously thought to be the sole driver.

1174.task: Watched a short video and did either a memory recall induction or a control induction, then 1-minute Alternate Uses Task and a 15-minute wind-turbine-blade repurposing task, in two sessions
1174.problem: Alternate uses of pencil and paperclip; repurposing retired wind-turbine blade sections
1174.prompt: List as many uses as possible for an everyday item; find creative uses for a section of a retired wind-turbine blade
1174.measured: Fluency, flexibility and elaboration on the Alternate Uses Task; scaled, feasible and appropriate idea fluency and flexibility for blade repurposing
1174.method_detail: Within-subjects lab study with counterbalanced induction order; memory versus control induction
1174.finding: After the episodic memory induction, alternate-use responses were more flexible and elaborate, and blade repurposing ideas were more appropriate and feasible, though fluency did not differ.

1175.who: 85 informal e-waste workers in rural Thailand (51 employers, 34 employees); 69 in a follow-up auction
1175.task: Ranked physical hand-tool prototypes in a face-to-face conjoint survey; later a bidding auction and a one-month follow-up survey on tool use
1175.problem: Hand tool for splitting electric motor stators in e-waste dismantling
1175.prompt: Rank prototype variants of a handled blade tool by preference (price, blade length, handle position, grip, blade thickness)
1175.measured: Stakeholder preference models (conjoint), distance between employer and employee optimal designs (SAM), AHP comparison, willingness to pay, tool use after one month
1175.method_detail: Field case comparing a new agreement metric with AHP; AHP stopped after the first 5 participants lost attention
1175.finding: The agreement metric's estimate matched later measures of stakeholder satisfaction, and AHP proved impractical in the field because its many comparisons tired participants.

1176.who: 16 undergraduates in a humanitarian engineering student organization (6 project teams; 13 completed post-intervention)
1176.task: Completed a questionnaire and interview and wrote design requirements for their project, then learned a cultural requirements method or a standard checklist, then repeated both
1176.problem: Student humanitarian projects for communities in South Carolina and Haiti
1176.measured: Information considered when making requirements (questionnaire, interviews), cultural content of design requirements, before-and-after change by group
1176.method_detail: Quasi-experimental pilot with control (checklist) and experimental (cultural method) teams, pre and post
1176.finding: The cultural requirements method increased designers' stated consideration of target-user culture, but the pilot could not show the method alone changed considerations or the requirements produced.

1178.who: 34 senior mechanical engineering students in 8 capstone design teams
1178.task: Wrote four design reports and a final report over a semester; researchers coded how teams justified their requirements and specifications
1178.problem: Sponsor-defined projects (assistive devices, university spaces, measurement tools, medical device)
1178.prompt: Each team received a short sponsor project description and developed a prototype to address a sponsor's problem
1178.measured: Types of justification for 84 user requirements and 103 engineering specifications, frequency of each, and change across reports
1178.method_detail: Inductive coding of capstone design reports (inter-rater kappa 0.86)
1178.finding: Teams justified requirements mostly through sponsor interactions and their own perceptions of user needs, rarely user data, and over a third of specifications lacked clear justification.

1179.who: 36 undergraduate and graduate students at one university
1179.task: After a contest experiment against a simulated opponent, answered five structured interview questions (about 150 seconds) on how they decided when to stop searching
1179.problem: Roller coaster track valley width (maximize rider enjoyment) in a competitive design contest
1179.prompt: Compete against an opponent to design the track valley width that maximizes rider enjoyment, without being given the enjoyment formula
1179.measured: Stopping criteria and strategies from interview content analysis, influence of opponent's past performance record on stopping decisions
1179.method_detail: Protocol-style content analysis of post-experiment interviews, following a behavioral experiment with or without opponent information
1179.finding: Participants stopped based on thresholds for target quality, resources spent and improvement sought, and these thresholds shifted with how competitive they judged the opponent to be.

1180.task: Practitioners were interviewed; students had a 10-minute tutorial, then 30 minutes designing an airplane with sliders under one of four uncertainty representations
1180.problem: Aircraft design with fuel consumption and failure rate objectives
1180.prompt: Choose airplane parameters giving both low failure rate and low fuel use, finding designs in three reward regions and on the combined Pareto frontier
1180.measured: Interview themes on uncertainty practice; feasible designs found, share in reward regions, points on combined Pareto frontier, understanding of the model
1180.method_detail: Half- to one-hour interviews with open coding, then a 4-condition between-subjects experiment (control, margin, two robust optimization sliders)
1180.finding: Robust optimization let participants explore the design space far more efficiently than control or safety-factor conditions, with little difference in their understanding of the model.

1181.who: 11 PhD-level experts in Earth-observing satellite design (10 in aerospace engineering)
1181.task: Used a data-exploration tool for 25 minutes on 6,655 satellite architectures, mapping concepts, then did multiple-choice, feature synthesis, design synthesis and self-assessment tests in a two-hour online session
1181.problem: Earth-observing satellite constellation architecture (cost versus science benefit)
1181.prompt: Find the features shared uniquely by the target set of designs, with high precision and recall, and record learnings in a concept map
1181.measured: Seven learning measures (concept map, feature and design identification and comparison, synthesis tasks) plus self-assessed learning, and their correlations
1181.method_detail: Single-condition online human-subject study testing new learning measures; no comparison of tools
1181.finding: Different measures captured different kinds of knowledge gained, and designers' self-assessed learning correlated with many measures, though taking measures during learning raised issues.

1182.who: 88 students in 21 teams across three six-week human-centered design courses (2017-2019)
1182.task: Teams chose three design methods per phase from a repository and wrote short justifications, 297 selections in total, which researchers coded by decision-making strategy
1182.problem: Student-chosen everyday problems (products, services, spatio-social systems)
1182.prompt: Choose a compelling problem you experience in daily life and apply human-centered design methods
1182.measured: Decision-making strategy behind each method choice (agent-, outcome- or process-driven), by design phase and innovation type, heterogeneity of selections
1182.method_detail: Coding of written method-selection justifications with a new framework (inter-rater reliability 0.86)
1182.finding: Teams used outcome-focused reasoning less than agent- or process-focused, shifted from user-focused to product-focused outcomes over phases, and strategy explained method choices better than project type.

1183.who: Anonymous café customers in a 8-week field study (number not reported); 295 valid online survey respondents
1183.task: Café customers took napkins from dispensers carrying positive, negative or feedback messages; separately, online respondents viewed the dispensers and rated emotions and perceived messages
1183.problem: Napkin dispenser designs to reduce napkin use
1183.measured: Napkins used per customer over time, environmental concern, emotions, perceived message and effectiveness
1183.method_detail: Field experiment in three cafés (baseline, intervention, post-baseline) plus Mechanical Turk survey
1183.finding: Positive information cut napkin use briefly, negative information changed use for longer and feedback did not change it, with emotions such as encouragement or guilt matching each message.

1186.who: 78 mechanical engineering students (46 sophomores/juniors, 32 seniors/masters) in 23 analyzed teams of three
1186.task: Designed trusses alone to measure proficiency, then in anonymous teams of three over two 10-minute sessions, with forced design-sharing points; teams built with highest or lowest proficiency members
1186.prompt: Design a truss that reaches a factor of safety of 1.25 with as little mass as possible
1186.measured: Individual and team design score, time to reach performance thresholds, regression on member proficiency, hidden Markov models of design actions
1186.method_detail: Behavioral study with team composition by proficiency and two student populations
1186.finding: Team performance depended mainly on its most proficient member, whose simpler designs were adopted by teammates, so upgrading the strongest member helps more than upgrading any other.

1187.who: 80 people in 16 teams: 8 managed (4 students plus a manager) and 8 unmanaged (5 students)
1187.task: Teams designed for 30 minutes with two constraints added later; managers gave preset prompts; discourse was transcribed and topic-modeled
1187.prompt: Design a low-cost, easy-to-make device that removes peanut shells for developing countries without electricity, handling large quantities with minimal damage to the nuts
1187.measured: Topics in team discourse (topic model with 15 topics), differences between managed and unmanaged teams, topic shift before and after manager interventions
1187.method_detail: Topic-model analysis of transcripts from an earlier controlled experiment; nominal teams excluded
1187.finding: Managed and unmanaged teams differed in topics tied to the interventions, and discourse shifted toward an intervention's topic right after the manager gave it.

1188.who: Data from 103 first-year engineering students used to simulate 13,482 four-person nominal teams (no live teams)
1188.task: Simulated teams by pooling ideas that individuals produced in a 20-minute ideation and later selected via a screening matrix, grouped by team trait empathy (average and spread)
1188.problem: Course project on healthy lives and well-being (water, vaccination, air pollution, road injuries)
1188.prompt: Original students chose one global health challenge and generated ideas individually; simulation had no brief
1188.measured: Team empathy elevation and diversity (28-item empathy survey), number of unique, useful and elegant ideas generated and selected
1188.method_detail: Bootstrapped simulation from an 806-idea repository, with hierarchical regression
1188.finding: Teams with higher average empathy generated and selected more unique ideas, and teams with more varied empathy generated more useful ideas.

1189.who: 6 practicing designers (3-17 years experience) in two teams of three
1189.task: Individually generated ideas and principles, then in teams spent 30 minutes agreeing a ranked list of design principles and 10 minutes sketching solutions; team talk was transcribed and analyzed
1189.problem: Reducing single-use plastic waste in a US city
1189.prompt: Develop concepts for a new product or system that lowers the environmental impact of single-use plastic in Omaha, Nebraska
1189.measured: Types and patterns of conversation showing sharedness of mental models, using conversation analysis of 350 minutes of recordings
1189.method_detail: Lab sessions of three hours; conversation analysis of the team phases
1189.finding: Designers built shared understanding through identifiable conversation patterns, and four types of sharedness (overlapping, complementary, distributed, similar) were found in unstructured design discussion.

1190.who: 207 first-year engineering students in 53 design teams (3-4 members)
1190.task: Sketched ideas individually for 15 minutes, screened team ideas as consider or not, chose four to prototype; five psychological safety surveys over the project
1190.problem: Course projects: food insecurity, healthy living, or a STEM water toy for children
1190.prompt: Address one of: food insecurity in developing countries, healthy lives for all ages, or a STEM water toy for ages 3 to 5
1190.measured: Team psychological safety (7-item survey), idea fluency, idea goodness, ownership bias in concept screening
1190.method_detail: Correlational field study across 8 course sections, 4- and 8-week projects
1190.finding: Psychological safety did not affect how many ideas teams produced but predicted higher idea goodness and a higher share of teammates' ideas being selected.

1191.who: 40 CAD-experienced participants in 20 pairs (10 per condition)
1191.task: After training and a solo baseline, pairs completed 45 minutes of prescribed CAD modeling tasks, either working in parallel or sharing one control, in a cloud CAD tool
1191.prompt: Follow a task list to edit and complete a CAD model of a phone holder, deciding unspecified dimensions with your partner
1191.measured: CAD model quality (completeness, conciseness, consistency, validity, effectiveness) scored with a rubric, and speed
1191.method_detail: Between-pairs lab experiment: parallel versus shared CAD control, random assignment
1191.finding: Pairs sharing one CAD control produced significantly higher quality, more complete and consistent models than pairs working in parallel, with a weak speed-quality trade-off only in the parallel mode.

1193.who: 30 people: 24 designers (students and professionals) and 6 interviewed users
1193.task: Designers watched recorded needfinding interviews and, at paused points, wrote what the user was thinking or feeling, which was compared with the user's own logged entries
1193.problem: Needfinding for products for musicians, car drivers and a blind person
1193.prompt: Infer as accurately as possible what the user was thinking or feeling at each paused moment of the interview video
1193.measured: Empathic accuracy of designers overall and for thoughts, feelings, design-related and non-design-related entries
1193.method_detail: Three sub-studies with video-based empathic accuracy task and blind raters scoring similarity (0-2)
1193.finding: Designers were consistently more accurate at inferring design-related user thoughts and feelings than unrelated ones, and feelings were inferred more accurately than thoughts, though less consistently.

1194.who: 215 participants pooled from five earlier behavioral experiments
1194.task: In the original experiments, participants chose sequential search points to find the minimum or maximum of a hidden function; this paper re-analyzed their first and second choices
1194.problem: Abstract function search tasks, including a roller coaster track design
1194.prompt: Find the minimum or maximum of an unknown function by choosing points one at a time, sometimes with a cost or opponent
1194.measured: Distribution of first search choices, second choice relative to first result, effect of opponent information, left-right and whole-number preferences
1194.method_detail: Secondary analysis of six datasets from earlier controlled behavioral experiments
1194.finding: Across experiments, participants' first choices were not uniform: they often bisected the range, anchored on prior data and favored whole numbers, suggesting informative priors for modeling designers.

1196.who: 70 first-year engineering design students in a fundamental design course
1196.task: Took a mental rotation test at semester start and three months later; in between sketched, modeled and drew an object shown in one of three media
1196.problem: Technical object to sketch, model and draw (spatial skills training)
1196.prompt: Sketch an unknown technical object with isometric and three main views, then model it in CAD and produce a technical drawing
1196.measured: Mental Rotation Test score (24 points) before and after, improvement by visualization medium and gender
1196.method_detail: Pre-post design in a course with random assignment to three media groups (2D drawing, 3D-PDF, 3D-printed model)
1196.finding: Mental rotation scores rose significantly over the semester for everyone, while the visualization medium had no significant effect, with only a slight trend favoring more interactive media.

1197.who: 8 professional designers (4 software, 4 graphic) with 3-17 years of experience
1197.task: In 3-hour individual sessions, read 16 information sheets, organized them on a whiteboard aloud, sketched ideas for 20 minutes, then explained them
1197.problem: Reducing pedestrian accidents caused by mobile-device distraction
1197.prompt: Develop concepts for a new product or system that reduces pedestrian accident rates due to distraction from mobile devices
1197.measured: Ways designers organized information (clusters, relations, nests), features of generated ideas, relation to designer background
1197.method_detail: In-depth lab sessions with think-aloud, idea analysis and interview content analysis
1197.finding: Designers structured information in three ways (clusters, relations, nests), and both background and organizing strategy were linked to the features of their ideas.

1198.task: Brainstormed and sketched concepts with no time limit while a near-infrared brain sensor recorded prefrontal cortex activity
1198.problem: Device to help elderly people raise and lower windows
1198.prompt: Design a device to assist the elderly with raising and lowering windows
1198.measured: Oxygenated hemoglobin changes in 22 prefrontal channels, brain network centrality over ten time deciles of each session
1198.method_detail: fNIRS neuroimaging with graph-theory analysis of network connectivity
1198.finding: Network centrality shifted between right, medial and left prefrontal cortex during brainstorming, consistent with alternation between divergent and convergent thinking.

1200.who: 24 participants (35 screened) in 12 pairs of internal-internal, external-external or internal-external locus of control
1200.task: Four individual and six paired slider-based parameter design tasks as fast as possible in a under-one-hour session, after five training tasks
1200.problem: Abstract cooperative parameter design (adjusting input sliders to hit output targets)
1200.prompt: Adjust the controlled sliders to bring all outputs into target regions as quickly as possible, alone or with a partner
1200.measured: Task completion time efficiency, designer behaviors such as action effectiveness, by locus of control pairing
1200.method_detail: Between-subjects pairing groups with 72 team task observations and regression analysis
1200.finding: Pairs with matching internal locus of control were most efficient and mixed internal-external pairs least, so trait similarity improved team efficiency.

1201.who: 50 US adults recruited on Mechanical Turk
1201.task: Online survey: saw autonomous car images with different messages, chose to cross or not, and rated confidence, perceived safety and trust
1201.problem: Autonomous vehicle message design for pedestrian crossing
1201.prompt: Decide whether to cross a two-way crosswalk with no signals, relying on the approaching car's message and the scene
1201.measured: Crossing decision, confidence, perceived safety and trust under informative, advisory and commanding styles, and with or without a follow-up reassurance message
1201.method_detail: Preliminary within-subject online survey experiment varying communication style and adaptive strategy
1201.finding: Advisory messages raised trust when a cross decision was expected, advisory and commanding messages raised it when not crossing was expected, and a follow-up reassurance message improved trust when crossing was expected.

1202.who: 32 senior product design teams of 17-20 students each over four course years (total people not stated)
1202.task: Teams used Slack during a 3-month course; researchers analyzed over 400,000 public-channel messages for networks, emoji use and topics, compared with expert-rated team strength
1202.problem: Student-identified product opportunities in a senior mechanical engineering product design course
1202.measured: Communication network density and centrality, emoji use and reactions by role, topic breadth and progression, stronger versus weaker team rating
1202.method_detail: Longitudinal analysis of exported Slack data with network, emoji and topic-model analysis
1202.finding: Stronger teams had lower average member centrality and used emojis more, and leaders and highly connected members used emojis most and held more central network positions.

1203.who: 5 industry professionals from five organizations of different sizes (large, SME and start-up)
1203.task: Took part in one-on-one semi-structured teleconference interviews of about 18 minutes about challenges in adopting crowdsourcing
1203.measured: Challenges of crowdsourcing coded from transcripts (problem formulation, resources, incentives, crowd selection, intellectual property), differences by organization size
1203.method_detail: Inductive content analysis of audio-recorded interviews with inter-rater reliability
1203.finding: Large organizations and start-ups were judged more likely to adopt crowdsourcing than SMEs, which struggle with resources, incentives, problem formulation and changing organizational culture.

1204.who: 12 engineering students experienced in additive manufacturing and CAD (4 control, 8 experimental)
1204.task: After a 15-minute inspection or checking task, redesigned a jet engine bracket in CAD for 45 minutes while thinking aloud, with or without a design-for-inspectability worksheet, then a post-survey
1204.prompt: Reduce the bracket mass by at least half while meeting the loading specifications; the experimental group also had to keep it inspectable by ultrasound
1204.measured: Final design models, think-aloud and screen-capture of process, self-rated confidence and time allocation, mass and strength
1204.method_detail: Preliminary lab study with random assignment to control and worksheet groups
1204.finding: Preliminary results suggest the inspectability worksheet changed the design process, making designers more selective in removing material and altering CAD tool choices, though the sample was small.

1205.who: 131 junior and senior mechanical engineering students in 32 teams of 3-5
1205.task: Built a robot-sumo robot over a 16-week course, with an early Alpha and a final Beta prototype, reporting time, cost and perceived value of each prototype in a survey system
1205.problem: Autonomous sumo robot (30 cm limit, $20 extra component budget)
1205.prompt: Design and build an autonomous robot no larger than 30 by 30 cm to push opponents out of a ring, with at most $20 on added components
1205.measured: Prototype time and money invested, perceived prototype value (success, requirements, problem learning, fabrication learning), competition outcome
1205.method_detail: In-situ study in a semester course with surveys after week 4 and week 14
1205.finding: No significant link was found between prototype cost and perceived value or outcome, but teams that reduced uncertainty early with Alpha prototypes did better, and top teams valued final prototypes less for learning.

1206.task: Defined function before and after building a function structure model on paper (video recorded); definitions topic-modeled and compared with literature and model quality
1206.measured: Topics in function definitions (LDA), definitions from literature, function model size (functions and flows), rubric-based model evaluation
1206.method_detail: Protocol study with pre/post surveys; exploratory text analysis, not a controlled experiment
1206.finding: Student definitions leaned toward a single topic while literature definitions mixed topics, and definitions stressing input/output and process went with larger function models; modeling changed how students defined function.

1207.who: 8 practitioners from Danish industry (7 in the focus group)
1207.task: Completed an online survey, then took part in a three-hour focus group with discussion and silent brainstorm about prototyping; content analysis of the data
1207.measured: Prototyping challenges, opportunities for improvement, and trends reported by practitioners
1207.method_detail: Small survey plus focus group, qualitative content analysis, mostly qualitative
1207.finding: Practitioners named 23 prototyping challenges, 15 opportunities and 5 trends, struggling most with decisions from few limited prototypes, virtual-physical gaps, medical regulation and misread prototypes.

1210.who: 28 engineering graduate students in 9 brainstorming teams
1210.task: Teams of about three brainstormed for 15 minutes with a human or a Wizard-of-Oz cognitive assistant facilitating, then chose a final idea; sessions coded and modeled
1210.problem: Reducing campus pedestrian accidents caused by cell phone distraction
1210.prompt: Brainstorm ideas to reduce pedestrian accidents on campus caused by phone distraction and select a final solution as a team
1210.measured: Interaction dynamics codes of team behavior, hidden Markov model group states, speaking time distribution
1210.method_detail: Two facilitation conditions (4 teams each analyzed); Interaction Dynamics Notation with Hidden Markov Models
1210.finding: Human facilitation led to more blocks, interruptions and responses and more equal speaking time, while cognitive assistant facilitation was linked to deviations and silence.

1211.task: Rated six brand-neutral vehicle fronts on friendliness, aggressiveness and gender, then compared pairs of fronts for belonging to the same brand
1211.problem: Vehicle front end (sedan) with smiling/frowning contours and curved/angular surfaces
1211.measured: Perceived friendliness, aggressiveness and masculinity of stimuli, brand affiliation of paired vehicle fronts
1211.method_detail: Online survey with rendered stimuli varying face contour and surface type
1211.finding: Both contour and surface type influenced brand affiliation, and respondents split into two groups, one pairing by friendly face and one by shared surface or aggressive look.

1334.who: 16 graduate mechanical engineering students in three specialized groups (5, 5, 6)
1334.task: Groups did conceptual design, detail design and fabrication over two 7-day rounds, first without communication, then with fax-like written exchange; focus groups after
1334.problem: Ping-pong ball herding machine (round 1), confetti-making machine from audio tape (round 2)
1334.prompt: Design and build a machine from scrap materials that herds ping-pong balls on a sinusoidal table, then one that cuts cassette tape into variable-length confetti
1334.measured: Information exchanged between groups across rounds, content of informal written messages, participant interview reflections
1334.method_detail: Course-based simulated project comparing no communication with asynchronous written communication; message and interview analysis
1334.finding: Asynchronous written communication tools were of little use to engineers doing design and manufacture, and substantial augmentation would be needed before engineers adopt them.

1337.who: 20 people: 6 expert mechanical designers, 7 graduate students, 7 non-design undergraduates
1337.task: Described aloud what they saw in 13 mechanical drawings, shown alone, then with a title, then with a short explanation; sessions videotaped
1337.problem: Reading 13 mechanical assembly drawings (couplings, valves, clutch, etc.)
1337.prompt: Describe aloud what you see in each drawing
1337.measured: Forms, design features and subfunctions mentioned, forward vs backward reasoning, whether overall function was identified; discriminant analysis across groups
1337.method_detail: Verbal protocol analysis with group comparison by expertise
1337.finding: Experts reasoned backward from overall function, while novices focused on geometry and graduate students resembled experts on familiar drawings and novices on others.

1340.who: Novice designers in four studies: first-year engineering and design students, plus 14, 1 and 17 senior students
1340.task: Across four experiments, designed a picnic table, a damping-cylinder test rig, an electric vehicle suspension, and final-year projects; sketches, videos and workbooks analyzed
1340.problem: Folding picnic table, rig for testing a hydraulic damping cylinder, electric vehicle suspension and transmission, final-year projects
1340.prompt: Design a folding picnic table within one week; develop concepts for a rig measuring hydraulic damping cylinder performance (4 hours, in groups of 2-4)
1340.measured: Sketch types and quality, number of design concepts, time share spent sketching, retrospective review of jottings and workbooks
1340.method_detail: Four studies with retrospective review, group videotape protocols, workbooks and activity sampling; builds a model of visual thinking
1340.finding: Novices' idea development is constrained by sketching; functional, geometric and pictorial sketches tie to concept stages, and the sketching interface can act as a barrier biased toward cognition or the physical.

1342.who: 4 engineers from industry (two pairs with 6-7 years experience)
1342.task: Pairs thought aloud while designing; speech, actions and drawings recorded; protocol turned into a semantic network to track attention
1342.problem: Rotating mechanism for an electric fan; jumping toy
1342.prompt: Each pair designed a rotating mechanism for an electric fan and a jumping toy meeting given specifications
1342.measured: Knowledge used in design, importance (activation) of concepts in a semantic network over time, drawing protocols
1342.method_detail: Protocol analysis with a CAD-like drawing recorder; methods paper with small sample
1342.finding: The authors show that design experiments with protocol analysis can reveal what knowledge designers use and how their attention shifts, using knowledge extraction and a connectionist concept network.

1344.who: A case-memory computer program (no human participants)
1344.task: System checked side effects and preconditions of events against a causal case memory to spot novel uses of familiar plans, on historical examples
1344.problem: Historical invention examples (e.g., Archimedes, Morse telegraph relay)
1344.measured: Whether the system recognizes familiar plans as relevant to blocked design goals
1344.method_detail: System description with worked examples, no empirical evaluation
1344.finding: A causal case memory that checks side effects and preconditions lets a system recognize when familiar plans can solve a blocked design problem in a novel way.

1346.task: Made modifications to existing designs from blueprints and specifications while asking questions and forming conjectures; audio and video recorded, with an examiner as information source
1346.problem: Redesign of aluminum plate dipping equipment (two engineers) and a plastic battery enclosure
1346.prompt: Given finished blueprints and original specifications, modify the design to meet two to four proposed specification changes
1346.measured: Questions asked and conjectures formed, who or what answered or confirmed them, taxonomy of information sought
1346.method_detail: Question-asking protocols of 1 to 2.75 hours each, with a warm-up session
1346.finding: Engineers sought information missing from blueprints; of 372 questions and conjectures, 31% concerned operation or purpose and 45% went unconfirmed, motivating intelligent CAD that stores design history.

1348.who: Mechanical designers from earlier protocol studies (graduate students, experienced designers; counts not reported)
1348.task: Paper describes a software tool for recording and querying design history, built from earlier protocols of designers and question-asking redesign sessions
1348.problem: Mechanical design history tool; source protocols covered production and one-off designs
1348.measured: Design history representation of constraints and decisions; questions and conjectures from earlier protocols that shape what to record
1348.method_detail: Tool description grounded on prior protocol data (46 hours); no new participant study
1348.finding: A design history tool built from protocol data can store the constraints, decisions and rationale behind each design object so that others can query why features exist.

1360.who: 5 mechanical designers (2 professors, 3 industry or independent designers with 8-25 years experience)
1360.task: Described aloud 13 mechanical assembly drawings while reading and analyzing them; protocols coded for geometric attributes then cluster analyzed
1360.problem: Reading 13 mechanical assembly drawings (motors, couplings, pumps, valves, razor, clutch)
1360.prompt: Describe aloud what you see while reading and analyzing each drawing
1360.measured: Geometric attributes in verbal descriptions, 61 design features, cluster analysis for distinctive features, discriminant analysis
1360.method_detail: Verbal protocol analysis with cluster analysis
1360.finding: Fifteen of 50 geometric attributes were minimally sufficient to distinguish the 61 design features, giving a basal set of distinctive features designers use to describe mechanical drawings.

1367.who: 3 design teams: faculty, industry designers, students (about 5 faculty, 5 students)
1367.task: Teams worked on a computer-based group design system with a manager, after a tutorial and a practice problem, until a concept was selected; transactions logged
1367.problem: Device to help a teenager with spastic cerebral palsy feed herself
1367.prompt: Design equipment aiding a quadriplegic teenager with uncontrollable arm movements to self-feed, minimizing impact of spastic motion
1367.measured: Time in transaction categories, response to management direction, sequence of transactions leading to the concept decision, member involvement
1367.method_detail: Three teams compared via logged transactions in a group design system
1367.finding: Systematic procedures seemed to encourage more equal participation, decisions less driven by individuals, and a flatter authority hierarchy.

1370.who: 65 junior and senior engineering students in a mechanical design class
1370.task: Took two timed concept generation tests (in-class 50 minutes plus take-home) before and after instruction; concepts counted and standardized by sample
1370.problem: Backup surface sampler for a Mars mission; household waste separation
1370.prompt: Generate as many distinct concepts as possible for a Mars backup surface sampler, later a way to separate municipal household trash
1370.measured: Number of concepts per student, standardized score by distinct concepts in sample, share of subjects identifying each concept
1370.method_detail: Two tests six class periods apart within a design course
1370.finding: Most concepts (60-70%) were produced by under 10% of students; standardizing by the sample's concept space worked for the in-class test.

1372.who: 16 senior-level simulation course students (graduate and undergraduate)
1372.task: Adjusted parameters of a manufacturing simulation by trial and error to restore base performance, with or without an expert advisor, in two activities
1372.problem: Tuning a discrete-event simulation of a manufacturing system
1372.prompt: After a specified technological change, adjust input rate (and workforce size) until throughput time and work in process match pre-change values
1372.measured: Number of simulations run, effects of queueing background and student status
1372.method_detail: Factorial design with two replications, treatment versus no advisor
1372.finding: Using the expert advisor reduced the number of simulations needed, though other factors may also affect trial and error.

1391.who: A company design team developing a riding lawn mower (no human participants reported)
1391.task: Described a design process that defined a frequency-weighted vibration measure and applied spectrum, modal and finite element analysis to optimize the mower
1391.problem: Rear-engine riding lawn mower vibration design
1391.measured: Goodness of Vibration factor at steering wheel, footrests and seat, modal behavior, excitation spectra
1391.method_detail: Engineering case of one product line; measurement and analysis, no participant study
1391.finding: A frequency-weighted Goodness of Vibration factor quantified operator perceived vibration, linked to modal behavior and excitation, and helped produce a comfort-optimized mower.

1393.who: 24 senior mechanical engineering students (3 groups of 8)
1393.task: Each group rated four design solutions twice, two weeks apart, using one of three design quality scales (test-retest)
1393.problem: Mount for an elliptical fire extinguisher
1393.prompt: Rate the quality of four given solutions to a fire extinguisher mount problem using the assigned scale
1393.measured: Test-retest reliability of ratings and weights per scale and dimension (ANOVA on session effects)
1393.method_detail: Within-subjects split-plot counterbalanced design with a two-week retest
1393.finding: One of the three psychometric scales gave unreliable judgments over time while the other two were reliable.

1394.who: Design engineers (number not reported) at 6 automotive companies in the US and Europe
1394.task: Engineers helped define performance attributes and gave preference judgments used to build multiattribute utility functions that ranked material system alternatives
1394.problem: Automotive structure and body skin material choice among steel, aluminum and polymer composites
1394.measured: Multiattribute utility of alternatives, acceptable attribute ranges, rankings and tradeoffs, sensitivity analysis
1394.method_detail: Application of a deterministic multiattribute utility method
1394.finding: The method ranked design alternatives and quantified tradeoffs, and results depended strongly on engineers' subjective preferences, with notable differences across similar alternatives.

1414.who: 318 first-year engineering and design students in 8 cohorts
1414.task: Brainstormed individually for 15 minutes on sheets with 8 or 20 idea cells while seeing no analogy images, six static images, or six new images every minute
1414.problem: Each team's own problem statement from its course project
1414.prompt: Generate as many ideas as possible for your project's problem, sketching each in a cell on the sheet
1414.measured: Number of distinct ideas, level of detail (1-5 rating by two researchers)
1414.method_detail: Between-cohort design crossing sheet format with analogy exposure condition
1414.finding: The 20-cell sheet produced more ideas, and continuous exposure to new analogy images raised both idea quantity and level of detail compared with static or no images.

1415.who: 10 designers aged 20-26 (4 male, 6 female, 1-6 years design experience)
1415.task: Made office chair designs with ChatGPT and Midjourney, then a 20-minute interview; outputs compared with 105 Red Dot chair entries
1415.prompt: Create novel office chair designs with help from two generative AI tools, submitting all satisfactory designs
1415.measured: Design feature keywords in AI text vs Red Dot designs, image feature diversity, designers' recognition of and responses to AI design fixation
1415.method_detail: One-on-one sessions with 96 AI-generated solutions, keyword analysis, and semi-structured interviews
1415.finding: AI-generated chair designs showed fixation at the feature level, with less emphasis on structural elements than human award-entry designs, and designers' recognition of and responses to this were examined.

1417.who: 10 expert engineers at one lawn equipment manufacturer
1417.task: Took part in a semi-structured interview, thinking aloud about a design problem and building knowledge networks with sticky notes on a whiteboard at three points
1417.problem: Reducing turf scalping on a zero-turn lawn mower
1417.prompt: Improve a recently launched mower design to cut the chance of scalping turf while keeping cut quality, striping and sustainability, with no budget
1417.measured: Knowledge network size (nodes, edges), growth rate across recognize, gather and evaluate phases, effect of years of experience
1417.method_detail: Interview with think-aloud and mind-mapping; network analysis
1417.finding: Networks grew similarly in the recognize and gather phases, with nodes added fastest in recognize, and more company experience went with more nodes and edges in the final network.

1418.who: 46 people in two studies: 20 (GPT-4 vs none) and 26 (GPT-4, XAI tool, raters)
1418.task: Study 1: divergent and convergent thinking tests with or without GPT-4. Study 2: proposed motorbike design elements with GPT-4 or an explainable AI tool; raters scored them
1418.problem: Study 2: environmentally friendly, fuel-efficient two-wheeled urban motorbike
1418.prompt: Propose 5 to 7 functions, behaviors and structures for an eco-friendly fuel-efficient urban motorbike, with a short explanation of the overall proposal
1418.measured: Fluency, originality, elaboration, creativity test scores; objective usefulness, feasibility, originality, subjective credibility of proposals
1418.method_detail: Two between-subjects online studies; second evaluates a proposed explainable AI framework
1418.finding: GPT-4 produced more ideas but less original individual responses and did better on convergent tasks; the explainable AI tool seemed to improve ideas and originality with small losses in feasibility and credibility.

1419.who: 12 graduate students in one design program at University of Michigan
1419.task: Four 10-minute ideation trials in groups of three, each with a different prompt and playlist (classical, pop, video game, none); sketched ideas, short survey
1419.problem: Four brief design prompts (e.g., safety in dark hours, helping people move, diaper waste)
1419.prompt: Generate as many ideas as possible in 10 minutes for the given design prompt, one idea per box, while listening to music or silence
1419.measured: Idea quantity, diversity, creativity (self-rated), preferred playlist
1419.method_detail: Exploratory within-subjects design with rotated playlist and prompt
1419.finding: Participants produced the most ideas and preferred the pop playlist, while the video game playlist produced the most creative and diverse ideas by self-report.

1423.who: 12 designers in 3 teams at NASA; 4 expert raters; GPT-3.5-turbo run as a third source
1423.task: Teams made Futures Wheel ideas on online whiteboards in a six-week design sprint; 120 sampled ideas from human, human-with-AI and AI sources were rated blind by experts
1423.problem: Speculative scenarios for the future of aeronautics
1423.prompt: Create scenarios that uncover threats and opportunities for the future of aeronautics, listing cascading outcomes of imagined events
1423.measured: Expert ratings of well-crafted, novel and useful (1-5), word count, local similarity of ideas
1423.method_detail: Field data from a design sprint; 40 ideas sampled per AI-use condition; ANOVA and consensus ratings
1423.finding: AI-generated and AI-assisted ideas were rated more well-crafted than human ideas and AI-generated ones more useful than AI-assisted, with no novelty difference and a smaller design space for AI ideas.

1424.who: A speech-recognition plus LLM classifier (Whisper, Phi-3.5-based model); tested on a NASA team of 13 consenting people
1424.task: Classified spoken sentences into 12 interaction dynamics labels in real time during a three-day remote design sprint; compared with human coding
1424.problem: Improving aviation connectivity in rural communities, including disaster relief
1424.measured: Agreement between automatic and human-coded interaction dynamics labels, per-label strengths and weaknesses
1424.method_detail: System build plus one case-study trial in a remote NASA design sprint (3 days, 4 hours each)
1424.finding: The automatic system matched human coders on 80.3% of sentences, similar to human inter-rater agreement, but struggled with humor and idea blocking.

1428.who: 4 GPT-4o-based AI judges (no human participants); 2 expert and 3 trained novice raters scored 934 sketches
1428.task: AI judges rated early-stage design sketches with different in-context prompts, three runs each; ratings tested for equivalence against experts and novices
1428.problem: Early-stage design sketches from earlier studies (934 sketches)
1428.measured: Uniqueness, creativity, usefulness, drawing quality (6-point); kappa, ICC, error, Spearman, top-set overlap, equivalence tests (TOST)
1428.method_detail: Statistical framework for expert equivalence, with text, image and reasoning prompt variants
1428.finding: The best AI judge (text and image examples with reasoning) reached expert-level agreement on uniqueness and drawing quality and matched or beat trained novices on all metrics.

1429.who: 20 people: 10 assistive-device designers interviewed, and 10 experts (5 clinical, 5 design) who validated a requirements list
1429.task: Designers were interviewed; separate experts judged a 30% sample of a requirements list as valid or not, assigned demand or wish, then were interviewed
1429.problem: Assistive devices for children with special needs (requirement elicitation)
1429.prompt: Review the categorized requirements for practical relevance, mark each valid or not, and assign priority and design category
1429.measured: Validity of requirements, agreement on demand versus wish and design category, expert interview comments
1429.method_detail: Validation Square framework with expert validation study plus interviews
1429.finding: Over half of requirements got unanimous demand or wish mapping, but experts disagreed on others and said requirements are context-specific, challenging a generic master list.

1430.who: 17 professional designers (architecture) plus 8 student wizards (two teams of four)
1430.task: Designers sketched a housing concept in 90-minute sessions while hidden student wizards, simulating an AI assistant, sent inspirational images, CAD plans and 3D models every five minutes
1430.problem: Family housing on a sloping terrain
1430.prompt: Conceive a family housing solution on a sloping site from a printed brief while receiving visual stimuli
1430.measured: Wizard time management and content creation, designer perception of the simulated AI, quality of data collected
1430.method_detail: Wizard of Oz application in 17 lab design sessions, with benefits and challenges of the method
1430.finding: Wizards produced stimuli on time with good content, designers perceived the simulation as real and positive, and the method gave rich data though it has costs and challenges.

1431.who: 128 online participants (native English speakers recruited on Prolific)
1431.task: Rated how similar 36 pairs of product images were by shape and by function on a 1-5 scale within six seconds each; reaction times recorded
1431.prompt: Rate how similar the two products are in shape, then in function, from not similar to very similar
1431.measured: Similarity ratings, reaction time as cognitive demand, accuracy of matched pairs, individual differences such as online shopping frequency
1431.method_detail: Online repeated-measures pairwise rating task with nine product images
1431.finding: Functional similarity judgments took more cognitive effort but were more accurate than appearance judgments, pointing to a functionality context schema; shopping frequency affected appearance judgments.

1432.who: 30 participants (graduate class at Virginia Tech and an ASME workshop attendees)
1432.task: Played an online multiplayer game with surveys, tutorial, free exploration and increasingly complex system architecting rounds with debriefs, to learn solver-aware heuristics
1432.problem: Abstract golf-based systems architecting problems with module and system-level decisions
1432.measured: Share identifying module-level heuristics, quality of system-level tradeoff decisions across rounds, learning over game stages, survey responses
1432.method_detail: Pilot of an educational game in one class and one conference workshop
1432.finding: By the end of the game all participants showed acceptable command of solver-aware heuristics for system-level tradeoffs, and 53% identified module-level heuristics well, suggesting the game supports higher-order learning.

1434.who: 32 senior mechanical engineering student teams (16 strong, 16 weak), 15-20 students each
1434.task: Researchers analyzed 251,744 Slack messages sent during a one-semester product design course, tracking user-related talk across design stages and topic models
1434.problem: Student-chosen consumer products (medical, fitness, accessibility, recreation, electronics)
1434.measured: Frequency and consistency of user-related messages over time, trends across divergent and convergent phases, topic co-occurrence with the word user
1434.method_detail: Secondary analysis of Slack data from 2016-2019 course offerings; topic modeling
1434.finding: Strong teams discussed users more consistently across the project and tied users more deeply to process terms, while weak teams talked about users sporadically.

1435.who: 8 undergraduates in 2 hackathon teams (5 in a team of strangers, 3 pre-existing teammates)
1435.task: Teams worked on self-chosen projects at hackathons while audio was recorded; conflict episodes were coded in transcripts and language compared with LIWC
1435.problem: Self-chosen hackathon projects (skin-tone outfit suggester, assistive wearable for visually impaired users)
1435.prompt: None given; teams were self-directed and chose their own project topics
1435.measured: Instances of conflict, LIWC language categories such as negative emotion, prosocial language, sentence complexity and cohesion, in conflict vs non-conflict talk
1435.method_detail: In-situ audio recordings at two hackathons, deductive coding then sentiment analysis
1435.finding: During conflict, teams used less negative emotion and prosocial language and focused on the task; the familiar team had fewer conflicts (28 vs 35) and resolved them with more complex sentences.

1436.who: 82 sophomore mechanical engineering students in 41 dyads (secondary analysis of earlier experiment)
1436.task: Pairs spent 20 minutes improving a sample design shown as text, sketch or CAD, then wrote individual reports; speaking time, words and turns analyzed from video
1436.problem: Peanut shelling and packaging machine redesign
1436.measured: Turn-taking counts, difference in speaking time, difference in words spoken between teammates
1436.method_detail: Between-subjects dyads by representation type (text 13 teams, drawing 14, CAD remainder); ANOVA on prior data
1436.finding: Equality of participation did not differ across text, sketch and CAD representations, so representation modality alone did not shape how evenly teammates contributed.

1437.who: 1,208 first-year engineering and computer science students in 378 teams (944 students analyzed in 297 teams)
1437.task: Teams of one, three or six wrote design requirements for 20 minutes after a guest lecture on requirements; requirements categorized for variety
1437.problem: Bookshelf retrieval device for wheelchair users, or bicycle safety lock
1437.prompt: Develop requirements for a mechanism helping wheelchair users reach high books, or for a lightweight bicycle lock permanently attached
1437.measured: Requirement category coverage (variety), frequency of categories, categories per requirement
1437.method_detail: Randomized team size across four course sections, two equivalent prompts
1437.finding: All team sizes covered about 60% of requirement categories, but teams of six had more categories in the highest-frequency band, so size raised emphasis, not breadth.

1438.who: 89 adults in two studies (23 in study 1, 66 in study 2), mostly university students
1438.task: Online survey rating ten AI-generated helmet concepts for feasibility and novelty and choosing which to advance, with labels or a power manipulation
1438.prompt: Evaluate each helmet concept on novelty and feasibility and decide which concepts should move forward in the design process
1438.measured: Perceived feasibility and novelty, concept selection decisions, effect of personal sense of power (high, control, low)
1438.method_detail: Two within-subjects online experiments; study 2 manipulated sense of power
1438.finding: Labeling concepts as AI- or human-generated had no effect, and sense of power had mixed effects on evaluation and selection of AI-generated helmets, contrary to prior literature.

1439.who: 1,208 first-year engineering and computer science students in 378 teams of one, three or six
1439.task: Teams wrote design requirements for 20 minutes; 4,310 requirements were coded by parts of speech for completeness (subject, modal, verb, modifier, object, target value)
1439.problem: Bookshelf retrieval device for wheelchair users, or bicycle safety lock
1439.prompt: Develop requirements for a mechanism helping wheelchair users reach high books, or for a lightweight bicycle lock permanently attached
1439.measured: Completeness of requirements via parts of speech use, including modals, objects, modifiers and target values
1439.method_detail: Randomized team size across course sections, two equivalent prompts, 297 teams analyzed
1439.finding: Individuals leaned on objects and modifiers, while teams of three and six used more modal terms and numeric target values, with little difference between three and six.

1440.who: 15 public sector innovation professionals in the Netherlands (8) and Sweden (7)
1440.task: Completed a pre-survey, then a 30-60 minute semi-structured interview about design and innovation in their organizations; thematic analysis
1440.measured: Use of dynamic design capabilities in public innovation, themes on innovation, design, context and capabilities
1440.method_detail: Semi-structured interviews with a pre-survey, thematic analysis
1440.finding: Dynamic design capabilities are not yet fully used in the public sector, though six emerging capabilities appear, such as design culture, integrated expertise and interdepartmental collaboration.

1441.who: 5 utility-scale solar developers at Michigan firms (small, medium and large)
1441.task: Took part in 60-75 minute semi-structured Zoom interviews about decisions, stakeholders and community engagement, with a process map
1441.measured: Key decision points, stakeholder interaction patterns, barriers to including community perspectives
1441.method_detail: Semi-structured interviews with process map integration, qualitative analysis
1441.finding: Developers saw community as fragmented, with landowners and officials as main decision-makers, neighbors emerging, and the public reached mostly through hearings, and they used limited engagement to manage risk.

1444.who: 42 engineering students (13 seniors, 29 juniors) at one college
1444.task: Read the original or a redesigned Pugh design specification tool for 10 minutes, listed factors for a design problem for 10 minutes, then answered questions on the tool
1444.problem: Retaining wall system for flood-prone Conewago Creek
1444.prompt: List the factors you would consider in designing a retaining wall system for a creek that floods during extreme weather, damaging nearby homes and farms
1444.measured: Depth and engagement with social and ethical factors in responses, perceived helpfulness of the tool
1444.method_detail: Random assignment to original or social-impact-centered tool in an online survey
1444.finding: Students using the redesigned tool gave more engaged and deeper responses on social and ethical factors and rated it more helpful for considering social impact.

1445.who: 5 panelists plus audience members at a conference session (about 30 gave affiliation, mostly academics)
1445.task: Attended a 2.5-hour session with talks, filled a short survey on what design justice means, joined a panel discussion and small group discussions; responses were coded
1445.prompt: What does justice in design mean to you and how does it show up in your work or research?
1445.measured: Definitions of design justice, how justice is integrated into research and practice, opportunities, challenges, future work
1445.method_detail: Special session at IDETC 2024 with open-ended survey, panel and group discussion transcripts; qualitative analysis
1445.finding: Participants framed design justice around community, implementation and impact, and pointed to power dynamics, long-term community engagement and institutional support as key challenges and needs.

1446.who: 7 participants in 3 teams (grouped by experience level)
1446.task: Teams of 2-3 read a fictional community description and six stakeholder cards, then had 30 minutes to propose one solution on video; stakeholder perspective-taking instances were coded
1446.problem: Water infrastructure grant for a fictional rural community
1446.prompt: Use a one-time federal water infrastructure grant to identify a potential early-stage solution that benefits the town most, considering six stakeholder viewpoints
1446.measured: 89 instances of stakeholder perspective-taking coded on a six-level spectrum from dismissal to adoption, individual and team signatures
1446.method_detail: Recorded 30-minute team design sessions; qualitative coding and visualization
1446.finding: Participants varied from dismissing to fully integrating stakeholder input, and visualizing coded instances as signatures showed distinct individual and team patterns of perspective-taking.

1449.who: A human-knowledge-embedded Bayesian optimization algorithm; 4 experienced machine operators supplied trial-and-error data
1449.task: Operators adjusted five roller spacings across conditions while adjustments were logged; SHAP extracted their knowledge to bound a Bayesian optimizer, compared with operators and standard optimization
1449.problem: Roll forming machine setup for customized building products
1449.prompt: Iteratively adjust five roller spacings under varying friction and material thickness until deformation reaches the target
1449.measured: Number of setup iterations and its spread versus operators and vanilla Bayesian optimization, SHAP importance of rollers
1449.method_detail: Case study with simulated roll forming setups
1449.finding: The method cut average trial iterations by 14.6% versus human operators and 76.6% versus vanilla Bayesian optimization, with benefits strongest when knowledge came from high-performing operators.

1451.who: 5 pilot participants from a university mechanical and industrial engineering department
1451.task: Did two IKEA-hacking tasks, one in CAD and one on paper (counterbalanced), with EEG and eye tracking
1451.problem: IKEA Hacking Task: build a new design from furniture parts
1451.prompt: Use at least three furniture parts, which may be combined, cut or connected, to create a new design
1451.measured: Creativity test scores (TTCT), EEG power spectrum and connectivity, eye tracking, design creativity under CAD vs pen and paper
1451.method_detail: Methodology review plus 5-person pilot of a within-subjects EEG and eye-tracking design
1451.finding: The pilot cannot support statistical conclusions but suggests the baseline and free-design tasks engage distinct neural processes and that CAD and pen-and-paper conditions differ in EEG patterns.

1452.task: Co-designed with a custom generative AI system using sketch and text prompts in one-hour think-aloud sessions (explore, function, form, free design); trust-related comments coded
1452.problem: In-law suite in a separate dwelling on an existing house (under 20 square meters)
1452.prompt: Design a small in-law suite with sleeping, bathroom, clothing and desk space, using the generative AI image tool
1452.measured: 896 trust-related think-aloud comments, factors causing trust to rise or fall
1452.method_detail: 12 hours of think-aloud protocol with incremental qualitative coding
1452.finding: Twenty-three factors drove trust fluctuation in co-design with generative AI, chiefly intent alignment, aesthetic quality and plausibility while keeping inspiration and avoiding fixation.

1453.who: 56 residents of Australia interviewed (plus 3 novice designers as interviewers); 112 simulated LLM personas as comparison
1453.task: Real users and GPT-4o-mini personas answered the same interview questions; three AI tools extracted themes, clustered into user needs
1453.measured: Themes and user needs from real versus simulated interviews, effect of demographic information on LLM answers, topic model comparisons
1453.method_detail: Comparison of 56 human interviews with 2 sets of 56 LLM interviews; human reviewers clustered needs
1453.finding: LLM interviewees reproduced general needs but missed deeper cultural and context themes, echoed the interview questions' emphasis, and demographic details barely changed their answers.

1454.who: 56 online participants without professional design experience, recruited via crowdsourcing
1454.task: Each used four versions of a chatbot design assistant in random order, generating and revising a sustainable household product concept with each, then rated trust and perceptions
1454.problem: Sustainable household products (washing machine, lighting, HVAC, toilet)
1454.prompt: Describe a sustainable design concept for the assigned household product to the chatbot and revise it after its critique
1454.measured: User trust in the AI, perceived effort, enjoyment, usefulness, effects of appearance, performance and empathy
1454.method_detail: Within-subjects fractional factorial design with four chatbot versions
1454.finding: Better system performance and empathetic behavior raised trust, and empathy improved perceived effort, enjoyment and usefulness even when performance was low.

1456.who: 28 undergraduate and graduate students in engineering and design (14 per condition)
1456.task: Watched a 5-minute video of a vacuuming or desk-setup activity and listed user needs, with or without an AI posture-analysis tool in the second half
1456.problem: User needs identification from video observation (vacuuming, office desk setup)
1456.prompt: Observe the person in the video and identify as many of their needs as possible, going beyond the obvious
1456.measured: Number and types of needs identified, level of detail, efficiency, participant experience and confidence
1456.method_detail: Formative between-subjects study of an AI ergonomic observation tool (REBA scoring from pose estimation)
1456.finding: The tool did not change the number or types of needs found but improved the level of detail and efficiency and raised designer confidence.

1460.who: 60 undergraduate civil engineering students (46 male) in a sustainability design course
1460.task: Thought aloud while identifying future constraints for a site, with or without ChatGPT, then ideated concepts unaided; transcripts were coded and prefrontal brain activity recorded with fNIRS
1460.problem: Sustainable redevelopment of a campus site
1460.prompt: Identify future environmental and climatic constraints for a campus site, then develop conceptual designs for its sustainable redevelopment
1460.measured: Number of constraints, number of design concepts by category, fNIRS prefrontal activation as cognitive effort
1460.method_detail: Random assignment to human-only or AI-assisted constraints identification; verbal protocol coding with fNIRS
1460.finding: AI-assisted students identified more constraints, later produced more sustainability-related concepts without AI, and showed lower neurocognitive effort in both phases.

1461.who: GPT-4o and GPT-4.5 agents (no human participants); design experts validated the knowledge space
1461.task: LLM agent followed C-K theory operations (concept-knowledge transitions) over 50 time steps under four conditions varying a penalizer feedback loop and concept memory
1461.problem: Creative nail holder for use while hammering
1461.measured: Transition history across C-K operations, diversity of concept space over time (determinantal point process, distance to centroid)
1461.method_detail: LLM agent simulation of C-K theory with two models and four conditions
1461.finding: The simulated agent was mostly stuck in concept-to-concept transitions and concept diversity declined over time in every condition, pointing to gaps in C-K theory around concept-to-knowledge and knowledge-to-concept steps.

1497.who: Student users (9 in the reported spring test) plus other student and industrial users not detailed
1497.task: Students designed a minimum-weight spring using a conventional spreadsheet or the proposed Designer's Spreadsheet; paper mainly describes the tool and its theory
1497.problem: Minimum-weight spring (among other practical design problems)
1497.measured: Weight of springs designed with each spreadsheet, ease of use and support for design problem solving
1497.method_detail: Tool paper with brief comparison test; fuller tests reported elsewhere
1497.finding: A spreadsheet built for preliminary parametric design was reported as intuitive and gave more support for design problem solving than a conventional spreadsheet.

1505.who: Senior mechanical engineering students (number not reported) split into two method groups
1505.task: Rated four to six design alternatives using either absolute ratings or relative comparisons, in two sessions two weeks apart, with usability and preference questionnaires
1505.problem: Mechanism for dipping each side of an aluminum plate into a chemical bath
1505.prompt: Evaluate the given design alternatives with the assigned assessment method
1505.measured: Reliability (test-retest), sensitivity between alternatives, validity of ranking, usability and preference
1505.method_detail: Between-subjects test-retest comparing absolute rating and relative comparison methods
1505.finding: The absolute rating method was more reliable and gave more valid rankings than relative comparison, which only matched it on sensitivity and was easier to use.

1506.who: 2 graduate students with 5 and 2 years of design experience
1506.task: Thought aloud while designing a bicycle lock for about an hour, after a warm-up problem; sessions audio and video taped, transcribed and coded
1506.prompt: Design a bicycle lock that is a single unit installed on the bike, rather than a separate U-lock; a bike and a sample lock were available
1506.measured: Informational activity (generate, access, analyze) per information fragment, amount of information handled (dims), level of abstraction
1506.method_detail: Verbal protocol analysis of two sessions
1506.finding: More than half of the information handled was newly generated, with access and analysis about a quarter each, and activity concentrated at labeled and associative abstraction levels.

1509.who: 13 mechanical engineers (7 with conventional tools, 6 with the KALEIT CAD system)
1509.task: Designed a device within 6 hours, asked to follow Pahl and Beitz methods; videotaped with heart-rate recording, then reviewed footage in a confrontation interview
1509.problem: Device connecting a washing machine's rotating table to an external motor
1509.prompt: Construct a device to connect the rotating table inside a washing machine to an external electric motor, using a written task and specification list
1509.measured: Heart rate and variability as strain, design variants and actions, time, quality of final layout rated by teaching assistants
1509.method_detail: Laboratory study, stress-and-strain analysis with video-confrontation
1509.finding: Methodical and non-methodical designers did not differ in time or design quality, and evaluating and selecting variants, calculating and reading the task caused the most strain.

1511.who: 13 mechanical engineers (7 with conventional tools, 6 with the KALEIT CAD system)
1511.task: Designed a washing-machine table drive within 6 hours while heart-rate was recorded; video-confrontation interviews on high-strain phases
1511.problem: Device connecting a washing machine's rotating table to an external motor
1511.prompt: Design a device that rotates the table in a washing machine, using design methods of Pahl and Beitz
1511.measured: Heart rate, heart-rate variability and 0.10 Hz power as strain, stress factors in software, time, drawing elements, sketches, layout quality
1511.method_detail: Laboratory study, results used to specify a simultaneous-engineering system
1511.finding: CAD users were slower, drew fewer elements and sketched more than conventional designers because screens hid information and lost old data, yielding user-interface requirements for the new system.

1516.who: Five groups of 2-3 mostly sophomore mechanical engineering students (exact total not reported)
1516.task: Designed a kitchen-scale mechanism blind, dissected two scales, drew free body diagrams, built a compact scale from a kit; videotaped
1516.problem: Kitchen scale mechanism (displacement to pointer rotation)
