1516.prompt: Design a mechanism that turns small vertical movement of the scale pan into large rotation of the pointer, then explore and redesign real scales
1516.measured: Questioning behavior, learning indicators, physical intuition, linkages to prior coursework, use of formal knowledge in practice
1516.method_detail: Video interaction analysis by an interdisciplinary team, in a credit-bearing course exercise
1516.finding: Integrating design, hardware dissection and analysis evoked student questions and supplied resources to answer them, showing students using formal knowledge and building intuition.

1522.who: 2 designers of very different experience (a 54-year-old experienced designer, a graduate student)
1522.task: Discussed and sketched ideas together for 30 minutes after a briefing; video-taped, transcribed and coded into activity objects and state diagrams
1522.problem: Animal trap redesign (reduce shock, add tensioning)
1522.prompt: Improve an existing predator trap so it minimizes initial shock and tensions and relaxes on the animal's leg, generating as many ideas as possible
1522.measured: Idea generation, clarification, evaluation and modification states, interaction densities, use of analogy, experience effects
1522.method_detail: Non-intrusive protocol study with two cooperating subjects
1522.finding: The experienced designer produced most ideas quickly, largely from analogies (about 55 percent), while the student fixated on one cuff solution, and evaluation followed only analogy-based ideas.

1527.who: 33 experienced workshop participants in four groups; one group's session analyzed
1527.task: Groups worked concurrently for 50 minutes on a blood sampling product, then held a design review; sessions videotaped, transcribed and coded with sense-making theory
1527.prompt: Develop a blood sampling product for the group's company using supplied specifications and background sheets; no leaders assigned
1527.measured: Information gaps, helps and decisions within and between groups across design situations
1527.method_detail: Video transcript coding (sense-making) of one business group's session
1527.finding: Early in group design most information needs concerned establishing the knowledge base and the design process, with many more intra-group gaps than helps or decisions and a clear need for exchange between groups.

1535.who: Freshman graphics classes at one university, about 40-80 students per term
1535.task: Students did a design and graphics project in successive course versions (tricycle, then personal-bug poster projects); instructors reviewed posters and revised teaching each term
1535.problem: Course projects: day-care tricycle, then self-chosen personal 'bug' solutions
1535.prompt: First version: design and document a tricycle for a day-care center; later versions: pick a personal need and design a better solution shown in drawings and a poster
1535.measured: Instructor judgments of project originality, sketching, poster communication and critical thinking level (Perry-based)
1535.method_detail: Reflective account of three years of course redesign, no formal assessment instrument
1535.finding: As teaching moved toward explicit connections, peer poster critique and sketching, student projects became more varied and personal and critical thinking moved from level 1 toward level 3.

1550.who: 22 engineering professors in a creativity workshop, plus 3 facilitators (25 total)
1550.task: Took the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator at the start and near the end of a faculty workshop on creativity in design education
1550.measured: Mean MBTI scores before and after, resolved into personality-type components on two orthogonal bases
1550.method_detail: Pre/post questionnaire; mainly a mathematical re-analysis of score vectors
1550.finding: Participants shifted from introversion and monitoring toward intuitive, feeling and perceptive preferences, summarized as a move from administrator toward facilitator.

1563.who: Core members of two workstation teams at one company (number not reported)
1563.task: Researchers disassembled two workstations, computed DFMA metrics, interviewed team members and discussed findings with the teams
1563.measured: Part and screw counts, Boothroyd Dewhurst assembly time and DFA index, assembly cost, engineering change orders, team perceptions
1563.method_detail: Product teardown with metrics plus interviews
1563.finding: The two products scored similarly on DFMA metrics, yet team perceptions of manufacturability differed from the metrics and shaped design decisions when metrics were unavailable.

1569.who: Elementary teachers in a training program (about 75 overall; 8 observed teaching)
1569.task: Took summer and academic-year institutes on engineering and design, did pre/post tests of engineering knowledge, and some were observed teaching a design activity
1569.problem: Elementary design briefs (e.g., rolling frame, toy, sunken ship rescue)
1569.prompt: Teachers worked hands-on design briefs themselves, such as raising a sunken toy boat with balloons
1569.measured: Pre/post engineering knowledge test scores (six questions, 0-3), observed teaching skills of novice versus experienced participants
1569.method_detail: Program description with pre/post testing and classroom observation
1569.finding: Teachers' post-test scores rose and trained teachers showed more engineering teaching skills, indicating more confidence in teaching math, science and engineering.

1570.who: Designers at 7 companies in 20 case studies (number not reported)
1570.task: Researchers observed designers at work and questioned them about information sources and decisions, mapping each access path onto information access diagrams
1570.problem: Real work tasks (e.g., gearbox casing design, bearing selection)
1570.measured: Information sources used and access paths, by design activity type (original, adaptive, variant, simple, complex, selection, new, previously done)
1570.method_detail: Twenty workplace case studies with a new diagramming technique
1570.finding: Designers relied heavily on their own memory, knowledge and experience when accessing information, and nine kinds of design activity were found beyond the classic original, adaptive and variant types.

1571.who: 6 designers (graduate students and one with 20 years of industrial experience)
1571.task: Thought aloud while designing for 51 to 120 minutes; transcripts segmented into information fragments and classified
1571.problem: Bike lock (two versions) and bike backpack fastener
1571.prompt: Design a bicycle lock, or a device fastening a backpack to a mountain bike
1571.measured: Informational activity, descriptor, subject class, level of detail and abstraction; information handled per minute (dims); verbal rate correlation
1571.method_detail: Verbal protocol analysis of six sessions
1571.finding: Designers handled information at a similar rate of about 8 dims per minute, and about 93 percent of conceptual design time involved non-quantitative levels of abstraction.

1584.who: 4 actors and 4 actresses supplying speech samples (no design participants)
1584.task: Recorded normal and angry conversation samples were digitized and analyzed by cepstrum, short-time energy and chunking to extract pitch and amplitude trends
1584.measured: Pitch frequency and maximum amplitude variation patterns, emotional expression trend
1584.method_detail: Signal processing of speech samples, preliminary
1584.finding: Anger could be separated from normal conversation by rising pitch and amplitude patterns, though other emotions were not yet distinguished.

1588.who: Laser-printer users in 10 focus groups of 4-6 (total not reported)
1588.task: Discussed ergonomics of a printer paper tray in focus groups led by one moderator, alternating a taxonomy-guided method (ELK) with a traditional focus group
1588.prompt: Discuss the ergonomic issues of the paper tray after a brief demonstration and adding paper to it
1588.measured: Number and quality of customer requirements elicited, scored by two judges with content analysis; time lines of requirements
1588.method_detail: Five ELK and five control focus groups, stopped early after large differences
1588.finding: The taxonomy-based ELK method elicited significantly more customer requirements than a traditional focus group in the same context.

1589.who: Managers and engineers at automakers and 15 suppliers (number not reported)
1589.task: Researchers interviewed respondents about development processes from concept to production over 1992-93, plus two in-depth case studies
1589.prompt: Respondents described their vehicle development process; interviewers probed how set-based it was
1589.measured: Degree of set-based design, concurrency and development practices at Toyota versus other firms
1589.method_detail: Interviews at several companies with two in-depth case studies
1589.finding: Toyota develops designs by narrowing sets of alternatives rather than iterating one concept, which looks inefficient but yields an effective and efficient overall process.

1593.who: Key staff of one small manufacturer (number not reported)
1593.task: Key staff took three 3-hour QFD workshops over 4 weeks, interviewed customers, and built a QFD matrix with coaching from university staff
1593.problem: Hydraulic cylinders (QFD applied to product requirements)
1593.measured: Company design practice, QFD adoption problems and lessons, types of customer needs captured
1593.method_detail: Action research collaboration between a university and a company
1593.finding: The company focused on explicit customer needs and struggled to adopt structured QFD, showing that new methods must show quick benefit and fit existing ad hoc practice.

1596.who: 10 engineers from two aerospace companies (experts and detail designers)
1596.task: Took 2-3 hour structured interviews and hosted 1-2 day follow-up visits including an audit of personal and group information stores
1596.measured: Design Information Profiles: workgroup organisation, information organisation and transactions, volumes and formats of stored information
1596.method_detail: Structured interviews plus workplace observation and file audit
1596.finding: Experts kept large personal information stores and distrusted company libraries, while detail designers relied on local group files, and only 10-20 percent of personal or group information was held on computer.

1597.who: 8 aerospace designers (4 experienced with 8-32 years, 4 novices with 8-30 months)
1597.task: Thought aloud for 90-120 minutes while doing their own real design work, then a 15-20 minute interview; transcripts coded into categories
1597.problem: Real work tasks (e.g., compressor blade design)
1597.prompt: No special task given; designers worked on their own ongoing design tasks
1597.measured: Twenty-one categories of thoughts and actions, e.g. trial and error, confidence in decisions, reference to past projects
1597.finding: Novices used trial and error and lacked confidence in decisions, and data, information and knowledge proved to be relative concepts that distinguish experts from novices.

1623.who: 1 team of 3 graduate mechanical engineering students with a sponsor and an industry mentor
1623.task: Team worked nine months on a sponsored project; researchers collected meetings, notes, calls and documents (about 1000 pages, 40 hours video) and extracted noun phrases
1623.prompt: Design, prototype and test a pedestrian-safe bumper for automobiles within nine months and a $15,000 budget
1623.measured: Noun phrases by medium and design activity, product versus process share, first-occurring, evolving and steady-state concepts
1623.method_detail: Ethnographic observation with text analysis of one student team
1623.finding: Over half of the noun phrases appeared in informal audio and video media and only 5 percent in formal reports, so concept generation occurs where capture tools are weakest.

1626.who: 98 junior and senior mechanical engineering students in one course (76 completed pre- and post-tests)
1626.task: Took a pre-test, used multimedia motor software in a lab session during a two-week Lego vehicle design project, then an identical post-test
1626.problem: Lego vehicle driven by a DC motor up an inclined pipe
1626.prompt: Select and deploy battery-powered DC motors and gears to drive a Lego vehicle up an inclined pipe with a specified payload
1626.measured: Pre/post test score gains on four motor questions, differences by gender, learning preference groups, preference questionnaire
1626.method_detail: Pre/post test in a course module, no control group reported
1626.finding: Scores rose significantly on all four questions, the software contributed to the gain, and the module especially helped female students close their prior-knowledge gap.

1629.who: Engineering, design and business students in 25 course teams, plus company design groups
1629.task: Course teams used ethnographic methods to study consumer needs; authors observed 350 team meetings and 100 presentations and interviewed companies
1629.problem: Course product opportunities (e.g., oven rack for elderly cooks)
1629.measured: Team behavior patterns in early product development, use of ethnographic insight and scenarios to set product criteria
1629.method_detail: Ethnographic observation of course teams and interviews with companies
1629.finding: Ethnographic methods let engineers and industrial designers turn consumer lifestyle insights into scenarios that guide product criteria in the fuzzy front end of development.

1634.who: 28 Delft residents in three age groups
1634.task: In a one-hour session viewed pictures of 4 products in 5 shape variants, ticked shape terms, rated 26 aesthetic properties, and answered a short interview
1634.problem: Judging door handles, computer housings, mugs and vases (no design task)
1634.measured: Shape description terms chosen, appreciation on 26 aesthetic scales, correlations, product clusters and discriminant functions
1634.method_detail: Laboratory questionnaire session with short interview
1634.finding: 13 shape terms correlated strongly with 21 aesthetic dimensions, and five product clusters with distinct appreciation profiles gave a first mapping from shape to aesthetic intent.

1636.who: A rehabilitation engineering team and clients, 24 clinic sessions (team size not reported)
1636.task: Team did everyday clinic work designing custom wheelchair seats; sessions were videotaped over three years and talk and physical actions coded
1636.prompt: No task set; real client seating design work
1636.measured: Talk type (question, comment, information, explanation, dimension, design proposal) and accompanying actions with artifacts, share of time spent artefacting
1636.method_detail: Video analysis of real practice, four sessions analyzed in depth
1636.finding: Talk was accompanied by action about 58 percent of the time and artefacting took roughly 46 percent of work time, making it a core mechanism of cross-discipline teamwork.

1638.who: About 44 designers in three experiment sets, students and industry
1638.task: Interpreted and improved sketches passed from others (think-aloud, then silent), and in 1997 used 6-3-5, C-Sketch and Gallery methods in 10-minute cycles with retrospective surveys
1638.problem: Boat propulsion, fencepost extractor, measuring cup for the blind, Robo Tug and others
1638.prompt: E.g., find alternatives to oars for propelling a boat; design a portable human-powered fencepost extractor
1638.measured: Cognitive process shares in transcripts, survival of original ideas, ratings of provocative stimuli, creative outcome and process (1-5), cycles to saturation
1638.method_detail: Three experiment sets simulating progressive idea generation; analysis partial
1638.finding: Participants preferred sketch-based methods and rated C-Sketch best at opening new paths; progressive methods reduced attachment to one's own first idea.

1648.who: 13 masters-level student design teams in one design course (1996-97; people count not reported)
1648.task: Teams worked a school year on sponsor projects with a web archive of past captured design records; web access logs analyzed
1648.measured: Web hit counts to prior-year versus current-year archives, project-specific versus logistical pages, access by team members versus outsiders
1648.method_detail: Web access log analysis plus informal observation
1648.finding: Prior-year design archives drew very little access (under 10 percent of hits) and project-specific information was under-used, prompting the DesignShare augmentation.

1656.who: 6 first-year Stanford undergraduates (3 women, 3 men) selected from 90 survey respondents
1656.task: Read and thought aloud through chapters of an engineering textbook in about 12 hours of videotaped sessions, followed by interview questions
1656.problem: No design problem (reading an engineering textbook)
1656.prompt: Read the textbook chapters aloud, voicing questions and reactions; notes allowed
1656.measured: Readability, comprehensibility and usability of the text, figure use, comments and post-reading interview answers
1656.method_detail: Video think-aloud protocol with researcher notes and interviews
1656.finding: The method surfaced text errors and unclear figures, showed all students used diagrams even when not referenced, and showed that learning from a text is active rather than passive.

1657.who: Senior mechanical engineering students over two semesters, plus junior comparison class (sizes not reported)
1657.task: Did a five-minute estimation problem about weekly (ten total), then a three-minute team estimate in groups of 3-4
1657.problem: Estimating machine component properties (bolt strength, spring constant, shaft power)
1657.prompt: Estimate the strength, load or power of a shown machine component within five minutes using a calculator but no notes
1657.measured: Share of answers within a factor of 2, 5 and 10 of the correct value, individual versus team estimates, seniors versus juniors
1657.method_detail: In-class quasi-experiment with a junior comparison group
1657.finding: Even seniors often missed by more than an order of magnitude, practice improved individual estimates only slightly, and teams estimated substantially better than individuals.

1670.who: 196 practicing engineers (4-20 years experience) rating solutions, plus 3 graduate-student engineer judges (199 total)
1670.task: Each engineer ranked 3-10 candidate solutions to a randomly assigned technological problem for inventiveness (1-7); three judges checked solutions against the SIT sufficient conditions
1670.problem: 20 engineering problems from mechanical, electrical and civil domains
1670.prompt: Rank each proposed solution to the technological problem by how inventive it is
1670.measured: Inventiveness ratings, judge agreement on sufficient conditions, point-biserial correlation of conditions with ratings
1670.method_detail: Three-stage empirical test of conditions underlying the SIT method
1670.finding: Solutions meeting the proposed sufficient conditions got the top creativity rating in 19 of 20 problems, with a correlation of 0.7, supporting the conditions behind SIT.

1685.who: Three-person student teams in one graduate mechatronics design course, 1992-93 (number of teams not reported)
1685.task: Teams wrote three requirements documents over seven months while developing a hardware prototype; researchers extracted noun phrases and compared them with project grades
1685.problem: Industry-sponsored mechatronic products (e.g., car door power lock, window regulator)
1685.prompt: Turn the client's product requirements into a working hardware prototype over three quarters
1685.measured: Number of distinct noun phrases in requirements documents per quarter, readability, word count, project grades, gamma association
1685.method_detail: Text analysis of project documents from a design course
1685.finding: Project grades were strongly associated (gamma above 0.7) with the number of distinct noun phrases and only weakly with readability or word count.

1694.who: Stanford graduate design students in teams of 2-4 (63 teams in experimental years)
1694.task: Students answered a short preference questionnaire (sampled from Myers-Briggs items) and were assigned to teams under constraints; teams entered a national design competition
1694.problem: Year-long course projects from manufacturers and hospitals
1694.prompt: Design, build, test and report on a device for a consumer or industrial problem suggested by a sponsor
1694.measured: Prize-winning share in the Lincoln Foundation design competition, prize quality, team satisfaction survey
1694.method_detail: Five-year field experiment compared with 13 earlier unconstrained years
1694.finding: With team composition constrained by personality preference, the share of prize-winning teams rose from 29 to 60 percent, with higher-quality prizes for teams with high creative composition.

1695.who: 8 male junior and senior mechanical engineering students in 4 pairs (3 analyzed)
1695.task: Pairs worked one hour on a toggle clamp task with paper only, with simulation software, or with Lego; videotaped and analyzed with learning theories
1695.prompt: Determine link lengths and positions of a four-bar toggle clamp meeting given force-magnification and size criteria
1695.measured: Problem-solving approach, affordances of resources, use of Kolb learning cycle modes, situated learning interpretation
1695.method_detail: Qualitative video analysis of three student pairs under different resources
1695.finding: The pair with simulation software used all four Kolb learning modes, the Lego pair three and the paper pair two, so simulation supported the richest learning situation.

1703.who: 10 near- or just-graduate industrial design engineering students
1703.task: Each designed alone for 2.5 hours with an experimenter as information source; events logged, activities sampled every 5 minutes, concept rated
1703.problem: Bicycle light generator concept (mechanical and electrical)
1703.prompt: Design a new light generator concept for a bike meeting ten given requirements, documented in a design document
1703.measured: Activities, requests and answers for information, results, activity changes, design quality as percent of requirements met
1703.method_detail: Exploratory design sessions with event protocol, no think-aloud
1703.finding: The amount of communicated information correlated significantly and positively with design quality, and analysis activities involved more information communication than synthesis or evaluation.

1705.who: 36 senior mechanical engineering design students in 6 blocks of 6, matched in triplets
1705.task: Thinking aloud on video, elicited manufacturability requirements from a moderator using 1, 2 or 3 taxonomy levels at early or late design stage
1705.prompt: List manufacturability requirements for the connector, either at product definition with a blank House of Quality or when judging a given concept with a decision matrix
1705.measured: Number of requirements, usefulness weights set by two judges, number of elicitations, time taken
1705.method_detail: 3 taxonomy levels by 2 design stages, ANOVA after removing five non-compliant subjects
1705.finding: Using the taxonomy yielded more and better requirements without slowing designers, though only for subjects who actually followed the taxonomy methodically.

1727.who: Simulation of design projects; 3 design-house engineers interviewed, 1 manager modeled a project
1727.task: Built a simulation of a finished project from timesheet data and compared results; a manager then modeled an ongoing 7-person project
1727.problem: Commercial product design projects (consumer product; 7-person, 32-week project)
1727.measured: Simulated versus actual activity sequences and times, project duration, sensitivity to agent working and communication efficiency
1727.method_detail: Two validation studies with design-house records and a manager's use of the software
1727.finding: The simulation reproduced timesheet-based project behavior reasonably well, and a manager could model an ongoing project and gain useful sensitivity insights about bottlenecks.

1729.who: 10 near- or just-graduate industrial design engineering students
1729.task: Each designed alone for 2.5 hours with an experimenter as information source; events logged, activities sampled every 5 minutes, concept rated
1729.problem: Bicycle light generator concept (mechanical and electrical)
1729.prompt: Design a new light generator concept for a bike satisfying ten given requirements and document it
1729.measured: Activities and information requests and answers, communication amounts per activity phase, design quality as percent of requirements met
1729.method_detail: Exploratory design sessions with event protocol, no think-aloud
1729.finding: More communicated information went with better design quality, and the analysis phase was more communication-intensive than synthesis and evaluation.

1730.who: 10 near- or just-graduate industrial design engineering students, compared with an independent expert designer's list
1730.task: Each designed alone for a session while requesting information from an experimenter; requested engineering aspects were compared with 22 issues an expert judged required
1730.measured: Engineering issues and aspects requested versus expert-required set, requirements met as weighted score
1730.method_detail: Ten-session observation with expert benchmark of required information
1730.finding: Subjects differed widely in which engineering aspects they requested, no aspect was requested by all, and requesting more different aspects significantly predicted better requirement fulfillment.

1731.who: Junior mechanical engineering students in 4 teams of 5 or 6 (exact total not reported)
1731.task: Teams designed, prototyped and delivered a web homepage on concurrent engineering with marketing, design and production roles, then wrote a reflective report and presented it
1731.problem: Web homepage on concurrent engineering (as a product)
1731.prompt: Work as a concurrent-engineering team to design, develop and deliver a homepage on the web about concurrent engineering
1731.measured: Features of the four web documents, students' reflective reports on concurrency and overlap analysis, evidence of reflective learning
1731.method_detail: Course exercise in an experiential-learning lab, assessed through reflective reports
1731.finding: Teams applied concurrent engineering ideas to build the web product and their reflective reports gave strong evidence of learning about concurrency and team processes.

1732.who: 152 sophomore design students plus 3 faculty on a course newsgroup
1732.task: Used a course newsgroup; all postings captured and analyzed afterward by author, topic, time, length, and Myers-Briggs type
1732.measured: Posting volume, thread length, communication matrix, topic affinity and robustness, newsgroup use by Myers-Briggs cognitive mode
1732.method_detail: Retrospective analysis of newsgroup logs, no intervention
1732.finding: Newsgroup communication patterns and topic relations could be measured, and students with analytical and invention cognitive modes used the newsgroup heavily while affiliation and implementation types used it little.

1733.who: 161 sophomores and 135 seniors in required MIT mechanical engineering courses
1733.task: Gave an unannounced lecture question: estimate a small DC motor's peak power (3 minutes) or a 9-volt battery's energy with work shown (5 minutes)
1733.problem: Estimating motor power and battery energy
1733.prompt: Roughly estimate the peak continuous power of the shown motor, or the energy in a 9-volt battery, and show your process
1733.measured: Estimates compared with actual values (orders of magnitude of spread), correct units, estimation process
1733.finding: Answers spread over 6 to 9 orders of magnitude, many lacked correct units, showing students could not estimate and had weak grasp of engineering fundamentals even as seniors.

1743.who: Engineers and desk workers rating photocopies (number not reported); 25 judged final images
1743.task: Rated photocopier output samples on adjective scales (semantic differential); results converted to function content, then 25 people compared images from optimized and original settings
1743.prompt: Rate each sample copy on pairs of adjectives such as clear-unclear and thick-thin
1743.measured: Function content of modifiers such as clearly and bright background, group differences, preference between optimized and original machine setting
1743.method_detail: Semantic differential rating experiment supporting a function-evaluation model
1743.finding: Engineers valued the clarity modifier more strongly than desk workers, and 17 of 25 judges preferred images made with parameters optimized by function content over the original design values.

1745.who: 15 male participants: 5 expert designers, 3 semi-experts, 7 engineering students
1745.task: Thought aloud while interpreting 8 mechanical drawings shown alone, then with a title, then with a short description; sessions videotaped and transcribed
1745.problem: Reading 8 mechanical engineering drawings (e.g., hydraulic spool valve)
1745.prompt: Reason aloud about each drawing and describe the device's function if you recognize it; revise when title and description are added
1745.measured: Forms, functions and relationships mentioned, correct identification of overall function, forward versus inverse reasoning
1745.method_detail: Verbal protocol analysis comparing three expertise groups
1745.finding: Experts reasoned inversely from the overall function more often and more successfully, while reasoning forward from components was costly and rarely correct, especially for novices.

1746.who: 18 mechanical designers across a redesign protocol, earlier data set and follow-up choice experiment
1746.task: Two designers thought aloud redesigning a water tank; five more solved industrial problems; 11 others chose a number of posts
1746.problem: Cattle water tank retrofit (antelope problem) and two simple industrial problems
1746.prompt: Raise the height of 6,000 range-cattle water tanks by 12 inches so antelope are discouraged from drinking
1746.measured: Types of constraints (given, introduced), constraint satisfaction as design quality proxy, distribution of choices of post number
1746.method_detail: Protocol analysis of two data sets plus a small follow-up choice experiment
1746.finding: Designers satisfied given constraints routinely, so quality differences came from constraints they introduced themselves, which narrow options to one solution rather than simply accepting the first acceptable one.
